plectis.label: Plectis
plectis.preview: Plectis is this project's public name, covering its mathematical research, formal proofs, and supporting software.
plectis.card: The website connects papers and working records with Lean source, reusable software components, and checks. It aims to make both the results and the process accessible for inspection and further work.
plectis.rule: Each paper or component has its own scope and evidence status.
plectis.deep: The project name is not a certification that every question is solved or every mechanism is complete. Some older technical identifiers retain the name Microcosm for compatibility with earlier files and links.

component.label: component
component.preview: A component is a distinct part of a system with a defined job and interfaces to other parts.
component.card: Plectis presents public components with their inputs, outputs, source, and checks. This lets a reader inspect one mechanism without first understanding the entire system.
component.rule: The component's description should make clear which behaviour it implements and tests.
component.deep: Combining components can introduce additional interactions. Evidence for each part helps assess the combination, but the combined behaviour may require its own checks and an explanation of how the parts fit together.

scope_limit.label: scope limit
scope_limit.preview: A scope limit states where a claim, permission, or piece of evidence stops applying.
scope_limit.card: For a component, it may restrict the supported inputs, checked behaviour, or conclusions allowed from a result. For mathematical work, it may identify a finite range or an unresolved hypothesis.
scope_limit.rule: The limit should name the actual boundary rather than offer a generic disclaimer.
scope_limit.deep: For example, a recorded test can establish that a specific forged note was rejected. That does not by itself establish that every forgery or every misleading report would be detected.

evidence_class.label: evidence class
evidence_class.preview: An evidence class identifies how a claim is supported, such as by a proof, test run, calculation, or citation.
evidence_class.card: The classification helps readers distinguish what has actually been checked from what has been inferred or proposed. Each class comes with its own assumptions and limits.
evidence_class.rule: The class must match the evidence attached to the particular claim.
evidence_class.deep: For example, exact arithmetic avoids rounding error in a calculation but does not automatically cover infinitely many cases. A formal proof can cover all cases in its statement while still depending on explicit hypotheses.

record.label: record
record.preview: A record is stored information about an object, event, decision, or result.
record.card: In Plectis it may be a structured row, file, or packet that can be reopened after a session ends. Its fields should make clear what it describes and where the information came from.
record.rule: Different records have different authority and evidence roles.
record.deep: A result record may describe one test run, while a registry record defines an object's identity. Keeping those roles clear prevents a summary of an action from being confused with the source or execution evidence behind it.

substrate.label: substrate
substrate.preview: Here, substrate means the underlying files, stored state, and tools on which the system operates.
substrate.card: It includes the concrete material an agent can inspect or change, beneath the pages and summaries that describe it. Plectis uses the term when distinguishing direct access to working material from access to a copied explanation.
substrate.rule: The source's role determines what it can authoritatively establish.
substrate.deep: A webpage can accurately describe a file without granting access to that file or permission to change it. Type A and Type B describe this access distinction in the project's actor vocabulary.

source_authority.label: source authority
source_authority.preview: Source authority identifies the record or implementation controlling a particular question in this system.
source_authority.card: A registry can own identity, code can define implemented behaviour, and an execution record can document a run. Generated pages select and explain information from these sources; each claim must trace to the appropriate owner.
source_authority.rule: Choose the controlling source by the question. A schema-valid record does not override implementation behaviour, and implementation code alone does not settle what happened in a particular run.
source_authority.deep: When a source and projection disagree, inspect their derivation and versions before deciding what needs correction. This local rule reconciles system records; it does not make one file or institution authoritative about every subject.

organ.label: organ (source identifier)
organ.preview: Organ is the source-code term for a bounded unit that the public site usually calls a component.
organ.card: It may appear in registry names and paths retained by the implementation. Each unit has a particular job, interfaces, and evidence describing its behaviour.
organ.rule: The biological word is internal terminology; it does not add a separate guarantee or capability.
organ.deep: When following a component card into source code, an organ identifier can refer to that same unit. The registry and linked source establish the identity and scope more precisely than the choice of label.

witness.label: check result
witness.preview: A check result records the outcome and evidence from a named software check.
witness.card: Local software uses witness for a verification record tied to a particular execution. Public pages call this a check result: it identifies what was checked, the inputs or source version, the method, and the reported outcome. The record can report failure or incomplete evidence as well as success.
witness.rule: Interpret a check result within its recorded method and scope. In mathematics, witness has a different meaning: an object satisfying an existence claim.
witness.deep: For example, 3 witnesses that some positive integer has square 9, with justification that 3 squared equals 9. That object and its proved property differ from a software log. A check record supports only what its producer and method establish; recording success alone does not prove a mathematical claim.

navigable.label: navigable
navigable.preview: Material is navigable when a reader has usable routes from its summary to the relevant detail or next action.
navigable.card: In Plectis, these routes can be links, anchors, source references, or commands. They help a person or agent move from a term or result to the object being described.
navigable.rule: A route must resolve to the intended material to be useful.
navigable.deep: The presence of a link alone does not ensure good navigation. Its label, destination, access requirements, and level of detail should fit the reader's question.

two_kernel.label: 2-kernel
two_kernel.preview: The 2-kernel of a sequence is the family of all subsequences \(n\mapsto a(2^{e}n+r)\), with \(e\ge 0\) and \(0\le r<2^{e}\).
two_kernel.card: At \(e=1\) it contains the even-indexed and odd-indexed subsequences. Higher levels split by residue classes modulo 4,8,…, and \(e=0\) includes the original sequence.
two_kernel.rule: A finite 2-kernel characterizes a 2-automatic sequence. For integer-valued sequences, 2-regularity instead asks that the integer module generated by this family be finitely generated.
two_kernel.deep: The #249 paper gives exact bases and ranks after stopping at a finite depth, then describes the full rational span. Unbounded finite-level ranks show that the totient sequence is not 2-regular. This kernel is a family of sequences, distinct from a linear map’s null space or Lean’s proof checker.

two_regular_sequence.label: 2-regular sequence
two_regular_sequence.preview: An integer-valued sequence is 2-regular when its dyadic subsequences generate a finitely generated module over the integers.
two_regular_sequence.card: Take all subsequences \(n\mapsto a(2^{e}n+r)\). Finite generation means finitely many sequences suffice to express every such subsequence as an integer linear combination. The analogous definition uses base \(k\ge 2\).
two_regular_sequence.rule: This is weaker than having only finitely many distinct dyadic subsequences. A theorem at each finite level does not establish finite generation across all levels.
two_regular_sequence.deep: The #249 paper computes the ranks of the totient sequence’s finite-level modules and shows that these ranks grow without bound. That proves nonregularity while also describing the exact finite-level structure; it does not settle the irrationality of the totient series value.

microcosm_instance.label: a microcosm
microcosm_instance.preview: A microcosm is a small example that reflects features of a larger system or situation.
microcosm_instance.card: Calling a local case a microcosm suggests that it makes a wider pattern easier to see. The comparison is useful only to the extent that the relevant relationships are actually shared.
microcosm_instance.rule: A representative example does not automatically establish every claim about the larger whole.
microcosm_instance.deep: This ordinary sense is distinct from Microcosm, the project's earlier name. When a component illustrates a general mechanism, its evidence still applies first to the particular case that was built and checked.

above_and_beyond.label: above and beyond
above_and_beyond.preview: In Plectis, “above and beyond” means doing the useful follow-through that makes a completed task easy to find, check, and continue.
above_and_beyond.card: Finishing a change can leave a broken link, an outdated instruction, or a lesson that exists only in the conversation. This term asks the agent to fix the directly related loose ends while the context is still available.
above_and_beyond.rule: The extra work needs a clear stopping point and must fit the user's authorised scope.
above_and_beyond.deep: For example, a new feature may need its existing guide updated and its check recorded so the next person can use it.

absolute_convergence.label: absolute convergence
absolute_convergence.preview: A series converges absolutely if the sum of the absolute values of its terms is finite.
absolute_convergence.card: For a real or complex series \(\sum a_{n}\), this means \(\sum |a_{n}|\) converges. It implies convergence of the original series and permits rearranging its terms without changing the sum.
absolute_convergence.rule: Ordinary convergence does not imply absolute convergence: the alternating harmonic series is a standard counterexample.
absolute_convergence.deep: For nonnegative terms, the two conditions coincide. Absolute convergence is useful in the papers when expanding denominators, regrouping contributions, or bounding an omitted tail by the sum of its magnitudes.

absolute_value.label: absolute value
absolute_value.preview: A number's nonnegative size, ignoring sign; for complex numbers it is distance from zero.
absolute_value.card: Absolute value measures size without sign. Thus \(|-3|=3\), while for the complex number \(z=3+4i\), \(|z|=5\) because the point \((3,4)\) lies five units from the origin. It is zero only at zero.
absolute_value.rule: The distance between real or complex numbers x and y is \(|x-y|\). Products satisfy \(|xy|=|x||y|\), and sums satisfy the triangle inequality \(|x+y|\le |x|+|y|\); cancellation can make the left side much smaller.
absolute_value.deep: In these papers absolute values measure approximation errors, bound nonzero integer expressions from below, and define polynomial regions such as \(\{|f(z)|<1\}\). For vectors or functions, the related size concept usually needs a separately specified norm.

accessibility.label: accessibility
accessibility.preview: Accessibility is the extent to which people, including disabled people, can perceive, understand, navigate, and use information or a system.
accessibility.card: Accessible design removes barriers such as controls that require a mouse, text with insufficient contrast, or images without useful alternatives. Different people need different ways to access the same content; a clear visual layout alone does not make a page accessible.
accessibility.rule: Assess accessibility against specific readers, tasks, technologies, and recognised criteria rather than treating it as a general claim of ease.
accessibility.deep: Accessibility concerns whether disabled people can perceive, understand, navigate, and operate a product or document. A feature can help one group while creating a barrier for another, so testing should cover concrete tasks and assistive technologies. Plectis uses keyboard controls, focus management, semantic HTML, and preserved mathematical accessibility data. Accessibility does not imply that specialist subject matter has become simple.

accountability_layer.label: accountability layer
accountability_layer.preview: The accountability layer is the evidence and source links that let someone check what the system says it did.
accountability_layer.card: A visible result should lead to the run that produced it, the inputs used, and the claim that was tested. Plectis groups those connections under this name so a reader can inspect the work behind a summary.
accountability_layer.rule: An evidence record supports the particular action or property it captures.
accountability_layer.deep: Keeping the record and its limits together helps expose a claim that has grown broader than the work supporting it.

achievement_set.label: achievement set
achievement_set.preview: An achievement set consists of all values obtained by selecting terms of a series and summing them, whenever those selected sums converge.
achievement_set.card: For nonnegative weights \(w_{n}\) with finite sum, it is \(\{\sum_{n}\varepsilon_{n}w_{n}: \varepsilon_{n}\in\{0,1\}\}\). It includes the empty selection, finite selections, and infinite selections.
achievement_set.rule: Different selections can give the same value unless additional conditions ensure uniqueness. Its possible shapes include intervals and Cantor sets.
achievement_set.deep: For the #257 Mersenne weights \(w_{n}=1/(2^{n}-1)\), every weight exceeds the sum of its successors. At the first differing selection digit, later terms cannot cancel the difference, so each achieved value determines a unique selection. This does not itself decide which rational targets are achieved by infinite selections.

actor_axes.label: actor axes
actor_axes.preview: Actor axes are separate descriptions of an agent's access, abilities, tools, and role in a task.
actor_axes.card: Plectis uses several axes because one ranking would mix different things. Type A and Type B describe access to the working system; capability describes what the actor can do; its role describes how it participates in the work.
actor_axes.rule: A model's reasoning ability does not determine its file permissions or access to evidence.
actor_axes.deep: The same model can have different authority in two sessions, depending on the tools and material available to it.

admitted_proof_step.label: admitted proof step
admitted_proof_step.preview: An admitted proof step fills a gap with an unproved assertion so unfinished formal work can continue.
admitted_proof_step.card: Lean's sorry placeholder marks a step whose proof has not been supplied. Surrounding development can proceed with a warning, but declarations depending on that step inherit the gap.
admitted_proof_step.rule: Audit the target declaration's dependencies, not just visible placeholders in its source. A gap can arrive through an imported lemma.
admitted_proof_step.deep: A stated hypothesis describes a conditional theorem; an admission supplies missing justification inside its development. Removing sorry is necessary for a finished result, while checking other axiom dependencies remains a separate audit task.

affine_function.label: affine function
affine_function.preview: A linear function followed by a translation, such as \(x\mapsto ax+b\).
affine_function.card: The function \(3x+2\) is affine. In linear algebra it is not linear, because a linear map must send zero to zero. Elementary algebra sometimes uses “linear” more broadly for equations whose graphs are straight lines.
affine_function.rule: In several variables an affine map has form \(Ax+b\); differences of outputs still transform linearly.
affine_function.deep: Prime-producing affine forms and affine tail recurrences organize arithmetic constraints throughout the papers.

affordance_row.label: affordance row
affordance_row.preview: An affordance row is a navigation entry that explains what an item is and what opening it lets you do.
affordance_row.card: Each row gives enough information to choose a next step: a label, a short explanation, and a route to the relevant material. Plectis can present the same entry as a brief line or a fuller card.
affordance_row.rule: The row should help a reader choose before loading the underlying files.
affordance_row.deep: Its source link matters because the menu is a summary; the referenced record or code contains the detail needed to act.

agent.label: agent
agent.preview: An AI agent is software that uses a model and tools to carry out steps towards a task.
agent.card: An agent may read files, run commands, or propose changes, depending on its tools and permissions. In Plectis, its work is expected to leave inspectable results that another person or check can assess.
agent.rule: The agent's written account and the evidence of its actions are separate things.
agent.deep: Type A and Type B describe its access to the working system. They do not rank the model's intelligence or guarantee that its work is correct.

agent_reliability.label: agent reliability and safety
agent_reliability.preview: Agent reliability is how consistently an AI agent completes its intended task under the conditions in which it is used.
agent_reliability.card: Plectis studies specific parts of this question, including whether an agent's report matches its actions and whether it respects the limits it was given. Tests deliberately introduce misleading notes or missing work to see whether a check detects them.
agent_reliability.rule: A successful test supports the behaviour and conditions that the test actually covers.
agent_reliability.deep: Safety also concerns harmful actions and permission boundaries. Neither reliability nor safety follows merely from a fluent answer or one passing example.

agent_seed.label: agent seed
agent_seed.preview: An agent seed is a saved record of an agent's observations and interpretations, with its author and sources identified.
agent_seed.card: Plectis keeps this material separate from raw seed, which preserves the operator's own words. That separation lets useful agent analysis survive a session without being mistaken for something the operator said or intended.
agent_seed.rule: An agent seed is material to assess and reuse, with authority appropriate to its sources.
agent_seed.deep: For example, an agent can record a recurring failure and the evidence behind its proposed explanation while preserving the original instruction unchanged.

agent_trace.label: agent trace
agent_trace.preview: An agent trace is a recorded sequence of events from an agent session, such as tool calls, outputs, and file operations.
agent_trace.card: The trace provides evidence against which to compare the agent's summary. It can show which command was invoked, what result returned, and what happened next, within the events the recording system captures.
agent_trace.rule: A trace is only as complete as its instrumentation and retention.
agent_trace.deep: An unrecorded event cannot automatically be treated as an event that never happened. Plectis audits should make that coverage boundary clear when they use traces as evidence.

ai_native.label: AI-native
ai_native.preview: AI-native describes a system designed from the outset for AI to take part in its normal operation.
ai_native.card: In Plectis, agents read structured context, use tools, make bounded changes, and leave records that later work can inspect. The files, interfaces, and checks are arranged to support that participation.
ai_native.rule: The term describes a design choice, not a measured level of intelligence or reliability.
ai_native.deep: Human direction, permissions, and independent checks still matter. A workflow can be built around AI and still need substantial supervision or correction.

mathematical_field.label: algebraic field
mathematical_field.preview: An algebraic field supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by nonzero elements under the usual commutative arithmetic laws.
mathematical_field.card: The rational, real, and complex numbers are fields. The integers are not: \(1/2\) is not an integer. Arithmetic modulo a prime also forms a field, showing that a field need not be infinite.
mathematical_field.rule: Zero and one must be distinct; every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, and multiplication distributes over addition. A data field and a vector field are different concepts.
mathematical_field.deep: The selected field determines the allowed coefficients in linear independence and supplies algebraic settings for polynomial and residue arguments.

algebraic_integer.label: algebraic integer
algebraic_integer.preview: An algebraic integer is a complex algebraic number satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients.
algebraic_integer.card: For example, \(\sqrt 2\) satisfies \(T^{2}-2\) and is an algebraic integer. A rational number is an algebraic integer exactly when it is an ordinary integer; \(1/2\) is not one.
algebraic_integer.rule: Being algebraic over \(\mathbb{Q}\) alone is weaker. A nonmonic integer polynomial may show algebraicity without showing integrality.
algebraic_integer.deep: The #243 reasoning surface compares its square obstruction with the general case of a nonsquare algebraic integer in a number field. Its actual cubic proof also excludes finitely many primes to handle denominators before reducing algebraic quantities. Those exclusions should not be replaced by an unsupported claim that every displayed element is integral.

algebraic_number.label: algebraic number
algebraic_number.preview: A complex number satisfying some nonzero polynomial equation with integer coefficients.
algebraic_number.card: Every rational number is algebraic because \(p/q\) solves \(qx-p=0\). The irrational number \(\sqrt 2\) is algebraic because it solves \(x^{2}-2=0\).
algebraic_number.rule: Algebraic does not mean rational. Numbers that satisfy no such integer polynomial, such as \(\pi\), are called transcendental.
algebraic_number.deep: The totient discussion explains that a digit-complexity theorem applying to algebraic irrationals cannot be used until algebraicity of the target sum is independently known.

algorithm.label: algorithm
algorithm.preview: An algorithm is an explicit procedure for turning permitted inputs into outputs or decisions.
algorithm.card: Algorithms range from sorting recipes to search and learning procedures. A description should identify valid inputs, steps, stopping conditions, and outputs. Correctness concerns whether the procedure meets its specification; efficiency concerns resources such as time and memory. An algorithm is the method, while one execution is a particular run on particular inputs.
algorithm.rule: A named algorithm does not establish that its implementation is correct, efficient, unbiased, or suitable for the present data.
algorithm.deep: An algorithm is an abstract procedure, independent of any particular programming language or machine. To assess one, specify its admissible inputs, output relation, sequence of steps, stopping behavior, and resource costs. Correctness asks whether every permitted execution meets the specification; complexity studies how time or space grows with input size. Randomized algorithms also expose a probability model. An implementation can mistranslate a sound algorithm, and a sound method can still be unsuitable for biased data, hostile inputs, or operational constraints.

almost_surely.label: almost surely
almost_surely.preview: A property holds almost surely when the set of outcomes where it fails has probability zero.
almost_surely.card: The phrase allows exceptional outcomes; it does not mean the property holds everywhere. On a continuous probability space, even a nonempty or infinite set of outcomes can have probability zero.
almost_surely.rule: Specify the measure and the property, including any quantifiers. Probability one for each separate event is not automatically a simultaneous assertion over an uncountable family.
almost_surely.deep: The #257 note's limiting profinite observable is infinite almost surely, although its values at positive integer inputs are finite. Those exceptional inputs do not contradict the measure-theoretic statement or justify a finite integral.

analytic_continuation.label: analytic continuation
analytic_continuation.preview: Analytic continuation extends a holomorphic function beyond its initial domain while agreeing with the original function wherever both are defined.
analytic_continuation.card: The geometric series \(1+z+z^{2}+\ldots\) defines \(1/(1-z)\) only for \(|z|<1\), but the rational function supplies an analytic continuation to every complex z except 1. Agreement on an overlap makes the extension unique on a connected domain.
analytic_continuation.rule: Continuation may proceed along paths and can fail at singularities. Different paths can lead to different branches unless a monodromy condition removes the ambiguity. It is more restrictive than any smooth extension because it must remain complex analytic.
analytic_continuation.deep: Here an inverse branch is continued across a larger disc. The proof must rule out critical or branch points and escape to infinity; merely writing the same formula outside the starting neighbourhood would not justify continuation.

analytic_function.label: analytic function
analytic_function.preview: A function that near every point is represented by a convergent power series; over the complex numbers this is equivalent to being holomorphic.
analytic_function.card: An analytic function agrees locally with the power series obtained from its derivatives. The exponential is an example. In real analysis, having derivatives of every order is weaker: a smooth function can have a Taylor series that fails to recover the function.
analytic_function.rule: Specify whether the variables are real or complex: complex analytic means holomorphic, while real analytic is stronger than merely smooth.
analytic_function.deep: A function is analytic on an open set if every point has a neighbourhood on which the function equals a convergent power series centred at that point. For functions of one complex variable, complex differentiability throughout an open set implies this power-series property, so analytic and holomorphic are equivalent there. For real functions, possessing derivatives of every order is insufficient: smooth functions can have Taylor series that fail to recover the function. References to analytic continuation or analytic inverse branches usually use the complex sense and require a connected domain and compatible local continuations.

annex.label: annex
annex.preview: An annex is Plectis's source-linked account of ideas or techniques drawn from an outside project.
annex.card: It records what an external framework, repository, or document offers and how a useful pattern might apply locally. The aim is to make prior work available before an agent invents another implementation.
annex.rule: The original source remains the authority on what the outside project actually does.
annex.deep: Adapting a technique requires a separate local decision and check; an annex does not establish that the technique has already been integrated or works here.

annihilator_subspace.label: annihilator of a subspace
annihilator_subspace.preview: The linear functionals that vanish on every vector of a specified subspace.
annihilator_subspace.card: For a linear subspace U of V, its annihilator \(U^{0}\) is \(\{\ell\in V^*: \ell(u)=0\text{ for every }u\in U\}\). It belongs to the dual space of linear functionals. In finite dimensions, \(\dim U^{0}=\dim V-\dim U\).
annihilator_subspace.rule: No inner product is needed. An orthogonal complement lives in the original space after choosing an inner product; identifying it with the annihilator requires that additional identification. Both the ambient space and scalar field must be specified.
annihilator_subspace.deep: The #269 torus proof studies the rational annihilator of the velocity-containing subspace. If two coordinate forms were dependent there, a rationally defined relation supported on those coordinates would yield an integer relation and contradict the irrational ratio of the corresponding logarithms.

annulus.label: annulus
annulus.preview: An annulus is the region between two concentric circles, usually written \(\{z: r<|z-a|<R\}\) with \(0\le r<R\).
annulus.card: The set \(1<|z|<2\) is an open annulus. Unlike a disc, it has a hole: a loop going once around the origin cannot be shrunk to a point while remaining in the annulus.
annulus.rule: Open or closed boundary conventions must be stated. In complex analysis, “annulus” often means the open region \(r<|z-a|<R\); a topological annulus may mean any space homeomorphic to such a region.
annulus.deep: The displayed inequality defines an open circular annulus; including one or both boundary circles gives a closed or partly closed version. When \(r=0\), the centre is still excluded, producing a punctured disc. The word is also used for regions with the same topology. In the paper, cutting an annulus along an arc joining its boundaries changes its topology and can remove the closed loops that carry winding information.

anti_principle.label: anti-principle
anti_principle.preview: An anti-principle names a recurring shortcut or failure pattern that the system is meant to avoid.
anti_principle.card: Where a principle describes a desired way of working, an anti-principle makes a specific bad practice recognisable. It connects the refusal to the requirement it protects, so the rule can be applied to real cases.
anti_principle.rule: The useful question is which concrete behaviour would violate the rule.
anti_principle.deep: For example, treating a plausible summary as evidence of a completed action would defeat a requirement to check the actual execution record.

apache_2_0.label: Apache-2.0
apache_2_0.preview: Apache-2.0 is an open-source licence allowing use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use, subject to its conditions.
apache_2_0.card: Redistribution requires a copy of the licence, retention of applicable notices, and prominent notices of changed files. An included NOTICE file can add attribution requirements. The licence also contains a patent grant and its conditions.
apache_2_0.rule: The licence attached to the particular repository or file determines what is covered.
apache_2_0.deep: Apache-2.0 does not grant general trademark rights and provides the work without warranties. The linked licence text controls the exact terms.

api.label: API
api.preview: An API is a defined interface through which software requests operations or data from another software component.
api.card: An API specifies available operations, input forms, returned values, and errors so separately built programs can cooperate. It may be a local library interface, an operating-system call, or a remote service.
api.rule: The API contract determines how callers interact with an implementation; transport over a network is common but not required.
api.deep: An API can expose functions inside one process, communication between local processes, hardware services, or requests to a remote server. Its documentation describes the public contract rather than the provider’s internal implementation. Versions may change accepted inputs or response fields. Authorization, quotas, latency, availability, pricing, and data retention are separate operational conditions. A successful API response proves that the interface returned that result under one request; interpreting or trusting the result still depends on provenance, semantics, validation, and error handling.

appeal_lifecycle.label: appeal lifecycle
appeal_lifecycle.preview: An appeal lifecycle is the process for challenging a system decision and recording how the challenge was resolved.
appeal_lifecycle.card: A disputed label or result is examined, its cause is identified, and responsibility for any repair is assigned. The outcome records the reasoning and supporting evidence so later work can tell whether the decision still stands.
appeal_lifecycle.rule: An appeal can confirm a decision, correct it, or reopen the question.
appeal_lifecycle.deep: Plectis uses the record to distinguish a faulty implementation from a faulty expectation: sometimes the check needs repair, and sometimes the rule being checked needs revision.

apply.label: apply
apply.preview: In Plectis, apply is the step that makes a specified change to a file or record.
apply.card: It follows observation or a proposal by naming the target and performing the permitted operation. The operation should check the conditions for the change and validate the resulting state.
apply.rule: A proposed change has not taken effect until the apply step succeeds.
apply.deep: Recording the operation, target, and result makes later inspection possible. Where an operation is reversible, its record can also explain how to undo it without disturbing unrelated work.

architecture.label: architecture
architecture.preview: Architecture is the high-level arrangement of a system’s parts, responsibilities, boundaries, constraints, and connections.
architecture.card: An architecture explains how information, control, authority, and failure move among components and why major responsibilities are separated. Software architecture is one domain use; buildings and organizations also have architecture, but this glossary emphasizes designed technical systems.
architecture.rule: Read an architectural claim by locating the real components, interfaces, ownership boundaries, flows, and constraints that the description says should exist.
architecture.deep: Architecture sits between purpose and implementation. It narrows which implementations fit while leaving local choices open. Useful views may show runtime communication, data ownership, deployment, security boundaries, or source-generation relationships; no single diagram necessarily captures them all. Boxes and arrows become architectural evidence only when they correspond to maintained objects and defined relations. The documented architecture can also drift from the running system, so source maps, tests, and operational observations are needed to verify that the intended structure remains real.

argument_principle.label: argument principle
argument_principle.preview: The change in argument of a meromorphic function around a boundary counts its zeros minus its poles inside.
argument_principle.card: If f is meromorphic on a neighbourhood of a positively oriented, piecewise smooth simple closed contour and its enclosed region, with no zero or pole on the contour, \(\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint(f\prime/f)\,dz\) equals the number of zeros minus the number of poles, each counted with multiplicity.
argument_principle.rule: Boundary zeros or poles invalidate this formula without a separate limiting or indentation argument. The counted quantity is a winding number, so it records multiplicity and orientation rather than geometric length.
argument_principle.deep: At regular lemniscate levels, #1041 uses the total argument change around a component to identify its root count. Combined with a coarea calculation and Cauchy–Schwarz, this supplies one input to the area-based connector estimate.

arithmetic_progression.label: arithmetic progression
arithmetic_progression.preview: A sequence obtained by repeatedly adding one fixed difference.
arithmetic_progression.card: The numbers 2,7,12,17,… form an arithmetic progression with first term 2 and common difference 5; its nth term is \(2+5n\) under zero-based indexing.
arithmetic_progression.rule: For a nonzero integer common difference d, extending the progression over all integer indices gives one residue class modulo \(|d|\). A geometric progression instead repeatedly multiplies by a fixed ratio.
arithmetic_progression.deep: Dirichlet's theorem supplies primes in suitable arithmetic progressions, letting the totient argument engineer prescribed congruence and fresh-prime behavior.

artifact.label: artifact
artifact.preview: An artifact is a stored item that someone can inspect or use, such as a file, report, dataset, or generated page.
artifact.card: Plectis uses the term for the concrete objects its work produces and maintains. An artifact has an identity and a role; it may be original source material, a record of an action, or a view generated from other data.
artifact.rule: Its role determines how it should be read and changed.
artifact.deep: A report about a test and the test's source code are both artifacts, but they provide different kinds of evidence.

artifact_kind.label: artifact kind
artifact_kind.preview: An artifact kind is a category of stored object, such as a standard, paper module, component, or result record.
artifact_kind.card: The category helps Plectis choose the right schema, editing rules, and navigation view for an item. A reader can start with a collection of one kind before choosing an individual object.
artifact_kind.rule: Two artifacts can concern the same subject while belonging to different kinds.
artifact_kind.deep: For example, a component implements a check, a standard states its requirements, and a result record describes one execution of it.

assimilation.label: assimilation
assimilation.preview: Assimilation is the process of incorporating a useful result into the system so later work can use it.
assimilation.card: After a finding has been checked and explained, Plectis puts it into the appropriate source, guide, rule, or record. The result then becomes available through the routes that future work already uses.
assimilation.rule: A note left only in a conversation has not completed that process.
assimilation.deep: Assimilation includes preserving the finding's scope and evidence. A successful local example should remain a local example unless there is support for a more general rule.

assistive_technology.label: assistive technology
assistive_technology.preview: Assistive technology is hardware or software that helps a disabled person perceive, operate, understand, or communicate with a system.
assistive_technology.card: Examples include screen readers, screen magnifiers, speech input, switch controls, alternative keyboards, and refreshable braille displays. People use them in varied combinations with browsers and operating systems.
assistive_technology.rule: An interface should expose meaningful names, roles, states, and reading order so the reader’s chosen technology can use it.
assistive_technology.deep: Assistive technology often relies on semantic structure, names, roles, states, focus order, and text alternatives exposed by an application. Visual appearance alone may not supply this information. Plectis preserves accessible mathematical markup and uses focus and description relationships for glossary help. Compatibility can vary across browser and technology combinations, so standards and representative testing both matter.

asymptotic_bound.label: asymptotic bound
asymptotic_bound.preview: An asymptotic bound compares the sizes of functions once their input is sufficiently large or approaches a specified limit.
asymptotic_bound.card: For example, \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) as n tends to infinity means \(|f(n)| \le C|g(n)|\) for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. The notation hides that constant and initial threshold.
asymptotic_bound.rule: It is a bound on growth, not an exact formula or necessarily an estimate valid at small inputs.
asymptotic_bound.deep: The papers use such comparisons to constrain potential counterexamples. Constants and parameter dependence must be recovered when an argument needs an explicit finite range.

asymptotic_density.label: asymptotic density
asymptotic_density.preview: Asymptotic density is the limiting proportion of positive integers up to N that belong to a set.
asymptotic_density.card: The even integers have density \(1/2\); the squares have density zero despite being infinite. Form \(|A\cap \{1,\ldots ,N\}|/N\) and let N grow.
asymptotic_density.rule: Ordinary density requires this limit to exist. Upper and lower density use limit superior and limit inferior; upper Banach density additionally considers translated intervals.
asymptotic_density.deep: Frequency is different from summability or independence. A density-zero support can have a divergent reciprocal sum, and long dense islands can coexist with ordinary density zero. The #251 theorem uses upper Banach density zero, which rules out a positive proportion in arbitrarily long intervals uniformly over their starting point.

asymptotic_equivalence.label: asymptotic equivalence
asymptotic_equivalence.preview: Two functions are asymptotically equivalent at a specified limit if their ratio tends to one.
asymptotic_equivalence.card: The functions \(n+1\) and n are asymptotically equivalent as n tends to infinity because \((n+1)/n\) tends to 1. Their difference remains 1, showing that asymptotic equivalence compares relative rather than absolute error.
asymptotic_equivalence.rule: Write \(f\sim g\) only after naming the limit and ensuring g is nonzero nearby. The statement means \(f/g\to 1\). It is stronger than \(f=O(g)\) and \(g=O(f)\), which allow a fixed multiplicative gap.
asymptotic_equivalence.deep: In the denominator and least-common-multiple arguments, asymptotic equivalence isolates the leading growth while suppressing lower-order terms. It does not supply exact equality, effective thresholds, or usable constants unless those are proved separately.

asymptotic_expansion.label: asymptotic expansion
asymptotic_expansion.preview: An ordered approximation whose truncation errors are controlled relative to successive smaller terms in a specified limit.
asymptotic_expansion.card: For example \(f(x)\sim a_{0}+a_{1}/x+a_{2}/x^{2}+\ldots\) means that every fixed finite truncation has the corresponding smaller-order remainder as x tends to infinity. The coefficients describe increasingly fine scales; the infinite series itself need not converge.
asymptotic_expansion.rule: State the limiting variable and region, and whether estimates are uniform in other parameters. Differentiating an expansion generally needs additional hypotheses. A two-term approximation does not establish a full expansion to arbitrary order.
asymptotic_expansion.deep: The #1049 paper computes a first coefficient correction of order \(1/k\) with an \(O(k^{-2})\) remainder. Summing its logarithm produces a power of N in the determinant asymptotic. The finer correction matters even though the dominant exponential and factorial factors are already known.

atlas.label: Atlas
atlas.preview: The Atlas is Plectis's navigable map of the system's parts and their relationships.
atlas.card: It helps a reader or agent move from an overview to a particular component, source, work record, or check. Its entries are derived from the system's stored information so the map can be refreshed as that information changes.
atlas.rule: The public site exposes a selected part of the wider system map.
atlas.deep: An Atlas entry is a route to inspect something; appearing on the map alone does not establish that the object is complete, current, or validated.

atom_feed.label: Atom feed
atom_feed.preview: An Atom feed is an XML document for syndicating entries such as articles or updates, with identifying and descriptive metadata.
atom_feed.card: Each entry commonly carries a stable identifier, title, update time, link, author information, and summary or content. A reader polls the published feed URL and decides locally how to display or retain new entries. Atom is an open syndication format related to RSS.
atom_feed.rule: A feed reports only entries the publisher includes; subscribing does not notify the publisher or prove that every site change appears in the feed.
atom_feed.deep: Atom defines XML elements and rules for identifying, dating, linking, and carrying entries. Stable entry identifiers help readers avoid duplicates when titles or URLs change, while updated timestamps signal revisions. Feeds can contain full content or summaries and may paginate or archive older entries separately. Polling frequency belongs to the reader, so delivery is not instantaneous. The format enables decentralized subscription without requiring an email address, but server logs may still record ordinary requests and therefore should not be described as absolute reader anonymity.

audit.label: audit
audit.preview: An audit is a systematic examination of records against stated requirements; here it often checks whether an agent's report matches its actions.
audit.card: For example, a completion audit can compare a claim that tests passed with the commands and results recorded for that session. This is narrower than deciding whether the tests adequately assess the software.
audit.rule: Read the audit's stated criteria to see which question it answers.
audit.deep: An accurate report of a poorly tested change can pass a report-faithfulness audit. Assessing the underlying change requires additional evidence and appropriate checks.

authentication.label: authentication
authentication.preview: Authentication is the process of checking a claim about who or what an actor is.
authentication.card: A system may authenticate a person, account, device, or service with passwords, keys, certificates, tokens, or multiple factors. Authentication differs from authorization, which determines permitted actions.
authentication.rule: State the identity claim and assurance method; successful authentication does not grant every permission.
authentication.deep: Authentication compares presented evidence with an identity system’s rules. It may establish control of an account or cryptographic key without proving a legal name or broader trustworthiness. Sessions often remember a successful check for a limited time. Plectis definitions of credentials, clients, webhooks, and HTTPS rely on this distinction: verifying identity is separate from deciding what that identity may read, change, publish, or trigger.

authority.label: authority
authority.preview: Authority is the recognised basis for settling a particular question or permitting an action.
authority.card: Plectis assigns authority by subject. Source code establishes what an implementation contains; an execution record reports a captured run; the operator's instructions determine intended scope. Each source can settle some questions and leave others unanswered.
authority.rule: Identify both the source and the kind of decision it can support.
authority.deep: A generated page can help you find authoritative material, but a convenient or confident summary does not acquire the authority of the source it describes.

authorization.label: authorization
authorization.preview: Authorization determines which actions a person, program, or role is permitted to perform on specified resources.
authorization.card: Authentication checks identity; authorization determines permitted actions. A policy can also allow an anonymous user to read public material without identifying them. Technical capability does not itself grant permission, and permission for one action need not cover another.
authorization.rule: An authorization decision binds an actor, action, target, conditions, and duration through policy, ownership, consent, role, or delegated authority.
authorization.deep: Authorization answers whether a particular actor may perform a particular operation on a resource under current conditions. The decision can come from access-control roles, explicit user consent, ownership, organizational policy, or delegated authority. Good authorization is scoped: permission to read one file does not imply permission to publish it, and approval to prepare a message does not imply approval to send it. Authentication supplies an identity claim but does not determine every allowed action. Authorization can also expire or be revoked, so past permission is not automatically authority for a materially different target or time.

axiom.label: axiom
axiom.preview: An axiom is a starting assumption of a mathematical theory; Plectis also uses the word for a fundamental system rule.
axiom.card: A mathematical proof derives its conclusion from its hypotheses and underlying axioms. On the software pages, a system axiom instead states a design constraint that other rules are expected to preserve.
axiom.rule: The surrounding subject determines which meaning is intended.
axiom.deep: For a Lean theorem, the relevant question is which logical assumptions its proof depends on. For a Plectis design rule, the question is how the implementation enforces it and what evidence shows that enforcement.

back_end.label: backend
back_end.preview: A backend is the processing, storage, and service layer behind a user-facing interface or another client.
back_end.card: Backends accept requests, apply business or domain logic, read and write data, call other services, and return results. Some systems have no visual frontend, and the boundary between frontend and backend depends on the architecture rather than on whether code is publicly visible.
back_end.rule: A backend claim should name the service boundary and behavior tested; being behind the interface does not make a component independently reproducible or more trustworthy.
back_end.deep: Backend is a relational role. Browser code may be frontend to a person while acting as a client of remote APIs; one service can consume another and provide results downstream. Backends may run on servers, local machines, embedded devices, or serverless platforms. Their correctness, security, privacy, availability, and performance require separate evidence. Source publication can make implementation inspectable, but an externally hosted backend may still depend on configuration, data, credentials, and infrastructure that readers cannot reproduce.

band.label: band
band.preview: A band is a named level of detail in a description, such as a brief label, a short summary, or a full explanation.
band.card: Plectis uses bands to let readers choose how much context to open. A compression profile specifies what each level must preserve and how it leads to the fuller source.
band.rule: A shorter band should reduce reading effort without changing the claim.
band.deep: For example, a glossary preview orients a reader quickly, while the expanded entry supplies the distinctions and examples needed to use the term accurately.

barrier.label: barrier
barrier.preview: A mathematical barrier is an obstruction showing why a specified approach cannot establish its intended result under stated conditions.
barrier.card: A barrier theorem proves a limitation of a method or construction. In these papers, such results help identify which attempted routes have failed and what a future approach would have to change.
barrier.rule: Check the hypotheses and the precise class of approaches ruled out.
barrier.deep: A method failing does not show that the original problem is impossible. A barrier can be useful progress by preventing repetition and revealing which assumption caused the obstruction.

base.label: base
base.preview: The base of a power is the number being raised to an exponent.
base.card: In \(b^{n}\), b is the base and n is the exponent. Decimal notation uses powers of ten for place values, while binary uses powers of two. The mathematics papers also raise rational bases such as \(3/2\) to powers without assuming ordinary integer-base digit rules.
base.rule: Check whether the passage concerns powers, positional digits, or both, and retain its stated restrictions on the base.
base.deep: For an integer base \(b>1\), the usual digits are 0 through \(b-1\), and the places after the radix point have weights \(1/b\), \(1/b^{2}\), and so on. More general positional expansions require their own digit conventions. In the irrationality papers, expressions involving a rational base can be studied as powers or series directly; conclusions about integer divisibility cannot be transferred without checking the assumptions.

basis.label: basis
basis.preview: In linear algebra, a basis gives unique vector coordinates; in an argument, its basis is the assumptions or evidence supporting it.
basis.card: A vector-space basis both spans the space and is linearly independent: every vector is a unique finite sum of basis vectors multiplied by scalars. One horizontal and one vertical unit vector form a basis for the ordinary plane.
basis.rule: The scalars and vector space are part of the mathematical definition; evidence supporting an argument does not have to form a vector space.
basis.deep: Plectis uses “named basis” for the stated sources or assumptions behind a claim. Naming those sources makes them inspectable; it does not by itself show that they support the conclusion.

benchmark.label: benchmark
benchmark.preview: A benchmark is a specified workload and measurement procedure used to compare performance against a baseline or other systems.
benchmark.card: A benchmark couples a task with a metric, dataset, environment, and scoring rule. Its result describes performance under those conditions; it does not automatically rank systems for workloads the benchmark did not test.
benchmark.rule: A comparison must identify the workload, scoring rule, environment, and any deliberately varied conditions; conclusions remain limited to what those choices represent.
benchmark.deep: Benchmarks measure properties such as speed, accuracy, reliability, resource use, or cost on a defined workload. Fair comparison fixes the relevant conditions or explicitly identifies what is being varied, including hardware, scoring, workloads, and treatment of failures. A single score can hide trade-offs, distribution shifts, or poor tail behaviour. Repeated optimization against a public test may also make the score less representative because systems adapt to its examples. In finance, benchmark can instead mean a reference index or rate; the shared idea is comparison with a declared standard, not a universal measure of quality.

bergman_kernel.label: Bergman kernel
bergman_kernel.preview: The kernel that reproduces square-integrable holomorphic functions by integration over their domain.
bergman_kernel.card: For the unit disc with ordinary area measure, \(K(z,w)=1/[\pi (1-z\cdot \overline{w})^{2}]\). If f is holomorphic and square-integrable there, \(f(z)=\int K(z,w)f(w)dA(w)\). The kernel is holomorphic in z and antiholomorphic in w.
bergman_kernel.rule: The normalization depends on the measure. Positive-definite kernel does not mean every kernel value is a positive real number. On the real diameter of the disc, this particular kernel is positive, which permits a special comparison.
bergman_kernel.deep: In #1041 the coefficient expansion of a Riemann map and Cauchy–Schwarz turn component area into a bound on the length of the image of a real interval. The positive disc kernel makes the resulting double integral explicitly computable.

bernstein_basis.label: Bernstein basis
bernstein_basis.preview: The degree-n polynomial basis \(\binom{n}{k}t^{k}(1-t)^{n-k}\) for k from 0 to n.
bernstein_basis.card: Each basis function is nonnegative on \([0,1]\), and the basis functions sum to one. Consequently a polynomial expressed in this basis lies between its smallest and largest Bernstein coefficients on that interval.
bernstein_basis.rule: Nonnegative coefficients are a sufficient positivity certificate, not a necessary condition in a fixed degree. Basis positivity holds on the stated interval; it cannot be used unchanged outside \([0,1]\). Bernstein approximation polynomials are a related construction, not this basis itself.
bernstein_basis.deep: The #1041 counterexample verifies inequalities by rewriting degree-fourteen polynomials along line segments in Bernstein form. Exact rational coefficients certify the whole interval, rather than only values at finitely many sampled points.

bertrand_postulate.label: Bertrand postulate
bertrand_postulate.preview: Bertrand’s postulate states that for every integer \(n>1\) there is a prime strictly between n and 2n.
bertrand_postulate.card: It guarantees a prime in a fixed multiplicative interval, without identifying which prime. For instance, at \(n=3\) the prime 5 lies between 3 and 6.
bertrand_postulate.rule: Endpoint conventions and the small cases matter when reformulating the theorem. It gives no claim that every short interval of an arbitrary fixed length contains a prime.
bertrand_postulate.deep: The #68 finite-gcd argument needs a prime ℓ with \(D/2<\ell \le D\). Bertrand supplies it for \(D\ge 3\) after treating the integer endpoints; \(D=2\) is handled directly. This interval ensures a unique largest factorial channel contributes the relevant prime valuation, ruling out a nontrivial common divisor.

big_o_notation.label: big-o notation
big_o_notation.preview: Big-O notation bounds the magnitude of one quantity by a fixed constant times another near a specified limit.
big_o_notation.card: The expression \(n+7\) is \(O(n)\) as n grows because \(n+7\le 8n\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The notation records an eventual constant-factor upper bound; it does not claim that \(n+7\) is approximately equal to n.
big_o_notation.rule: The statement \(f=O(g)\) near a specified limit means \(|f|\le C|g|\) there for some fixed C after a threshold. Any parameters on which C may depend must be stated, often by a subscript such as \(O_{\varepsilon}\).
big_o_notation.deep: Big-O lets the papers separate a main arithmetic contribution from controlled errors or bound the number of exceptional indices. It hides constants and a finite initial range, so it cannot by itself certify a numerical inequality at a particular input.

biholomorphic_map.label: biholomorphic map
biholomorphic_map.preview: A bijective holomorphic map whose inverse is also holomorphic.
biholomorphic_map.card: A biholomorphism gives complex domains the same analytic structure. Translation and nonzero complex scaling are examples. A local biholomorphism has such an inverse near each point; it can still identify distinct points globally.
biholomorphic_map.rule: In one complex variable a holomorphic map with nonzero derivative is locally biholomorphic. A global conclusion also needs injectivity and the specified target. Biholomorphic maps preserve angles locally but generally change lengths and areas.
biholomorphic_map.deep: The square-root coordinate in #1041 becomes a global biholomorphism only after properness and simple connectivity are established. Its inverse turns a segment in the coordinate domain into a root-connecting curve. Estimating that curve requires a separate bound on the inverse derivative, rather than topology alone.

bijection.label: bijection
bijection.preview: A bijection is a function that reaches every element of its codomain exactly once.
bijection.card: Equivalently, it is both injective and surjective: different inputs produce different outputs, and every element of the codomain is reached. The integer map \(n\mapsto n+1\) is bijective, with inverse \(m\mapsto m-1\).
bijection.rule: Bijective functions admit two-sided inverses and show that their domain and codomain have the same cardinality.
bijection.deep: A bijection alone need not preserve distance, addition, or continuity. Statements requiring those properties must supply them separately; a conformal bijection in the geometry papers carries much more structure than an arbitrary pairing.

binary_expansion.label: binary expansion
binary_expansion.preview: A binary expansion writes a number with digits 0 and 1, using powers of two as place values.
binary_expansion.card: For example, \(0.101\) in binary is \(1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8\), or \(5/8\). The digit positions turn questions about a real number into questions about a sequence of zeros and ones.
binary_expansion.rule: In base two, rational numbers have eventually repeating expansions.
binary_expansion.deep: Numbers with a terminating expansion also have an alternative ending in repeating ones. Arguments about uniqueness or periodicity must account for this familiar ambiguity.

binomial_coefficient.label: binomial coefficient
binomial_coefficient.preview: A binomial coefficient counts ways to choose a fixed number of elements from a finite set, without regard to order.
binomial_coefficient.card: For integers \(0\le k\le n\), “n choose k” is \(n!/[k!(n-k)!]\). For example, five elements have ten two-element subsets. Choosing none or choosing all gives one possibility.
binomial_coefficient.rule: These formulas specify nonnegative integer parameters. Generalized binomial coefficients extend the notation to other parameters and need their own convention.
binomial_coefficient.deep: The coefficients also appear in \((1+x)^{n}\). In #1049, ordinary binomial coefficients occur in exponents of q-polynomials, while Gaussian binomial coefficients are a different polynomial analogue. Their value at \(q=1\) recovers the ordinary coefficient; the two should not be identified at an arbitrary q.

boolean_selector.label: Boolean selector
boolean_selector.preview: A Boolean selector is a sequence or function taking values 0 and 1 that records which objects are included.
boolean_selector.card: Given terms \(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots\), a selector \(\varepsilon _n\) forms the chosen subseries \(\sum \varepsilon _n a_n\): \(\varepsilon _n=1\) keeps the nth term and \(\varepsilon _n=0\) omits it. The selector is the indicator function of the selected index set.
boolean_selector.rule: “Boolean” here means two-valued, not that logical operations are necessarily being performed. The selector encodes membership but does not by itself impose finiteness, randomness, periodicity, or independence on the chosen set.
boolean_selector.deep: In the Mersenne-support paper, one binary selector determines the coefficient sequence and hence the support subseries. This makes combinatorial choices into arithmetic data that can be transformed by Möbius-type identities.

borel_cantelli_lemma.label: Borel–Cantelli lemma
borel_cantelli_lemma.preview: The Borel–Cantelli lemmas relate sums of event probabilities to whether infinitely many events occur.
borel_cantelli_lemma.card: For a sequence of measurable events on one probability space, the first lemma says that a finite sum of probabilities implies only finitely many events occur almost surely; independence is unnecessary. The second says that mutual independence and a divergent sum imply infinitely many occur almost surely.
borel_cantelli_lemma.rule: Do not infer the second conclusion from divergence alone. State the independence or other sufficient dependence condition used.
borel_cantelli_lemma.deep: In the #257 profinite argument, prime divisibility events are independent and have probabilities 1/p with divergent sum. The second lemma explains the infinitely-many-occurrences step, which makes the proposed limiting observable unsuitable as a finite integrable average.

bound.label: bound
bound.preview: A bound is a value that a quantity is proved to stay above or below under stated conditions.
bound.card: An upper bound M gives \(x \le M\); a lower bound m gives \(m \le x\). Bounds can also depend on a parameter, such as the number of terms in a sum.
bound.rule: A bound need not equal the quantity it controls or be the best possible bound.
bound.deep: In these papers, bounds often control the error left after a finite calculation, allowing a statement about an infinite process to follow from finite information.

branch_point.label: branch point
branch_point.preview: A branch point is a location around which continuing a multivalued function can lead from one branch to another.
branch_point.card: For the complex square root, continuing a chosen value around zero once changes its sign: starting with one square root returns to the other. No single continuous square-root choice works on the entire punctured plane.
branch_point.rule: This concerns continuation around the point, not merely a formula that is inconvenient to evaluate there.
branch_point.deep: Avoiding branch points lets the selected inverse of a polynomial continue as one injective holomorphic branch.

bridge.label: bridge
bridge.preview: A bridge is Plectis's mechanism for sending a bounded task to an outside worker and returning its response.
bridge.card: The controlling agent selects the instructions and context to send. The returned material is then assessed before it is incorporated into the working system. This exchange can support an external reasoning or research pass.
bridge.rule: The bridge itself does not grant the outside worker direct control of the local files.
bridge.deep: The worker's answer remains a proposal or source of evidence until the receiving agent checks it and performs any authorised changes.

bundle.label: bundle
bundle.preview: A bundle is a group of related files packaged together for inspection or use.
bundle.card: For a Plectis component, an evidence bundle can include the source code, test inputs, and result record associated with a run. Keeping them together lets a reader inspect which inputs were used, which checks ran, and what those checks returned.
bundle.rule: The bundle's inventory and source versions determine what it actually contains.
bundle.deep: A bundle may document a recorded run or provide material for repeating it. The accompanying instructions should say which of those uses it supports.

cache.label: cache
cache.preview: A cache stores a reusable copy of data or a computed result so later access can avoid repeated work.
cache.card: Caches improve speed or reduce load by serving previously stored values. That benefit creates a freshness problem: the cached copy may no longer agree with its source after the source changes.
cache.rule: A functioning cache has a key that identifies reusable work, a policy for admitting and removing entries, and an expiration, invalidation, or refresh path when source state changes.
cache.deep: A cache keeps data closer to a consumer or preserves the result of an expensive computation. A cache hit reuses a matching entry; a miss fetches or computes the value and may store it. Keys determine which requests count as equivalent, while capacity and eviction policies determine what remains available. Expiration limits age, and invalidation removes entries known to be stale. No single policy guarantees both perfect freshness and maximum reuse. Browsers, processors, applications, databases, and build systems all use caches, but their consistency requirements and failure consequences differ.

calibration.label: calibration
calibration.preview: Calibration compares measurements with a reference standard or compares stated forecast probabilities with observed event frequencies.
calibration.card: Instrument calibration characterizes or adjusts readings against a known standard. Forecast calibration asks whether events assigned similar probabilities occur at corresponding rates across a suitable collection of predictions.
calibration.rule: Measurement calibration requires a traceable reference and stated conditions; probability calibration requires comparable forecast-event pairs and enough observations to assess frequency agreement at the claimed resolution.
calibration.deep: Calibration has two common technical senses. A measuring instrument is calibrated by comparing its readings with reference values under controlled conditions, then estimating bias, uncertainty, or an adjustment. A probabilistic forecaster is calibrated when, among comparable events assigned probability p, approximately a proportion p occur over repeated cases. This is a group-frequency property, so one correct or incorrect forecast says little about calibration. A forecaster can be calibrated yet uninformative by always giving the base rate. Conversely, sharp predictions can be useful but miscalibrated if their stated probabilities systematically overstate or understate observed frequencies.

callback.label: callback
callback.preview: A callback is a function supplied to other code so that code can call it when a specified event or stage occurs.
callback.card: Callbacks let a caller provide behaviour without controlling the whole operation. They are common in event handling, asynchronous work, validation, and library extension points.
callback.rule: Check who invokes the callback, when it may run, what arguments it receives, and how errors or repeated calls are handled.
callback.deep: The code receiving a callback chooses when to invoke it and what arguments to supply. A sorting function might call a supplied comparison function immediately; a browser might call a registered click handler much later. Callbacks can therefore be synchronous or asynchronous. Plectis evaluators use them for checks that vary between cases while a shared runner performs the common steps.

canonicalisation.label: canonicalisation
canonicalisation.preview: Canonicalisation is the process of putting something into a standard, representative form.
canonicalisation.card: In the mathematical research discussion here, it means consolidating a result into a natural statement and an understood proof that others can reuse. Equivalent formulations and routine supporting lemmas may become part of one clearer account.
canonicalisation.rule: A repository can simplify its own presentation, but it cannot declare that the mathematical community has adopted it.
canonicalisation.deep: This is a later question than whether a proof checks: it concerns which formulation and explanation become useful, recognised tools for other work.

cardinality.label: cardinality
cardinality.preview: Cardinality measures how many elements a set has, extending finite counting to infinite sets through bijections.
cardinality.card: The set \(\{2,4,6\}\) has cardinality 3. Two sets have the same cardinality when their elements can be paired by a bijection. Consequently, the natural numbers and the even natural numbers have the same infinite cardinality via \(n\mapsto2n\).
cardinality.rule: Infinite cardinalities need not all be equal: the real numbers cannot be put in a bijection with the natural numbers.
cardinality.deep: A proper subset can have the same infinite cardinality as the containing set. Cardinality is therefore different from length, area, probability, or asymptotic density, each of which answers a different question about size.

care.label: care
care.preview: Care means attending to the people, correctness, and future maintenance affected by a piece of work.
care.card: Plectis uses the word as a practical standard for an agent's conduct. A change should be understandable, checked to the appropriate extent, and left in a state that another person can continue.
care.rule: Care is expressed through decisions and follow-through, rather than through enthusiastic language.
care.deep: For example, preserving unrelated edits and updating an instruction made inaccurate by a change both reduce avoidable costs for the next person working on the system.

catalog.label: catalog
catalog.preview: A catalog is an organised inventory; on Plectis's architecture page it lists patterns available for use in the system.
catalog.card: Each catalog entry identifies a pattern and provides the information needed to select it. The architecture then connects the selected pattern to requirements, an implementation route, and evidence from its use.
catalog.rule: This particular catalog is distinct from the site's collection of papers or skills.
catalog.deep: Generating the inventory from registered source material makes omissions and stale entries easier to detect, although the generated catalog still needs to be refreshed and checked.

cauchy_determinant_formula.label: Cauchy determinant formula
cauchy_determinant_formula.preview: An exact product evaluation for a matrix with entries that are reciprocals of pairwise sums.
cauchy_determinant_formula.card: For \(C_{ij}=1/(x_i+y_j)\), its determinant is \(\frac{\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)(y_j-y_i)}{\prod_{i,j}(x_i+y_j)}\). The formula assumes that every denominator is nonzero. Distinct x-values and distinct y-values make the numerator nonzero.
cauchy_determinant_formula.rule: The multiplicative version with entries \(1/(1-x_i y_j)\) follows by a change of variables and has its own displayed factors. Keep signs, indexing and normalization consistent. This identity evaluates one structured determinant; it is different from Cauchy–Binet.
cauchy_determinant_formula.deep: The #1049 paper first evaluates the equal-weight geometric moment determinant exactly by this formula. That solved model helps isolate the additional effect of nonconstant moment weights in the later asymptotic theorem.

cauchy_product.label: Cauchy product
cauchy_product.preview: The Cauchy product of two series groups products of terms by the sum of their indices.
cauchy_product.card: For \(\sum a_{n}\) and \(\sum b_{n}\), its nth term is \(c_{n}=\sum _{k=0}^{n}a_{k}b_{n-k}\). If both numerical series converge absolutely, then \(\sum c_{n}\) converges absolutely and equals their product.
cauchy_product.rule: Convergence of each series without further conditions is not enough for this conclusion. For formal power series, the same finite coefficient formula defines multiplication without analytic convergence.
cauchy_product.deep: The #1049 factorization of the weight generating function turns its product into finite coefficient convolutions. The paper handles the formal identity through coefficient finiteness and proves the analytic identity through locally uniform convergence inside its specified disc. This separates the algebraic coefficient rule from justification of numerical products.

cauchy_binet_formula.label: Cauchy–Binet formula
cauchy_binet_formula.preview: The Cauchy–Binet formula expresses the determinant of a rectangular matrix product as a sum of products of matching square minors.
cauchy_binet_formula.card: If A is \(N\times M\) and B is \(M\times N\) with \(M\ge N\), then \(\det (AB)=\sum _{s} \det (A[:,S])\det (B[S,:])\), where S runs over N-element subsets of the intermediate indices.
cauchy_binet_formula.rule: The finite formula is algebraic. Passing to infinitely many intermediate indices requires a separate convergence argument.
cauchy_binet_formula.deep: In #1049, a finite-node moment matrix factors through evaluations of powers. Cauchy–Binet yields squared Vandermonde determinants; entrywise convergence and positivity then justify the paper’s infinite-node limit.

cauchy_schwarz_inequality.label: cauchy–schwarz inequality
cauchy_schwarz_inequality.preview: The absolute inner product of two vectors is at most the product of their lengths.
cauchy_schwarz_inequality.card: For real lists \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{n}\) and \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{n}\), Cauchy–Schwarz says \(|\sum a_{i}b_{i}|\le \sqrt{\sum a_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum b_{i}^{2}}\). For example, it bounds a mixed sum using two simpler square-sums, with equality only when the lists are proportional.
cauchy_schwarz_inequality.rule: Identify the vectors, functions, or sequences and the inner product before applying the inequality. Infinite-dimensional or integral versions also require the square-size quantities on the right to be finite.
cauchy_schwarz_inequality.deep: The lemniscate analysis uses Cauchy–Schwarz to convert energy control into a perimeter or path-length estimate. The inequality does not create smallness alone: one still needs useful bounds for both factors on its right-hand side.

ceiling_function.label: ceiling function
ceiling_function.preview: The ceiling of a real number x is the smallest integer at least x, written ⌈x⌉.
ceiling_function.card: For example, \(\lceil 2.3\rceil =3\), \(\lceil 2\rceil =2\), and \(\lceil -2.3\rceil =-2\). It rounds toward positive infinity, not toward the integer with greatest absolute value.
ceiling_function.rule: It satisfies \(x\le\lceil x\rceil<x+1\). Ceiling differs from rounding to the nearest integer and from floor, which chooses the greatest integer at most x.
ceiling_function.deep: In the landing page’s #243 example, ceiling converts \(n\cdot a_{n}^{2}/(n+3)\) into an integer recurrence term with a one-sided error smaller than one. This rounding bound matters when checking the recurrence’s asymptotic rate.

certificate.label: certificate
certificate.preview: A certificate is data that a specified checker can use to verify a particular claim.
certificate.card: The data might provide a witness, a calculation trace, or the finite cases needed for a result. Producing the certificate and checking it can be separate tasks, with different costs and trust requirements.
certificate.rule: The guarantee depends on what the checker verifies and how that check connects to the claim.
certificate.deep: A collection of verified cases establishes a general theorem only when a further argument shows that those cases cover everything the theorem asserts.

challenge_solution_pair.label: Challenge/Solution pair
challenge_solution_pair.preview: A Challenge/Solution pair packages a precise Lean problem with a proposed solution that can be checked against it.
challenge_solution_pair.card: The challenge states the required result and allowed assumptions. The solution supplies the implementation or proof intended to meet that requirement. Plectis uses the pair as an independently inspectable unit in its Comparator and Palomar material.
challenge_solution_pair.rule: The solution must satisfy the actual challenge, including its hypotheses and restrictions.
challenge_solution_pair.deep: Checking one pair establishes that result within its stated setting. It does not automatically settle neighbouring statements or the original open problem from which the challenge was derived.

changelog.label: changelog
changelog.preview: A changelog is a reader-facing record of notable changes between versions.
changelog.card: It helps users understand additions, fixes, removals, compatibility breaks, and migration needs without reconstructing history from every commit. A changelog selects and explains relevant changes, while Git history records a finer-grained ancestry of snapshots.
changelog.rule: A changelog should name versions and dates and should not imply that omitted internal changes never occurred.
changelog.deep: A changelog is curated communication for users, organized around named versions or dates. It selects additions, fixes, removals, compatibility breaks, security notes, and migration requirements that matter outside the development process. Git history serves a different purpose: commits preserve repository trees and ancestry at finer granularity, often with messages unsuitable as release documentation. A useful changelog links claims to versions, distinguishes planned from shipped behavior, and states omissions.
