It should not be read as exhaustive evidence that every internal alteration, dependency update, or deployment event was recorded.

chebotarev_density_theorem.label: Chebotarev density theorem
chebotarev_density_theorem.preview: The Chebotarev density theorem says that primes with any prescribed Frobenius conjugacy class occur with a predictable positive density in a finite Galois extension.
chebotarev_density_theorem.card: For an abelian extension, each allowable Frobenius element occurs among unramified primes with density reciprocal to the Galois-group size. This generalizes familiar statements about primes in arithmetic progressions.
chebotarev_density_theorem.rule: The standard theorem excludes ramified primes and prescribes a conjugacy class, not necessarily one distinguished group element. An effective version adds quantitative error bounds; the paper explicitly uses only the qualitative finite-Galois form.
chebotarev_density_theorem.deep: The argument needs existence of infinitely many primes whose reductions realize a chosen field symmetry. Chebotarev supplies exactly that bridge from Galois data to primes.

chebyshev_polynomial.label: Chebyshev polynomial
chebyshev_polynomial.preview: A polynomial family whose first-kind members satisfy \(T_{n}(\cos \theta )=\cos (n\theta )\).
chebyshev_polynomial.card: The first members are \(T_{0}=1\), \(T_{1}=x\) and \(T_{2}=2x^{2}-1\). For \(n\ge 1\), \(T_{n}\) has leading coefficient \(2^{n-1}\) and alternates between \(-1\) and 1 at \(n+1\) points of \([-1,1]\). This oscillation gives its extremal approximation property.
chebyshev_polynomial.rule: For \(n\ge 1\) the monic comparison polynomial is \(2^{1-n}T_{n}\); for \(n=0\) it is \(T_{0}=1\). Different Chebyshev families use different normalizations; the first-kind convention is the one used for the collinear-root argument.
chebyshev_polynomial.deep: In #1041 the appropriately scaled first-kind zeros attain the sharp bound for an adjacent root segment when all roots are collinear. Alternation supplies both the comparison and the equality case, connecting a geometric root problem with uniform polynomial approximation.

check.label: check
check.preview: A check is an examination of whether something satisfies a stated condition.
check.card: On this site, a check usually has a runnable command, specified inputs, and a recorded result. It may test a behaviour, validate a file, compare copies, or verify a proof.
check.rule: The result should say what was examined and which condition passed or failed.
check.deep: Useful checks can distinguish relevant failures from success. Reading a recorded result tells you about that run; repeating the command supplies evidence about your own copy and environment.

checker.label: checker
checker.preview: A checker is a program or procedure that evaluates an input against specified rules.
checker.card: A syntax checker, link checker, and proof checker each answer a different question. Their outputs are useful when the rules, inputs, and failure conditions are clear enough to inspect.
checker.rule: A pass establishes satisfaction of the implemented rules, subject to the checker's own correctness.
checker.deep: The rules may still omit something important to the wider task. Plectis therefore connects checker results to specific claims rather than treating every pass as general approval.

chinese_remainder_theorem.label: Chinese remainder theorem
chinese_remainder_theorem.preview: The Chinese remainder theorem solves simultaneous congruences with pairwise coprime positive moduli.
chinese_remainder_theorem.card: It says that any prescribed remainders occur together in exactly one class modulo the product of the moduli. For example, \(x\equiv1\) modulo 2 and \(x\equiv2\) modulo 3 combine to \(x\equiv5\) modulo 6.
chinese_remainder_theorem.rule: Without coprimality, the prescribed remainders must satisfy compatibility conditions.
chinese_remainder_theorem.deep: The papers use the theorem to arrange several divisibility conditions at once. It gives a controlled arithmetic construction rather than merely evidence that a computer found one suitable integer.

circuit_break.label: circuit-break
circuit_break.preview: To circuit-break a process is to interrupt a loop that would otherwise keep running or reinforcing itself.
circuit_break.card: In Plectis's research discussion, the loop is self-confirmation: the same people or tools produce work and judge its value. An outside reader can interrupt that loop by questioning the evidence, interpretation, or direction.
circuit_break.rule: An interruption prompts reassessment; it does not itself decide which conclusion is true.
circuit_break.deep: Automated checks remain useful for errors they can detect. Independent judgement addresses questions of meaning and value that repeating the internal checks may never raise.

claim.label: claim
claim.preview: A claim is an assertion that can be examined for truth or support.
claim.card: Plectis records what a component or mathematical result is said to establish and links that wording to evidence. This makes it possible to compare the public explanation with the source, proof, or recorded test.
claim.rule: The strength of the wording should match the strength and scope of the evidence.
claim.deep: For example, a successful test on specified inputs supports that tested behaviour. A claim covering every possible input requires a different argument or a suitable proof.

claim_registry.label: claim registry
claim_registry.preview: A claim registry is a structured list of assertions and the evidence, scope, and status attached to each.
claim_registry.card: For the formal mathematics, it connects reader-facing statements to particular declarations or other supporting material. This gives reviewers a way to check that the explanation says what the mathematics actually establishes.
claim_registry.rule: Registration records how a claim is presented and supported; it is not peer review.
claim_registry.deep: When the wording or proof changes, their connection must be checked again. A large number of formal declarations does not by itself imply an equally large number of distinct research contributions.

classical_logic.label: classical logic
classical_logic.preview: Classical logic allows excluded middle and principles such as eliminating a double negation.
classical_logic.card: Excluded middle asserts P or not P even when no method is known to decide which alternative holds. It supports familiar forms of proof by contradiction and nonconstructive existence arguments.
classical_logic.rule: A classical proof can establish existence without yielding an executable procedure for the object. Its accepted logical assumptions should remain explicit.
classical_logic.deep: The local Lean sources use classical blocks to make classical instances available. This permits standard mathematical reasoning while axiom audits report the resulting dependencies; the source keyword alone does not list every assumption of a theorem.

denominator_clearing.label: clearing denominators
denominator_clearing.preview: Clearing denominators multiplies an equation or expression by a suitable nonzero common denominator to remove its fractions.
denominator_clearing.card: For example, multiplying \(x/2 + y/3 = 1\) by 6 gives \(3x + 2y = 6\). Every term must receive the same multiplier for the equation to remain equivalent.
denominator_clearing.rule: If a denominator contains a variable, its nonzero condition must be preserved.
denominator_clearing.deep: The papers use this operation to obtain integer equations from rational quantities. Divisibility and congruence arguments can then study the resulting integers without losing the original denominator assumptions.

client.label: client
client.preview: A client is a program or device that requests data or a service from a server.
client.card: Client and server describe roles in an interaction. The same program can be a client in one exchange and a server in another, and a client may present a command line, library API, or graphical interface.
client.rule: Identify the service and protocol when calling something a client; the label alone does not state its permissions or trust.
client.deep: A client constructs requests, sends them through a protocol, interprets responses, and handles failures such as timeouts or rate limits. It may cache data or retry, subject to the service contract. Plectis component prose distinguishes a provider client from a theorem prover or local runner: the client communicates with a provider but does not supply the provider’s guarantees. Client input and server output both need validation at their boundaries.

clone.label: clone
clone.preview: To clone a repository is to create a local copy of its files and Git history, with options to limit what is downloaded.
clone.card: A normal full clone lets you inspect earlier revisions and work on the project locally. A shallow clone downloads limited history; other options can defer file contents or restrict the working checkout.
clone.rule: The public repositories linked here can be cloned for local inspection and checks.
clone.deep: A clone records a particular state. To compare your results with a published example, use the stated revision and environment rather than assuming that every copy contains the same files.

closed_route.label: closed route
closed_route.preview: A closed route is a recorded approach that has been ruled out within a stated set of assumptions or methods.
closed_route.card: The working records keep the reason for closure, such as a counterexample or a proved obstruction. This lets later researchers understand the failure before trying a similar idea.
closed_route.rule: Closure applies to the described approach, not automatically to the original problem.
closed_route.deep: A materially different method or hypothesis may avoid the obstruction. The record should make clear what would have to change, and whether the closure rests on proof, exact calculation, or weaker evidence.

closed_set.label: closed set
closed_set.preview: A set containing all of its limit points; equivalently, its complement is open.
closed_set.card: The closed unit disc \(\{z:|z|\le 1\}\) includes its boundary circle. If a sequence of its points converges, the limit remains in the disc.
closed_set.rule: Closed does not mean bounded: the entire real line is closed. A set can be both open and closed, depending on the surrounding space.
closed_set.deep: Closed discs and closed coefficient classes retain limiting configurations, which is essential when compactness arguments pass from approximating polynomials to a limit.

closeout.label: closeout
closeout.preview: A closeout is the final record of a unit of work: what changed, what was checked, and what remains unresolved.
closeout.card: It gives the next person enough information to continue without reconstructing the session. Plectis expects the record to distinguish completed work, deliberate scope limits, and unfinished obligations.
closeout.rule: Claims of completion should point to the resulting files or execution evidence.
closeout.deep: A useful closeout also explains any condition that should trigger another pass. That makes a bounded stopping point understandable without implying that every related problem has been solved.

topological_closure.label: closure of a set
topological_closure.preview: The smallest closed set containing a given set.
topological_closure.card: The closure of the open interval (0,1) is \([0,1]\): it adds the two boundary points approachable by sequences from inside. Points already in the set remain.
topological_closure.rule: A point lies in the closure exactly when every neighbourhood of it meets the original set. Closure is not the same as solving or completing an argument.
topological_closure.deep: Density and lower-semicontinuity arguments prove results first on generic polynomial configurations, then extend them to the closure containing limiting nongeneric cases.

coarea_formula.label: coarea formula
coarea_formula.preview: The coarea formula rewrites an integral over a region as integrals over level sets of a function, with a gradient factor accounting for how the levels are spaced.
coarea_formula.card: For a height function on a rectangle, integrating a quantity over the rectangle can be done by integrating along each horizontal slice and then over height. In curved settings, \(|\nabla u|\) supplies the needed Jacobian.
coarea_formula.rule: Precise hypotheses depend on dimension and regularity, commonly a Lipschitz map and measurable integrand. Critical levels may require measure-theoretic treatment. The formula is an identity, not automatically an inequality or a bound.
coarea_formula.deep: The paper uses coarea to integrate geometric information over polynomial level curves. Combined with winding or the argument principle, it translates two-dimensional analytic energy into one-dimensional boundary-length information.

code_map.label: Code Map
code_map.preview: Code Map is a generated view of the code's parts and their dependencies.
code_map.card: It helps readers see which modules belong together and which other modules they use. Plectis derives this view from source information so the diagram can be refreshed when the implementation changes.
code_map.rule: Open the linked source when a dependency matters to a proposed change.
code_map.deep: The map reflects the relationships its analysis captures. Dynamic behaviour or indirect connections may require further inspection, and the view can become stale if it has not been rebuilt.

coding_agent.label: coding agent
coding_agent.preview: A coding agent is an AI agent equipped to work with source files and development tools.
coding_agent.card: Depending on its permissions, it can inspect a repository, edit code, run commands, and examine results. Plectis provides routes and checks that let a person use such an agent to work on a bounded task.
coding_agent.rule: Its report should distinguish actions it performed from actions it merely recommends.
coding_agent.deep: Tool access makes execution possible; it does not guarantee a sound solution. The resulting change still needs appropriate validation, and the agent's permissions remain separate from its reasoning ability.

codomain.label: codomain
codomain.preview: The codomain is the set in which a function's outputs are declared to lie.
codomain.card: A function from integers to integers given by \(f(n) = n^{2}\) has the integers as its codomain, although it never produces a negative integer. Its image is the smaller set of outputs it actually attains.
codomain.rule: A function is surjective exactly when its image equals its codomain.
codomain.deep: Keeping this distinction explicit prevents “every output” from changing meaning halfway through an argument. Restricting the codomain to the image makes a function surjective onto that smaller set, but says nothing new about which values its formula produces.

coefficient.label: coefficient
coefficient.preview: A number multiplying a variable, power, basis element, or series term.
coefficient.card: In \(3z^{2}-7z+4\), the coefficients are 3, -7, and 4. A missing power has coefficient zero: the coefficient of \(z^{3}\) in this example is 0.
coefficient.rule: A coefficient may be an integer, rational, real, or complex number depending on context. In a series, coefficients form a sequence and need not be polynomial coefficients.
coefficient.deep: Plectis uses coefficients both to describe polynomial families and to weight infinite series, so the surrounding formula determines which meaning applies.

coefficient_sequence.label: coefficient sequence
coefficient_sequence.preview: A coefficient sequence is the indexed list of coefficients in a series or expansion, including any zero coefficients.
coefficient_sequence.card: In \(\sum c_n x^{n}\), the list \(c_0,c_1,\ldots\) is the coefficient sequence. Zeros matter because they mark missing powers or omitted series terms; the support is the set of indices where \(c_n\) is nonzero.
coefficient_sequence.rule: The surrounding expansion determines what the coefficients belong to. A coefficient sequence can be finite or infinite and need not converge by itself. It is data, distinct from the value of the resulting series.
coefficient_sequence.deep: The Mersenne paper obtains its coefficient sequence by a divisor transform of a Boolean selector. That sequence then determines the support and arithmetic behavior of the associated series.

coercion.label: coercion
coercion.preview: A type coercion is a designated conversion inserted to use a value where another type is expected.
coercion.card: For example, a natural number can be converted to an integer when an integer operation requires it. Coercion can also expose a structure's underlying set or function, making mathematical notation more convenient.
coercion.rule: Inspect the conversion when types matter. A coercion is a function or mechanism with defined behaviour, not an assertion that two types are identical or every conversion loses no information.
coercion.deep: The #243 Lean source moves among natural numbers, integers, residue types, and finite sets viewed as sets. Explicit ↑ notation and cast lemmas make those transitions visible when an arithmetic proof depends on them.

cofinal.label: cofinal
cofinal.preview: A subset of an ordered set is cofinal if it reaches at least as far as every element of that set.
cofinal.card: More precisely, for each x there is an element y in the subset with \(x \le y\). For indices in the natural numbers, this means that qualifying indices occur arbitrarily far out.
cofinal.rule: Cofinality does not mean that every sufficiently large index qualifies.
cofinal.deep: For example, the even natural numbers are cofinal among all natural numbers. This distinction matters when a proof needs infinitely many suitable indices rather than a property that eventually holds everywhere.

cold_agent.label: cold agent
cold_agent.preview: A cold agent starts a task without the earlier conversation or session context.
cold_agent.card: It must recover the task's meaning and current state from available files, instructions, and navigation routes. Plectis uses this situation to judge whether knowledge has been preserved well enough for work to continue.
cold_agent.rule: “Cold” describes missing context, not a lack of reasoning ability.
cold_agent.deep: A source link, clear status, and recorded next step can let a new agent resume correctly. A conclusion kept only in a previous conversation cannot do that.

cold_clone.label: cold clone
cold_clone.preview: A cold clone is a fresh repository checkout used to test whether someone new can follow the published instructions.
cold_clone.card: The test starts without the author's local caches, private files, or unrecorded setup. It checks whether the stated dependencies and commands are enough to reproduce the advertised example.
cold_clone.rule: Any additional setup must be stated for the test to be meaningful.
cold_clone.deep: A successful cold-clone run supports portability to that tested environment. It does not promise identical behaviour on every operating system, dependency version, or machine.

collaboration.label: collaboration
collaboration.preview: Collaboration is people working together on a shared task or result.
collaboration.card: Here it can take the form of a proof, correction, explanation, implementation, or useful account of a failed approach. The public records give contributors something concrete to inspect and improve together.
collaboration.rule: Attribution should identify the people responsible for the work and describe tool assistance accurately.
collaboration.deep: Agreement with the project is not required to help it: a well-supported correction or objection can be as useful as extending an existing result.

combinatorics.label: combinatorics
combinatorics.preview: Combinatorics studies how discrete objects can be selected, arranged, counted, and related.
combinatorics.card: Typical questions concern subsets, permutations, graphs, and patterns that must occur in sufficiently large collections. Some problems ask for an exact count; others ask whether a configuration exists at all.
combinatorics.rule: The objects and allowed arrangements must be specified before a counting argument applies.
combinatorics.deep: In the papers here, combinatorial structure can turn a broad number-theory question into a finite collection of cases or expose patterns that an arithmetic argument must address.

command_shell.label: command shell
command_shell.preview: A command shell interprets commands and coordinates the programs, files, and data streams they act on.
command_shell.card: For example, a shell can run a test program, pass its output to another program, and save errors in a file. Bash and Zsh are shells. The terminal displays the interaction; the shell parses the command language and carries out its instructions.
command_shell.rule: Quoting, variable expansion, and redirection are shell operations that can change which arguments a program receives and where its output goes.
command_shell.deep: The website’s runnable instructions depend on the stated shell and working directory. A shell also runs scripts without an interactive terminal, and some commands are built into the shell rather than separate programs. Reproducing an instruction requires preserving its arguments and relevant environment, not merely copying the visible program name. A successful shell invocation establishes only the outcome reported by the invoked operation.

command_line_interface.label: command-line interface
command_line_interface.preview: A command-line interface lets someone control software through textual commands, usually with arguments and options.
command_line_interface.card: A command such as a tool name followed by --help uses a command-line interface. Arguments identify inputs or subcommands, while options modify behaviour. The interface can be used interactively or called from a script, which makes repeated operations easier to reproduce.
command_line_interface.rule: The interface describes how instructions are supplied; the shell and terminal are separate programs that may help supply and display them.
command_line_interface.deep: The system exposes checks and builders through command-line interfaces so a reader can repeat a named operation and inspect its output. Commands can also be invoked directly by another program without a shell. Exit codes, standard output, and standard error are common ways to report results. A graphical interface may offer the same underlying operation with buttons and forms instead of typed commands.

commit.label: commit
commit.preview: A Git commit records a complete repository-tree snapshot, parent link or links, and identifying metadata.
commit.card: A commit names one state in Git history. It points to the full tree, links to its parent commit or commits, and records metadata such as author, time, and message; a diff is computed by comparing commits.
commit.rule: The commit object binds content, ancestry, and metadata; it excludes uncommitted working-tree changes and does not itself encode a unique change when it has multiple possible comparison bases.
commit.deep: Git stores a commit as an object that refers to one complete tree, zero or more parent commits, and metadata including author, committer, timestamps, and message. Its identifier therefore depends on both the recorded content and its history links. An ordinary commit usually has one parent; a merge commit can have several. The perceived change is not stored as an intrinsic patch: Git calculates a diff against a chosen parent or other revision. A commit neither includes unstaged work nor implies that anyone reviewed, tested, released, deployed, or approved the snapshot.

common_sense.label: common sense
common_sense.preview: In Plectis, common sense means choosing a proportionate action using the task, available evidence, and relevant constraints.
common_sense.card: It applies when no instruction spells out every detail. An agent should infer routine next steps, inspect what already exists, and choose an action that advances the user's aim without silently widening it.
common_sense.rule: Judgement remains accountable to evidence, permissions, and the consequences of being wrong.
common_sense.deep: For example, updating a link broken by one's own change is ordinary follow-through; starting an unrelated redesign requires a different justification.

compact.label: compact
compact.preview: Compact means concise in the software descriptions, while mathematical compactness requires every open cover to have a finite subcover.
compact.card: A compact software view preserves the information needed for its purpose in little space. In topology, an open cover is a collection of open sets containing every point of a space; compactness means finitely many of those sets already cover it.
compact.rule: In Euclidean space, compact sets are exactly the closed and bounded sets; other spaces require their own compactness test.
compact.deep: The software use concerns presentation. The mathematical use supports arguments about convergent subsequences and continuous functions. A short description and a small-looking geometric set do not establish the same property.

compactness.label: compactness
compactness.preview: A space is compact if every collection of open sets covering it has a finite subcollection that still covers it.
compactness.card: In Euclidean space, a set is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. For metric spaces, compactness is also equivalent to every sequence having a subsequence converging to a point in the set.
compactness.rule: These equivalent tests require their stated setting; boundedness alone is not enough in general.
compactness.deep: The papers use compactness to extract limits from families of candidates. A separate continuity or closure argument is needed to show that the limit retains the required property.

comparator.label: Comparator
comparator.preview: Comparator is a Lean tool for checking a submitted solution against a separately specified challenge.
comparator.card: Keeping the challenge separate helps detect a submission that proves a different or weakened statement. The challenge and checking configuration determine the requirements, including any restrictions on assumptions.
comparator.rule: Read the checked pair and configuration to see exactly what was accepted.
comparator.deep: Plectis uses this separation to support external inspection of formal results. A successful comparison concerns the specified challenge; it does not establish the importance of the result or its agreement with an informal claim.

compatibility_route.label: compatibility route
compatibility_route.preview: A compatibility route keeps an old address or identifier usable after an item has moved or been renamed.
compatibility_route.card: It may be a redirect, alias, or explanatory page leading to the current location. Plectis keeps such routes so existing citations and bookmarks can still reach the intended material.
compatibility_route.rule: The destination identifies the current item; the old address preserves continuity.
compatibility_route.deep: A migration record can state the old route, new route, and expected behaviour. This makes it possible to test the transition instead of relying on readers to discover the move themselves.

compiled_binary.label: compiled binary
compiled_binary.preview: A compiled binary is machine-readable output from compilation, such as an object file, library, bytecode module, firmware image, or executable.
compiled_binary.card: Compilation can produce several binary artifact kinds, and some are neither native machine code nor directly executable. Their exact bytes depend on source, tools, flags, dependencies, target platform, and environment. Running may require linking, loading, interpretation, or a virtual machine.
compiled_binary.rule: A binary’s presence proves neither provenance nor safety; bind it to source revision, build recipe, platform, and digest when identity matters.
compiled_binary.deep: Compiled binary is a broad term for machine-readable output produced by compilation; it need not be a native executable. The result may be an object file, shared or static library, bytecode module, firmware image, executable program, or another platform-specific artifact. Its bytes depend on source, compiler and linker versions, flags, dependencies, target architecture, and build environment. Running may require a loader or virtual machine. Identity, safety, and provenance need separate evidence such as digests, signatures, reproducible builds, and a binding to the corresponding source revision.

compiler.label: compiler
compiler.preview: A compiler translates one structured representation into another under defined transformation and checking rules.
compiler.card: A programming-language compiler may turn source into machine code, bytecode, or another language. A repository compiler may transform governed records into HTML, indexes, or other deterministic projections rather than executable code.
compiler.rule: Compilation is characterized by its input language and authority, transformations, target representation, diagnostics, compiler version, and guarantees established during translation.
compiler.deep: Compilers can parse, resolve names, check types, optimize, link, or generate output, but the exact stages and target vary. Machine code is only one possible result; source-to-source translators, template engines, schema compilers, and documentation builders also compile representations. Successful compilation establishes compliance with the checks the compiler performs, not the truth of input claims or correctness for every runtime case. Generated output remains reproducible when the input, compiler version, options, dependencies, and environment are fixed and its provenance stays traceable.

completely_multiplicative_function.label: completely multiplicative function
completely_multiplicative_function.preview: A completely multiplicative function takes 1 to 1 and turns every product of positive integers into the product of their values.
completely_multiplicative_function.card: It satisfies \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(mn)=f(m)f(n)\) for every positive m,n. The function \(f(n)=n\) is an example: \(f(9)=f(3)f(3)=9\), even though the factors are not coprime.
completely_multiplicative_function.rule: For a prime p and integer \(k\ge 0\), \(f(p^{k})=f(p)^{k}\). Ordinary multiplicativity only assumes a product rule for coprime factors; Euler’s totient has \(\varphi (9)=6\) but \(\varphi (3)^{2}=4\), so it is not completely multiplicative.
completely_multiplicative_function.deep: The #249 long record uses \(c(n)=n\) as a completely multiplicative comparison sequence in a Mersenne-tail example. Its conclusions concern the specified coefficient sequence; a separate argument is needed for Euler’s totient coefficients.

complex_number.label: complex number
complex_number.preview: A number \(a+bi\) with real a,b and \(i^{2}=-1\).
complex_number.card: The complex number \(3+2i\) is represented by the point \((3,2)\) in the complex plane. Its modulus \(|3+2i|=\sqrt{13}\) is its distance from 0.
complex_number.rule: Real numbers are the special case \(b=0\). Addition works coordinatewise, while multiplication uses \(i^{2}=-1\) and combines rotation with scaling.
complex_number.deep: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root and factors fully into linear factors. Its modulus level sets form the lemniscate geometry studied here.

complex_plane.label: complex plane
complex_plane.preview: The complex plane represents every complex number \(a+bi\) by the point with Cartesian coordinates \((a,b)\).
complex_plane.card: The horizontal coordinate is the real part and the vertical coordinate is the imaginary part. The number \(3+2i\) lies at \((3,2)\), and its distance from zero is \(\sqrt{13}\). This identifies the complex numbers with a two-dimensional real plane.
complex_plane.rule: Multiplication by a nonzero complex number acts as a rotation and scaling; complex multiplication supplies additional structure beyond the plane’s real coordinates.
complex_plane.deep: The lemniscate papers draw roots, critical points, curves, and regions in this plane. A complex number is one element; the complex plane is the whole ambient space. A set of roots can be finite while the surrounding plane is infinite. Real coordinates make geometric distances visible, and the complex arithmetic determines how polynomial maps transform those points. The complex plane is distinct from the Riemann sphere, which adds a point at infinity.

compression.label: compression
compression.preview: Compression reduces the amount of information needed to store, transmit, or read something.
compression.card: In Plectis's navigation, it means producing a shorter view of source material under rules about what must be preserved. The view keeps a route to the fuller source and makes important omissions or limits recoverable.
compression.rule: This use allows deliberate loss of detail, so preserving meaning requires judgement and checks.
compression.deep: A glossary preview, for example, should retain the defining idea while leaving examples and qualifications to the expanded entry.

compression_profile.label: compression profile
compression_profile.preview: A compression profile specifies how one kind of material should be presented at different levels of detail.
compression_profile.card: It defines what a short view must include, what it may omit, and how it links to the fuller account. Plectis uses profiles to make summaries of the same artifact kind follow consistent expectations.
compression_profile.rule: The profile governs the shape of a summary; the source governs its facts.
compression_profile.deep: For example, a result card may always need its claim and evidence status even when a very short version leaves out the supporting calculation.

computer_science.label: computer science
computer_science.preview: Computer science is the study of computation, algorithms, information, and the systems that process them.
computer_science.card: It includes theoretical questions about what can be computed as well as practical questions about languages, software, hardware, and reliable execution. CS is the usual abbreviation.
computer_science.rule: Formal verification is one part of this wider field.
computer_science.deep: On this site, computer-science contributions may concern the architecture, tools, checks, or reproducibility of the research workflow. They can improve how the mathematical work is produced and examined without themselves proving a mathematical claim.

concept.label: concept
concept.preview: A concept is an idea or category used to understand and organise a subject.
concept.card: Plectis also uses Concept as a structured record type: a recurring idea receives a stable identifier, definition, sources, and relationships. Other records can then refer to it consistently.
concept.rule: The record explains what the idea denotes; procedures describe how to act on it.
concept.deep: This separation helps detect vocabulary drift. If two mechanisms use the same name for different things, their shared concept reference provides a place to examine and resolve the mismatch.

concurrency.label: concurrency
concurrency.preview: Concurrency is the organization of multiple tasks whose execution or waiting periods overlap.
concurrency.card: Concurrent tasks can interleave on one processor or execute simultaneously on several processors. When they share mutable state or limited resources, their possible orderings require explicit coordination.
concurrency.rule: Concurrency permits overlapping progress but does not imply simultaneous execution; correctness depends on how shared state, ordering, cancellation, failures, and resource limits are coordinated.
concurrency.deep: Concurrency allows more than one task to be in progress during the same interval. A scheduler may interleave them on one processing unit, or hardware may run them in parallel. Overlap can improve responsiveness and resource use when one task waits for input or a service. It also creates several hazards: races depend on timing, deadlocks leave tasks waiting on one another, duplicate work can violate uniqueness assumptions, and concurrent writes can lose updates. Locks, transactions, message passing, immutable data, and ownership rules are different ways to control those interactions.

conditional_reduction.label: conditional reduction
conditional_reduction.preview: A conditional reduction proves that a target statement follows if a specified further condition holds.
conditional_reduction.card: The implication can be a complete theorem even while the condition remains unresolved. The reduction is useful when it exposes a more tractable question or clarifies exactly what additional evidence is needed.
conditional_reduction.rule: The target is still open until the required condition is established or another proof is found.
conditional_reduction.deep: A one-way implication need not give an equivalent problem. The new condition may be stronger than the target, so its difficulty and plausibility need separate assessment.

conditional_theorem.label: conditional theorem
conditional_theorem.preview: A conditional theorem proves a conclusion under stated hypotheses.
conditional_theorem.card: Mathematical theorems commonly have hypotheses. Here the label is especially useful when an important hypothesis remains unproved, so the theorem establishes an implication without yet establishing the desired conclusion on its own.
conditional_theorem.rule: Read the assumptions together with the conclusion, including assumptions supplied as parameters in Lean.
conditional_theorem.deep: A checked proof of “if H, then C” can be fully valid while H and C remain open. It is different from a proof containing an admitted step.

configuration.label: configuration
configuration.preview: Configuration is the set of selected values and options that determines how a program or system operates in a particular environment.
configuration.card: Configuration can choose paths, features, limits, credentials, service addresses, or policy modes without changing the program’s source code. Different configurations can produce different behaviour from the same version.
configuration.rule: Record the relevant configuration with a result when those settings can affect interpretation or reproduction.
configuration.deep: Configuration may live in command-line options, environment variables, structured files, deployment systems, or stored service settings. Defaults are also configuration choices even when no user edits a file. Plectis source contracts name configuration paths when routes depend on them. A configuration can be syntactically valid yet unsafe or unsuitable, so validation must check both form and permitted combinations.

conformal_map.label: conformal map
conformal_map.preview: A conformal map preserves angles locally; in planar complex analysis, it is a holomorphic map with nonzero derivative.
conformal_map.card: A conformal map locally acts like a rotation and a positive scaling, with the scale allowed to vary between points. For example, \(z\mapsto z^2\) is conformal away from zero. It preserves local angles but can change lengths and areas.
conformal_map.rule: For planar complex domains verify that the map is holomorphic and has nonzero derivative; global one-to-one correspondence additionally requires injectivity and is not part of local conformality alone.
conformal_map.deep: A conformal map preserves oriented angles between intersecting curves at every point. For maps between open subsets of the complex plane, a holomorphic function is conformal wherever its derivative is nonzero. Such a map may stretch lengths and areas, but infinitesimally it acts as a rotation followed by a positive scaling. A conformal bijection has a conformal inverse and gives an equivalence of domains. A Riemann map is a special conformal bijection between a proper simply connected planar domain and the unit disc, so conformal map and Riemann map are not interchangeable names.

congruence.label: congruence
congruence.preview: Two integers are congruent modulo m if their difference is divisible by m.
congruence.card: For a positive modulus, this is equivalent to having the same remainder. Thus \(17 \equiv 2\) modulo 5 because \(17 - 2 = 15\) is divisible by 5.
congruence.rule: Congruence is weaker than equality: infinitely many different integers can be congruent to one another.
congruence.deep: The papers use congruences to keep only the remainder information relevant to an argument. A nonzero remainder can rule out divisibility even when the original expression is too large to inspect directly.

conjecture.label: conjecture
conjecture.preview: A conjecture is a precise mathematical claim proposed as true but not yet established by proof.
conjecture.card: Examples, calculations, and partial results may make a conjecture plausible. A proof must cover its full statement; a counterexample must satisfy its hypotheses while violating its conclusion.
conjecture.rule: Evidence from many cases does not by itself settle a claim about all cases.
conjecture.deep: The papers can give equivalent formulations or sufficient conditions for a conjecture. Those are useful results, but the conjecture stays unresolved unless the additional work actually establishes or refutes it.

conjugacy_class.label: conjugacy class
conjugacy_class.preview: The conjugacy class of a group element g is the set \(\{hgh^{-1}:h\text{ in the group}\}\).
conjugacy_class.card: In an abelian group every conjugacy class has one element because \(hgh^{-1}=g\). In a nonabelian symmetry group, conjugate elements represent the same action after changing the coordinate or labeling used to describe it.
conjugacy_class.rule: Conjugacy is an equivalence relation on group elements. It is not complex conjugation, although complex conjugation itself can be a particular group element. A theorem prescribing a class is weaker than choosing one distinguished element.
conjugacy_class.deep: Changing the prime ideal above a fixed base prime conjugates its Frobenius element. Chebotarev therefore naturally counts base primes by Frobenius conjugacy classes.

connected_component.label: connected component
connected_component.preview: A connected component is a connected subset that cannot be enlarged while remaining connected within the surrounding space.
connected_component.card: Connected means that the part cannot be separated into two disjoint, nonempty relatively open pieces. Each point belongs to exactly one connected component.
connected_component.rule: Connectedness need not provide a continuous path between every pair of points in an arbitrary space.
connected_component.deep: In the lemniscate papers, components distinguish separate regions around polynomial roots. Statements requiring an actual path or a length bound need more than merely identifying which connected component contains a point.

connected_set.label: connected set
connected_set.preview: A set that cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open pieces relative to that set.
connected_set.card: An interval is connected, while two separated intervals are not. Connectedness says the set is one topological piece even when no particular path has yet been supplied.
connected_set.rule: Path connected implies connected, but the converse can fail in general spaces. Do not silently replace a connected-set claim by a stronger path claim.
connected_set.deep: The lower-bound argument applies to every connected set containing two selected roots, so it is stronger than checking only straight segments or one chosen curve.

constructive_proof.label: constructive proof
constructive_proof.preview: A constructive proof uses constructive inference and supplies the information required by its conclusions.
constructive_proof.card: For an existence claim, this usually means producing an appropriate witness with justification of its property. Constructive logic does not use unrestricted excluded middle or double-negation elimination as general inference rules.
constructive_proof.rule: State the constructive framework and assumptions when computational content matters. An explicitly described object inside an otherwise classical argument need not make the whole proof constructive.
constructive_proof.deep: The external-verification notes distinguish constructive dyadic-rank arguments from other evidence routes. Lean can check constructive and classical developments, so being machine-checked alone does not identify which logical methods a result uses.

context_packet.label: context packet
context_packet.preview: A context packet is a selected collection of information supplied for a particular task.
context_packet.card: Plectis uses packets to give an agent the relevant question, source routes, constraints, and current evidence without requiring it to read the whole repository. Public reader packets serve a similar orientation purpose.
context_packet.rule: A packet should make its scope and source versions clear.
context_packet.deep: Selection necessarily leaves things out. Links to the underlying material let a reader recover missing detail and check whether a summary still agrees with the sources it describes.

context_window.label: context window
context_window.preview: A context window is the bounded sequence of tokens a language model can use during a generation.
context_window.card: The window can contain instructions, conversation, retrieved documents, tool results, and tokens generated so far. These compete for finite space, although input and output limits vary by model. Token capacity measures available context, not comprehension, permanent memory, or factual reliability.
context_window.rule: A larger window permits more input but does not guarantee that every included detail is used accurately or with equal attention.
context_window.deep: A context window bounds the tokens a language model can directly condition on for one generation. Instructions, conversation, retrieved passages, tool results, and the requested output budget all consume capacity. Content outside that window has no direct effect unless another mechanism retrieves or summarizes it back in. Large capacity does not create durable memory, guarantee recall, or ensure equal attention across positions. Tokenization also means character count and word count do not map uniformly to available space, especially across code, mathematics, and languages.

continuous_integration.label: continuous integration
continuous_integration.preview: Continuous integration is the practice of frequently combining code changes and automatically checking that they work together.
continuous_integration.card: A CI service reacts to selected repository changes by running declared builds, tests, linters, or policy checks in a controlled environment. It gives collaborators evidence about whether changes integrate and preserves logs and status. The result covers the configured jobs and their environment.
continuous_integration.rule: A green CI result means the configured checks passed for that revision; it is not proof of correctness, security, deployability, or review.
continuous_integration.deep: Continuous integration combines small repository changes frequently and runs declared automation against each selected revision. Typical jobs compile code, execute tests, check formatting, scan dependencies, or build documentation in a controlled environment. The practice detects integration faults early and leaves reviewable logs, but its authority ends at configured checks, fixtures, platforms, and permissions. A green result establishes only what the completed checks justify; a skipped job or an untested requirement is not covered by the colour of the overall status. Reproducibility also depends on pinned dependencies and a faithfully described runner environment.

contradiction.label: contradiction
contradiction.preview: A contradiction is an impossibility obtained from assumptions, such as a statement and its negation both being true.
contradiction.card: In proof by contradiction, one assumes the opposite of the desired conclusion and derives such an impossibility. Classical reasoning then rules out that opposite assumption.
contradiction.rule: Each inference must follow from the assumptions actually available at that point.
contradiction.deep: For example, an irrationality argument may assume a number equals a fraction in lowest terms, then show both numerator and denominator must share a factor. That conflicts with the lowest-terms assumption.

contrapositive.label: contrapositive
contrapositive.preview: In classical logic, the contrapositive of “if P, then Q” is the equivalent statement “if not Q, then not P”.
contrapositive.card: For example, “every multiple of 4 is even” gives “an odd integer is not a multiple of 4”. Either version expresses the same implication through a different route.
contrapositive.rule: The converse, “if Q, then P”, is a different statement and need not hold.
contrapositive.deep: The papers often prove that rationality would force a property, then establish failure of that property to deduce irrationality. The reasoning must negate the exact consequence, with its quantifiers intact.

contribute.label: contribute
contribute.preview: To contribute is to supply work that helps a shared project advance or correct itself.
contribute.card: Here useful contributions include proofs, counterexamples, clearer explanations, software fixes, and reproducible reports of failed approaches. The public repositories provide concrete material against which a contribution can be inspected.
contribute.rule: Acceptance and attribution should follow the work and evidence, not the confidence of its presentation.
contribute.deep: A mathematical result remains attributable to the people who established it. Using Plectis as a tool or starting point does not transfer priority for their result to the project.

contributor_credit.label: contributor credit
contributor_credit.preview: Contributor credit records who supplied a piece of work and what that contribution was.
contributor_credit.card: Plectis aims to preserve attribution for accepted results, corrections, and other useful work, including when later work builds on them. Describing the contribution makes the credit more informative than simply listing a name.
contributor_credit.rule: Human authorship and the use of AI or other tools should be recorded distinctly.
contributor_credit.deep: The project's contribution record is not a substitute for scholarly priority or publication conventions. A result's authors retain credit for establishing it, including when this system helped them work.

convergence.label: convergence
convergence.preview: Convergence means approaching a specified limit; for an infinite series, it means that its partial sums approach a finite value.
convergence.card: For a real sequence, every chosen positive tolerance must eventually contain all later terms around the limit. For a series, apply that condition to the sums of the first n terms.
convergence.rule: Terms tending to zero are necessary for a series to converge, but are not sufficient.
convergence.deep: For example, \(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + \cdots\) diverges. Proving convergence also leaves separate questions about whether the sum is rational, algebraic, or transcendental.

convex_combination.label: convex combination
convex_combination.preview: A weighted sum whose weights are nonnegative and add to one.
convex_combination.card: One quarter of x plus three quarters of y lies on the line segment between x and y.
convex_combination.rule: Allowing negative weights while keeping their total equal to one gives an affine combination. A general linear combination need not have weights summing to one.
convex_combination.deep: The trinomial root equation places normalized polynomial values inside the convex hull of two controlled quantities.

convex_envelope.label: convex envelope
convex_envelope.preview: The convex envelope of a function is the greatest convex function that lies everywhere at or below the original function.
convex_envelope.card: On the interval \([-1,1]\), the function \(f(x)=-x^{2}\) bends downward and is not convex. Its convex envelope is the constant function \(-1\): that constant stays below f, and convexity prevents any convex function below f from rising above the chord joining the two endpoint values.
convex_envelope.rule: State the convention and domain. Here “convex envelope” means the lower convex envelope of a function. It is not the convex hull of a set, although the envelope can be constructed from convex combinations and is closely related to the convex hull of the function’s epigraph.
convex_envelope.deep: On a convex domain, take the pointwise supremum of all convex functions g satisfying \(g\le f\). Equivalently, minimize weighted averages of f over finite convex combinations representing each point. If no finite convex minorant exists, the envelope may take \(-\infty\) under an extended-value convention. A closed convex envelope additionally requires lower semicontinuity; that condition can change boundary values. The function construction is related to convex hulls through the epigraph, the set of points on or above a graph.

convex_hull.label: convex hull
convex_hull.preview: The convex hull of a set is the smallest convex set containing it, equivalently all finite weighted averages of its points with nonnegative weights summing to one.
convex_hull.card: For three non-collinear points in the plane, the convex hull is the filled triangle, including its edges and interior. For two points it is their line segment. It fills all straight mixtures between the original points.
convex_hull.rule: A set is convex when the segment between any two of its points remains inside. The convex hull contains points, not merely the polygonal boundary; repeated or interior generating points do not change it.
convex_hull.deep: In the polynomial paper, a point is located relative to the convex hull of several partial sums. That geometric containment encodes every possible convex combination of those sums and gives stronger information than membership in their union.

convexity.label: convexity
convexity.preview: A set is convex when it contains every line segment between its points; a function is convex when its graph lies at or below each chord joining two graph points.
convexity.card: A filled disc is a convex set because every segment between two points stays inside; a crescent need not be. The function \(f(x)=x^{2}\) is convex because its graph lies below every chord. These are related meanings: the epigraph lying on or above a convex function is a convex set.
convexity.rule: Identify the object. For a set, test whether \(tx+(1-t)y\) remains inside. For a function, test whether \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)\). Convex does not mean increasing, and strict convexity is stronger.
convexity.deep: For a set C, convexity requires \(tx+(1-t)y\) to belong to C whenever x and y do and \(0\le t\le 1\). For a real-valued function on a convex domain, it requires \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)\). A linear function is convex, so convex does not mean strictly curved. The polynomial papers use convex combinations and convex hulls to turn weighted relationships between points into geometric information.

coprime.label: coprime
coprime.preview: Two integers are coprime if their greatest common divisor is 1.
coprime.card: They have no positive common divisor other than 1, or equivalently no common prime factor. For example, 8 and 15 are coprime even though neither is prime.
coprime.rule: A fraction is in lowest terms when its numerator and denominator are coprime.
coprime.deep: In modular arithmetic, an integer has a multiplicative inverse modulo m exactly when it is coprime to m. This is why coprimality often appears among the hypotheses of statements about multiplicative order.

corpus.label: corpus
corpus.preview: A corpus is a collection of material studied or managed as a body of work.
corpus.card: The site uses the term for collections such as formal declarations, papers, or recorded examples. A particular revision or manifest can fix which items belong to the collection being described.
corpus.rule: Any reported count or check should identify the corpus and version it covers.
corpus.deep: A corpus can grow or change over time. Results about one snapshot should not silently be treated as results about every later version or every related repository.

countable_set.label: countable set
countable_set.preview: A set is countable when its elements can be injected into the natural numbers; finite sets are included.
countable_set.card: An infinite countable set can be listed in a sequence covering every element. A finite set is also countable, and the empty set qualifies. Countably infinite explicitly excludes these finite cases.
countable_set.rule: Countability bounds cardinality, not density, size of individual values, or existence of an efficient enumeration algorithm.
countable_set.deep: The #257 divisor-cover discussion permits finite or countable families of finite covering sets. This permits an indexed sum over the cover without asserting that the covered support itself is finite or that an optimal cover has been computed.

counterexample.label: counterexample
counterexample.preview: A counterexample is a case that satisfies a claim's assumptions but makes its conclusion false.
counterexample.card: One counterexample disproves a universal statement. For instance, 2 is a counterexample to “every prime number is odd”, because it is prime and even.
counterexample.rule: An example outside the assumptions does not refute the statement.
counterexample.deep: Counterexamples in the working records may target an attempted lemma or method rather than the original open problem. Naming the exact statement they refute preserves that distinction and explains what a revised approach must avoid.

coverage.label: coverage
coverage.preview: Coverage is the measured portion of a declared population, requirement set, behavior space, or source surface that has been examined or represented.
coverage.card: The denominator and matching method determine what the number means. Test coverage can report executed statements or branches; corpus coverage can report linked records; proof coverage can report which stated obligations have formal evidence. None of these automatically establishes correctness of covered items.
coverage.rule: Ask what total set was declared, how membership and matches were determined, when measurement occurred, and which uncovered cases remain.
coverage.deep: Coverage converts a bounded inventory into a numerator, denominator, and method. High test coverage can coexist with weak assertions or missing behaviors. Complete proof coverage may mean every declared obligation has a proof while the specification itself omits an important requirement. Source or documentation coverage can be exact within a known catalogue yet silent about objects outside it. Comparisons are meaningful only when inventories and methods align. A useful receipt therefore preserves the authority for the denominator, exclusions, measurement version, and concrete uncovered set.

covering_map.label: covering map
covering_map.preview: A map whose target has neighbourhoods that lift to separate copies, each mapped homeomorphically onto that neighbourhood.
covering_map.card: A covering map is a continuous surjection with this evenly covered neighbourhood property. The real line covers the circle by \(t\mapsto \exp (it)\). The map \(z\mapsto z^{2}\) covers the punctured plane twice, but branches at zero.
covering_map.rule: A finite cover has finitely many sheets. Local invertibility alone does not establish a covering: the neighbourhood must work simultaneously for every preimage.
covering_map.deep: The #1041 paper removes the critical values attained in the chosen polynomial component. The remaining restriction is a covering. On its simply connected slit domain, each chosen root determines an inverse sheet. These topological prerequisites do not themselves bound the lifted path length.

credential.label: credential
credential.preview: A credential is evidence used to support a claim about identity, qualification, role, or authority.
credential.card: In computing, credentials include passwords, keys, tokens, and certificates used during authentication. In professional settings, credentials include degrees, licences, and recognised appointments.
credential.rule: Determine which claim a credential supports; holding it does not grant every permission or prove every relevant competence.
credential.deep: Technical credentials help a system check an account, service, or role: examples include passwords, signed certificates, and access tokens. Some are secret; a public certificate need not be. Institutional credentials instead record training, qualifications, or position. Plectis uses both senses. Neither possession of a credential nor a person’s qualifications replace checking the specific permission or research argument involved.

critic_posture.label: critic posture
critic_posture.preview: Critic posture is a deliberate way of examining an idea for weaknesses before relying on it.
critic_posture.card: Plectis uses it to ask concrete questions: whether an abstraction fits the evidence, whether a proposed route can be executed, and whether a necessary rule or check is missing.
critic_posture.rule: A useful criticism identifies the affected claim and the evidence that would resolve it.
critic_posture.deep: This turns an objection into work that can be assessed. The critic's role is to test the idea, while any resulting change still needs an owner and validation.

critical_point.label: critical point
critical_point.preview: A critical point of a differentiable real or complex function is an input where its derivative vanishes; in several real variables, all first partial derivatives vanish there.
critical_point.card: For a complex polynomial p, a critical point c satisfies \(p'(c) = 0\). For \(p(z) = z^{2} - 1\), the critical point is 0, whereas the roots are 1 and \(-1\). In several real variables, all first partial derivatives must vanish together.
critical_point.rule: A critical point is an input where the derivative vanishes; its image is a critical value. Neither need be a root, and distinct critical points can share one critical value.
critical_point.deep: Some elementary conventions also include points of nondifferentiability. The polynomial setting here is differentiable everywhere, and critical points matter because the Newton expression \(-p/p'\) is undefined there.

critical_value.label: critical value
critical_value.preview: A critical value is the output of a function at one of its critical points.
critical_value.card: For \(p(z) = z^{2} - 1\), the critical point 0 has critical value \(-1\). The point and value lie on different sides of the function: one is an input and the other is its image.
critical_value.rule: The modulus \(|p(c)|\) is the magnitude of a critical value, not the value itself.
critical_value.deep: The lemniscate arguments compare these magnitudes and directions to study how regions can meet. Distinct critical points can share a critical value, and different values can have the same magnitude.

css.label: CSS
css.preview: CSS is a language for describing how structured documents are presented.
css.card: CSS rules select parts of an HTML document and assign visual or layout properties such as colour, spacing, type, position, and responsive behaviour. The document remains HTML; CSS changes its presentation.
css.rule: CSS controls presentation, including layout and interaction cues such as visible keyboard focus.
css.deep: A browser combines the document tree with matching CSS rules to calculate its presentation. When rules compete, the cascade resolves their origin, importance, layer, specificity, and order; some properties are inherited from a parent. Plectis shares a stylesheet across generated pages and uses it for screen layouts, print output, readable contrast, and reduced-motion preferences.

curve_parametrisation.label: curve parametrisation
curve_parametrisation.preview: A function from a parameter interval into a space whose image traces a curve.
curve_parametrisation.card: The map \(t \mapsto (\cos t,\sin t)\), for \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), traces the unit circle once counterclockwise. A parametrisation specifies a position for every parameter value, and a differentiable parametrisation also determines direction and speed.
curve_parametrisation.rule: Separate the parametrised map from its image: different parametrisations can trace the same geometric curve, with different speeds or orientations.
curve_parametrisation.deep: A parametrisation of a curve is a map gamma from an interval into a space, usually Euclidean or complex space. Its image is the geometric set traced by gamma. When gamma is differentiable, gamma'(t) gives velocity; if that derivative never vanishes, the parametrisation is regular. Replacing t by a suitable increasing function changes speed without changing orientation or image, while a decreasing replacement reverses orientation. Curve length is unchanged by sufficiently regular one-to-one reparametrisation, but a map that retraces part of the curve can count that part more than once.

cyclotomic_polynomial.label: cyclotomic polynomial
cyclotomic_polynomial.preview: The nth cyclotomic polynomial is the monic integer polynomial whose roots are exactly the primitive nth roots of unity.
cyclotomic_polynomial.card: \(\Phi _{1}(x)=x-1\), \(\Phi _{2}(x)=x+1\), and \(\Phi _{4}(x)=x^{2}+1\) because \(\pm i\) are the primitive fourth roots. The factorization \(x^{n}-1=\prod _{d\mid n} \Phi _d(x)\) organizes all roots of unity by exact order.
cyclotomic_polynomial.rule: A primitive nth root has exact multiplicative order n. Cyclotomic polynomials are irreducible over the rationals, but “cyclotomic factor” in a calculation may mean one copy appearing inside a larger product.
cyclotomic_polynomial.deep: The paper cancels cyclotomic factors before estimating rational-base denominators. The factorization isolates predictable roots-of-unity divisibility, allowing the remaining numerator and denominator growth to be measured more sharply.

field.label: data field
field.preview: A data field is a named part of a structured record that holds a value with an expected meaning and form.
field.card: A result record might have fields for its status, timestamp, and source revision. A schema states which fields are required, what values they accept, and how absence or an empty value is interpreted. This computing meaning differs from an algebraic field or a field of study.
field.rule: A field name identifies its role within a record or schema; the same name in another schema can have a different meaning.
field.deep: Fields let programs locate specific information without inferring it from free text. Their values can be numbers, strings, lists, nested records, or other allowed data. A missing field, an explicit null value, and an empty string may express different states. The site uses fields to preserve exact identifiers and checking results across generated views. Merely recording a value does not show that it is accurate, current, or supported by evidence; those properties require their own checks.

database.label: database
database.preview: A database is an organized collection of data maintained so it can be accessed, queried, and updated.
database.card: A relational database organizes records in tables; document, graph, and key-value databases use other models. A database management system provides the software for storing, querying, and changing those records. Everyday computing prose often uses “database” for both the data and that running service.
database.rule: Database behavior is defined by its data model, schema, query and update semantics, consistency, transactions, indexes, access controls, replication, and backup policy.
database.deep: A database is the organized data, managed through software often called a database management system; a dataset groups records for a particular analysis or other purpose. A query result may reflect one transaction snapshot, a replica lag, cached values, permissions, or later updates. Constraints can prevent some invalid states but cannot establish that recorded facts are true. Replication improves availability yet introduces consistency choices. Reliable interpretation names the database instance or export, schema version, query, time, and whether the result came from live, cached, replicated, or archived state.

dataset.label: dataset
dataset.preview: A dataset is an organized collection of observations or records intended to be considered together.
dataset.card: A table of measurements, labelled images, survey responses, documents, or synthetic examples can each be a dataset. Its meaning depends on what was collected, from whom, when, and how.
dataset.rule: A dataset is characterized by its population, sampling and collection process, fields, units, labels, exclusions, version, and known transformations.
dataset.deep: Datasets do not speak independently of their construction. Missing groups, duplicated records, measurement error, label ambiguity, selection bias, data leakage, later corrections, and incompatible versions can change an analysis. A dataset may be representative for one question and unsuitable for another. Synthetic data reflects assumptions of its generator rather than direct observation. Train, validation, and test partitions are roles assigned to records, not different kinds of evidence. Reproducible conclusions identify the exact version and preprocessing used.

decidability.label: decidability
decidability.preview: A decision problem is decidable when an algorithm always terminates with the correct yes-or-no answer.
decidability.card: In Lean, Decidable P is a type containing either a proof of P or a proof of its negation. A computational instance can be evaluated by decide, connecting executable decisions to logically justified outcomes.
decidability.rule: Classical reasoning can supply a noncomputable Decidable instance. Its existence in the logic is not an executable decision algorithm for an arbitrary problem.
decidability.deep: Finite certificate checks use decidable arithmetic tests. The distinction matters when a proof has a classical instance available but evaluation cannot reduce it: type-level availability and practical computation are different requirements.

declaration.label: declaration
declaration.preview: A declaration introduces a named item in a programming or proof language, such as a definition, theorem, or structure.
declaration.card: In Lean, the declaration's source states its type and, where applicable, its value or proof. Later declarations can use that name, creating a chain of dependencies.
declaration.rule: A declaration count combines different kinds of items and is not a count of distinct mathematical discoveries.
declaration.deep: To assess a theorem, inspect its exact statement, proof dependencies, and assumptions. Supporting definitions and routine lemmas may be necessary without being separate research contributions.

integral.label: definite integral
integral.preview: A definite integral accumulates a function’s values over a specified region using a rule for measuring that region.
integral.card: For example, integrating 2x from 0 to 1 gives 1, the area under that graph over the interval. Integrals can also describe mass, averages, energy, and curve length. Signed values can cancel, so an integral need not equal the total unsigned area.
integral.rule: Check the integration domain, variable, and notion of integration; finite Riemann integration and Lebesgue integration agree for continuous functions on compact intervals but have different general scope.
integral.deep: A definite integral combines the values of a function over a specified domain. The Riemann integral is built from limits of weighted sums over finer partitions and is well suited to bounded functions on finite intervals. The Lebesgue integral groups values using a measure and handles wider classes of functions and limit operations. Continuous functions on a closed bounded interval are integrable in both senses with the same value. An improper integral is a limit used for an unbounded domain or singular integrand, so convergence must be proved rather than assumed.

definitional_equality.label: definitional equality
definitional_equality.preview: Definitional equality is equality recognized by a formal system's built-in computation and conversion rules.
definitional_equality.card: Two expressions can be recognized as the same after evaluating a function or unfolding a definition. For example, a numerical expression such as \(2+3\) can reduce to 5 without a separate theorem asserting their equality.
definitional_equality.rule: Do not assume every mathematically equal expression is definitionally equal. A more substantial identity may require a propositional equality proof.
definitional_equality.deep: Lean uses this relation when matching a term's type to an expected type. The local hypothesis-extraction tool promises to recover the actual binder type, avoiding a transcription that might merely look equivalent or introduce different definitions.

polynomial_degree.label: degree of a polynomial
polynomial_degree.preview: The degree of a nonzero polynomial is the highest exponent with a nonzero coefficient.
polynomial_degree.card: For example, \(3z^{4} + 2z - 1\) has degree 4, while a nonzero constant has degree 0. Over the complex numbers, a degree-n polynomial has n roots counted with multiplicity.
polynomial_degree.rule: The zero polynomial needs a separate degree convention because it has no nonzero coefficient.
polynomial_degree.deep: Degree constrains possible algebraic behaviour without determining the locations or distinctness of roots. The lemniscate papers use degree in quantitative estimates and sometimes prove results only for particular degree ranges.

demo_take.label: Demo Take
demo_take.preview: Demo Take is the system's recording tool for capturing a demonstration and its accompanying material.
demo_take.card: It brings screen recording, transcript capture, and still frames into one workflow. The resulting files can then support a prepared demonstration without reconstructing the session from separate recordings.
demo_take.rule: A recorded demonstration shows the particular run and material that were captured.
demo_take.deep: It is useful for explanation and review, while repeatability still depends on the source, inputs, environment, and commands behind what appears on screen.

denominator.label: denominator
denominator.preview: The denominator is the divisor in a fraction: the b in \(a/b\), where b is nonzero.
denominator.card: In \(3/4\), the denominator is 4. For a positive fraction interpreted as equal-sized parts, it specifies that the whole has been divided into four parts.
denominator.rule: Cancelling a common factor changes the written denominator without changing the fraction's value.
denominator.deep: Number-theory arguments often require the denominator in lowest terms. For example, whether a fraction terminates in a chosen numeral base depends on the prime factors of that reduced denominator.

dense_subset.label: dense subset
dense_subset.preview: A subset whose closure is the whole surrounding space.
dense_subset.card: The rational numbers are dense in the real line: every open interval, however short, contains a rational. They still omit most real numbers, so dense does not mean equal to the surrounding space or large by counting.
dense_subset.rule: A subset is dense when its closure is the whole space, equivalently when every nonempty open region meets it. Density depends on the surrounding topology; changing the space can change the verdict.
dense_subset.deep: In the running-LCM paper, an irrational rotation has a dense orbit, allowing points arbitrarily close to any target location on the circle. Topological density concerns proximity, while asymptotic density concerns proportions of integers; any connection requires specifying the set and surrounding space.

dependency.label: dependency
dependency.preview: A dependency is an object, service, fact, or earlier result that another component or conclusion requires.
dependency.card: A software component may depend on a library, file, service, or build step; an argument may depend on a premise or earlier theorem. The dependency identifies a necessary input, not merely a related object.
dependency.rule: A dependency relation has a direction: the dependent item requires the upstream item, and a change or failure upstream can require downstream rebuilding, rechecking, or withdrawal.
dependency.deep: Dependencies connect work into a directed structure. In software, a package can require a particular library version, a generated file can require its source, and a service can require another service to answer. In reasoning, a conclusion depends on its premises and supporting results. Required dependencies prevent the dependent route from working when absent; optional dependencies affect only features that use them. Because changes can propagate downstream, dependency records often include versions, identities, and compatibility conditions. Cycles require special handling because no member can be prepared independently of the others.

dependent_type.label: dependent type
dependent_type.preview: A dependent type is a type whose form can depend on a value, not only on another type.
dependent_type.card: For example, Fin n is the type of natural numbers below n, so changing n changes the available values. A function can likewise return a value whose type depends on its input, expressing constraints directly in its signature.
dependent_type.rule: Read the value parameter as part of the type. An object of Fin 3 cannot simply be used as an object of Fin 2 without the required justification.
dependent_type.deep: The #243 Lean source uses functions indexed by Fin k to represent finite families. Their index bounds are tracked by types, allowing proofs about every member while preventing indices outside the declared family.

deployment.label: deployment
deployment.preview: Deployment places a software version or configuration into an environment where it can run or serve users.
deployment.card: Building and testing an application creates candidate artifacts; deploying selects one and installs or activates it in development, staging, production, or another target environment.
deployment.rule: Deployment status identifies the artifact, target environment, configuration, rollout state, and whether traffic or users actually reach it.
deployment.deep: Deployment is distinct from committing source, merging a pull request, publishing a release, and proving that the service works correctly. A rollout may be partial, staged, paused, rolled back, or active only for selected users. Database migrations, secrets, feature flags, infrastructure, and cached assets can make two deployments of the same code behave differently.
