Forecast quality also depends on question selection, base rates, missing outcomes, revisions, and whether forecasters could observe information that later evaluators treat as unavailable.

formal.label: formal
formal.preview: Formal means expressed within explicitly specified rules; in mathematics, it usually concerns a precise logical language and inference system.
formal.card: A formal statement identifies its objects and conditions in that language. A formal proof follows the system's rules to derive a conclusion from assumptions.
formal.rule: Precision of form does not ensure that the statement expresses the intended question.
formal.deep: The papers connect formal statements with ordinary mathematical explanations so readers can examine both the validity of the derivation and whether the encoded result matches the claim being made.

formal_mathematics.label: formal mathematics
formal_mathematics.preview: Formal mathematics expresses definitions, statements, and proofs in a language governed by explicit logical rules.
formal_mathematics.card: Proof assistants such as Lean can check the resulting derivations mechanically. Authors may use tactics and automation to construct proofs, while the accepted proof must satisfy the system's checking rules.
formal_mathematics.rule: The exact statement and assumptions determine what has been established.
formal_mathematics.deep: Formal checking reduces dependence on unchecked inference steps. It leaves separate work in choosing the right formulation, explaining the ideas, assessing significance, and ensuring that the formal statement corresponds to the intended mathematics.

formal_power_series.label: formal power series
formal_power_series.preview: A formal power series is an infinite coefficient sequence written as powers of a symbol, with arithmetic defined coefficient by coefficient.
formal_power_series.card: Over a coefficient ring, \(\sum a_{n}z^{n}\) is an algebraic object. Addition is termwise, and each coefficient of a product is a finite sum \(\sum _{k=0}^{n}a_{k}b_{n-k}\).
formal_power_series.rule: Formal series do not require numerical convergence. Substitution into an infinite series needs its own algebraic condition, such as a substituted series with zero constant term.
formal_power_series.deep: The #1049 moment sums define formal series because only finitely many summands contribute to each coefficient. Its determinant proof can truncate modulo a fixed power before taking limits. The manuscript separately proves convergence when q is a real number between zero and one.

formal_proof.label: formal proof
formal_proof.preview: A formal proof is a derivation expressed in a logical system whose rules make each step precisely checkable.
formal_proof.card: In Lean, a proposition is represented by a type and its proof by a term of that type. A term can be written directly or constructed by tactics; its derivation depends on definitions, hypotheses, and axioms.
formal_proof.rule: Distinguish a formal proof from a formalised statement with an unfinished proof. Also distinguish being formally expressible from having passed a recorded checker run.
formal_proof.deep: A checked conditional theorem establishes its conclusion under its hypotheses. Applying it requires those hypotheses and a formal statement matching the intended claim. Paper-to-source links expose that comparison but do not settle it automatically.

formal_verification.label: formal verification
formal_verification.preview: Formal verification uses logic and mathematical models to establish a stated property against a precise specification.
formal_verification.card: In software or hardware, the property might concern an implementation model or all reachable states. In the mathematical work here, Lean checks whether a proof term establishes its formal theorem. These are different applications of mathematical checking.
formal_verification.rule: Identify the specification, model, assumptions, and trusted checking method before interpreting the guarantee. Passing sample tests supports a different kind of conclusion.
formal_verification.deep: Exact verification can concern an incomplete model or a specification missing the intended question. Reviewing that correspondence remains necessary. Locally, the linked declaration fixes what Lean checked, while the paper explains why that statement addresses the research problem.

formalisation.label: formalisation
formalisation.preview: Formalisation translates definitions, statements, or arguments into a language with explicit logical rules.
formalisation.card: Mathematical formalisation chooses representations, states hypotheses and quantifiers, and expresses conclusions precisely. The Lean developments here also connect their declarations to statements discussed in accompanying papers.
formalisation.rule: Report the stage reached: formal definitions, an encoded statement, a finished proof, and an inspected correspondence with the informal claim are distinct achievements.
formalisation.deep: Representation choices can uncover hidden assumptions or change a theorem's formulation. Software specifications can likewise be formalised before anyone proves that an implementation satisfies them. Pinned locators let readers inspect this translation at a fixed source revision.

forward_invariant_set.label: forward-invariant set
forward_invariant_set.preview: A set is forward invariant when trajectories starting in it remain there for as long as their forward evolution is defined.
forward_invariant_set.card: For the differential equation \(x'=-x\), every solution starting in \([-1,1]\) moves toward zero and remains in that interval. Hence \([-1,1]\) is forward invariant, although reversing time can drive points outward.
forward_invariant_set.rule: Forward invariance means a trajectory stays in the set for every later time for which its evolution is defined. It depends on the chosen dynamics and makes no promise about backward motion or continuation through singular points.
forward_invariant_set.deep: Along regular Newton trajectories, the polynomial modulus decreases, so a polynomial sublevel set is preserved. This alone does not justify extending a trajectory through a critical point where the vector field -f/f′ is undefined.

fraction.label: fraction
fraction.preview: A fraction writes a quotient as \(a/b\); for a rational number, a and b are integers and b is nonzero.
fraction.card: The numerator a is divided by the denominator b. Different fractions can represent the same number: \(2/4\) and \(1/2\) are equal because the common factor 2 can be cancelled.
fraction.rule: “In lowest terms” means that numerator and denominator are coprime.
fraction.deep: An expression written as a quotient is not necessarily a rational number if its numerator or denominator is non-integer. For example, \(\sqrt 2/1\) is still irrational.

fractional_part.label: fractional part
fractional_part.preview: For a real number x, its fractional part is x minus the greatest integer at most x, so it lies in \([0,1)\).
fractional_part.card: For example, 3.7 has fractional part 0.7, while -1.2 has fractional part 0.8 because the floor is -2. Fractional parts record position modulo one and are central when a sequence is studied around the unit circle.
fractional_part.rule: The fractional part \(\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\) is zero exactly when x is an integer. Negative inputs still give a value in \([0,1)\), unlike a signed decimal tail produced by truncation.
fractional_part.deep: Here the paper studies fractional parts of factorially scaled numbers. Saying they vanish eventually means every sufficiently late scaled value is an integer. Bounds on fractional parts can force arithmetic conclusions even without proving that those parts are evenly spread.

freshness.label: freshness
freshness.preview: Freshness describes whether stored information still reflects the source or state it is meant to represent.
freshness.card: A generated page, cached result, or copied file may have been accurate when created and become outdated after its source changes. Plectis uses source versions and refresh rules to assess that relationship.
freshness.rule: A recent timestamp alone does not show that the right source was read.
freshness.deep: A useful freshness record identifies the source, the version examined, and the condition that requires another check. Different kinds of information can have very different refresh needs.

frobenius_automorphism.label: Frobenius automorphism
frobenius_automorphism.preview: In characteristic p, Frobenius sends x to \(x^p\); it is an automorphism when this power map is onto, as it always is for a finite field.
frobenius_automorphism.card: In \(F_{4}\), the map \(x\mapsto x^{2}\) fixes 0 and 1 and swaps the two other elements, so it is a nontrivial automorphism. More generally, if \(q=p^{n}\), the p-power Frobenius generates the cyclic Galois group \(Gal(F_q/F_p)\) and has order n.
frobenius_automorphism.rule: On every field of characteristic p the p-power map is injective, but it need not be surjective on an infinite imperfect field. On \(F_q\) itself, \(x\mapsto x^q\) is the identity. On \(F_{q^m}\) over \(F_q\), the q-power map is an automorphism of order m and generates \(Gal(F_{q^m}/F_q)\).
frobenius_automorphism.deep: The binomial identity \((x+y)^p=x^p+y^p\) in characteristic p makes Frobenius a field endomorphism. In characteristic p, a field is perfect precisely when this map is surjective and hence an automorphism; all finite fields are perfect because an injective self-map of a finite set is surjective. In number-field reduction, a Frobenius element at P above p acts on the upstairs residue field \(\kappa (P)\) by \(x\mapsto x^q\), where \(q=|\kappa (p)|\) is the base residue-field size. That action is a field Frobenius automorphism, but the Frobenius element also records how it lifts into the number-field Galois group.

frobenius_element.label: Frobenius element
frobenius_element.preview: A Frobenius element is a field symmetry attached to an unramified prime in a finite Galois extension of number fields; it describes a power map after reduction modulo a chosen prime above it.
frobenius_element.card: In a number-field extension, reducing algebraic integers modulo a prime gives a finite field. Raising to the qth power is identity on the base residue field, and its lift records how that prime splits upstairs.
frobenius_element.rule: The exponent q is the cardinality of the base residue field \(\kappa (p)\), not the usually larger upstairs field \(\kappa (P)\). Choosing P determines an element of the decomposition group; changing P conjugates it, so a base prime canonically determines only a conjugacy class.
frobenius_element.deep: Let P lie above an unramified base prime p and put \(q=|\kappa (p)|\). Under the arithmetic-Frobenius convention, the element \(\sigma _P\) satisfies \(\sigma_P(x)\equiv x^q\pmod P\) on integral elements and acts by the q-power map on \(\kappa (P)\). Choosing another prime above p conjugates \(\sigma _P\), so p canonically determines a conjugacy class. Some geometry texts call the inverse element geometric Frobenius; the convention must be stated.

front_end.label: frontend
front_end.preview: A front end is the part of a software system through which a user interacts with it.
front_end.card: It may present screens, controls, and views over data supplied by a back end. In the site's “Why” walkthrough, the term refers to the larger system's operator interface shown in the videos.
front_end.rule: That demonstrated interface has a different scope from the public website you are reading.
front_end.deep: Both can present views of related source objects. Their appearance alone does not establish which actions or private data are available through each interface.

frontier.label: frontier
frontier.preview: Here, the mathematical frontier is the stated boundary between established results and unresolved questions for a problem.
frontier.card: A useful account identifies the strongest relevant results, the assumptions still needed, and the approaches that have been ruled out. It helps another researcher choose a next question without reconstructing all earlier work.
frontier.rule: A convenient intermediate target is not automatically equivalent to the original problem.
frontier.deep: Moving the frontier requires a meaningful mathematical change, such as removing a hypothesis or proving a new obstruction. More declarations or a new presentation alone do not show that change.

function.label: function
function.preview: A mathematical function assigns one output to each allowed input; a software function is a callable piece of code.
function.card: Mathematically, a function specifies a domain, a codomain, and an assignment: \(f(n) = n^{2}\) sends each integer to its square. A software function runs instructions when called and may return a value, change state, report an error, or fail to terminate.
function.rule: Different mathematical inputs may have the same output, but each input in the domain has exactly one output.
function.deep: Software behaviour can depend on arguments and surrounding state. Treating code as an implementation of a mathematical function requires specifying those inputs and checking the intended behaviour. A shared name does not establish that correspondence.

function_composition.label: function composition
function_composition.preview: Function composition applies one function to the output of another.
function_composition.card: The notation \(g \circ f\) means “first f, then g,” so \((g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))\). If \(f(x) = x+1\) and \(g(x) = 2x\), then \(g \circ f\) gives \(2x+2\), while \(f \circ g\) gives \(2x+1\).
function_composition.rule: The first function's outputs must lie in the second function's domain, and the order generally matters.
function_composition.deep: The same idea connects stages of a software pipeline, but effects, errors, and state may add conditions beyond a mathematical function's domain. A valid sequence of individually defined operations still needs compatible inputs and outputs at each connection.

function_domain.label: function domain
function_domain.preview: The domain of a function is the set of inputs on which that function is defined.
function_domain.card: For \(f(x) = 1/x\) over the real numbers, zero must be excluded from the domain. The formula alone does not determine every permitted input: the same expression can be considered on integers, real numbers, or complex numbers with different restrictions.
function_domain.rule: Statements about every input of a function quantify over its declared domain.
function_domain.deep: Changing the domain changes the mathematical function and can change properties such as injectivity or continuity. In software, a function's accepted arguments and preconditions play a related role; a website domain is a different meaning of the word.

galois_closure.label: Galois closure
galois_closure.preview: The Galois closure of a finite separable field extension is the smallest Galois extension containing it, inside a chosen algebraic closure.
galois_closure.card: It adjoins all conjugate copies of the original extension so its algebraic symmetries act within one field. For a number field, separability holds automatically.
galois_closure.rule: The closure can be larger than the original extension. Its defining minimality is taken inside the chosen algebraic closure; it does not mean that every field extension is already Galois.
galois_closure.deep: In #243, a hypothetical nonsquare \(\alpha ^{2}-1\) gives \(K(\beta )\) with \(\beta ^{2}=\alpha ^{2}-1\). The proof takes its Galois closure over \(\mathbb{Q}\) so the sign-changing automorphism can be expressed through Frobenius behavior at suitable primes. This produces the contradiction with the square condition in the prime field.

galois_extension.label: Galois extension
galois_extension.preview: A Galois extension \(L/K\) is an algebraic field extension that is normal, so it contains every conjugate root required by its equations over K, and separable, so those roots are distinct.
galois_extension.card: For example, \(Q(i)/Q\) is Galois: the polynomial \(x^{2}+1\) splits into the two distinct roots i and \(-i\) inside \(Q(i)\). Its automorphisms fixing Q are the identity and complex conjugation. By contrast, \(Q(\sqrt[3] 2)/Q\) omits the two nonreal conjugates of \(\sqrt[3] 2\), so it is not normal and therefore not Galois.
galois_extension.rule: Galois is relative to a named base field K. In characteristic zero, algebraic extensions are separable, but normality still must be checked. The equality \(|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)|=[L:K]\) characterizes the Galois property only for finite extensions; infinite Galois groups also carry a natural topology.
galois_extension.deep: Normality says that if an irreducible polynomial over K has one root in L, then all of its roots lie in L. Separability says those roots are distinct rather than repeated. Together these conditions make the K-fixing automorphisms of L rich enough to form the Galois group \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\), which permutes conjugate roots while preserving every arithmetic relation over K. The paper places several algebraic quantities inside one finite Galois extension so a chosen automorphism can later be realized as Frobenius behavior at suitable primes.

galois_group.label: Galois group
galois_group.preview: The Galois group \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\) is the group of field automorphisms of L that fix every element of K.
galois_group.card: For \(Q(i)/Q\) the group has two elements: the identity and complex conjugation. Composition is the group operation. For a finite Galois extension, the group size equals the extension degree.
galois_group.rule: The base field is part of the notation and changes the group. Automorphisms must preserve addition and multiplication and fix K pointwise; arbitrary permutations of elements or roots do not qualify.
galois_group.deep: The paper selects an automorphism with prescribed action on algebraic quantities, then uses Chebotarev to realize its conjugacy class as Frobenius behavior at infinitely many primes.

gate.label: gate
gate.preview: A gate is a checkpoint that permits an action only when specified conditions are satisfied.
gate.card: Plectis uses gates before changes or publication that require evidence, such as a successful check or a matching source version. The gate records which requirement determined its decision.
gate.rule: A gate's pass means that its particular conditions were met.
gate.deep: It cannot establish requirements that it never examines. A blocked gate can indicate missing evidence, a failing check, or an unavailable dependency, and those cases may require different next steps.

gaussian_binomial_coefficient.label: Gaussian binomial coefficient
gaussian_binomial_coefficient.preview: A Gaussian binomial coefficient is the q-analogue of an ordinary binomial coefficient, written [n choose k]_q and defined by a product of q-power differences.
gaussian_binomial_coefficient.card: For prime-power q, [n choose k]_q counts the k-dimensional subspaces of an n-dimensional vector space over the finite field with q elements. As a function of q it is a polynomial with nonnegative integer coefficients.
gaussian_binomial_coefficient.rule: Despite the name, it is unrelated to the Gaussian probability distribution. At \(q=1\) its polynomial limit is the ordinary binomial coefficient. Different texts use q, X, or another indeterminate.
gaussian_binomial_coefficient.deep: The paper treats the Gaussian binomial as a polynomial in X and uses its degree and coefficient positivity inside a cyclotomic calculation.

generalise_up_propagate.label: generalise-up-propagate
generalise_up_propagate.preview: Generalise-up-propagate means turning a supported local lesson into guidance that future relevant work will actually encounter.
generalise_up_propagate.card: Plectis first identifies what the case teaches and how broadly the lesson applies. It then places the refinement in an existing rule, skill, standard, or other source used by the affected workflow.
generalise_up_propagate.rule: A single example should not become a universal rule without an argument for that scope.
generalise_up_propagate.deep: The change should preserve the source case and its limits. Updating the shared owner can prevent repeated mistakes more effectively than adding another isolated note.

generating_function.label: generating function
generating_function.preview: A generating function encodes a sequence as coefficients of a power series; the ordinary version is \(A(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_{n}z^{n}\).
generating_function.card: The coefficient of \(z^{n}\) recovers \(a_{n}\). Products encode additive convolutions of sequences, while other series operations can translate recurrences into functional identities.
generating_function.rule: The series may be formal or analytic. Evaluating it at a number requires convergence; a formal coefficient identity alone supplies no convergence claim. Exponential generating functions instead use \(a_{n}z^{n}/n!\).
generating_function.deep: The #1049 weight generating function packages all moment weights into one series in w and factors it into two product terms. The paper establishes both the formal coefficient identity and analytic convergence in the stated disc. Totient and divisor generating series also appear in #249 and its related reading surfaces.

geodesic.label: geodesic
geodesic.preview: A curve that is locally straight according to the geometry of its surrounding space.
geodesic.card: On a flat torus, geodesics lift to straight lines in Euclidean space. A line whose direction is proportional to a nonzero lattice vector gives a closed geodesic; an irrational direction on a two-dimensional torus instead gives a dense nonclosed line.
geodesic.rule: A geodesic need not be the globally shortest route between its endpoints. A segment can wind around a torus before reaching an endpoint that is nearby by another route.
geodesic.deep: The #269 walls are closed geodesics because they are defined by integer linear equations modulo 1. Each wall family can have several components when its integer normal vector has a common factor. The proof counts their intersections and faces; it does not use a shortest-path claim.

geometric_majorant.label: geometric majorant
geometric_majorant.preview: A geometric majorant bounds terms or their magnitudes by a geometric sequence with a fixed ratio.
geometric_majorant.card: If \(|a_{N+k}|\le Cr^k\) for \(k \ge 0\) and \(0 \le r < 1\), the entire tail's absolute sum is at most \(C/(1 - r)\). This turns infinitely many bounds into a usable finite estimate.
geometric_majorant.rule: The same ratio and initial bound must work throughout the claimed tail.
geometric_majorant.deep: Rapidly growing factorial denominators can supply such comparisons. The starting index matters because a ratio bound may fail for early terms even when it holds for all later ones.

geometric_series.label: geometric series
geometric_series.preview: A geometric series adds terms formed by repeatedly multiplying an initial value by a fixed number.
geometric_series.card: Its terms are a, ar, \(ar^{2}\), and so on, where a is the initial value and r is the common multiplier. When \(|r| < 1\), the infinite sum is \(a/(1-r)\); for example, \(1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + \ldots = 2\).
geometric_series.rule: For a nonzero initial value, the infinite sum converges exactly when \(|r| < 1\). With initial value zero, every term and the sum are zero.
geometric_series.deep: Geometric series and their differentiated forms give explicit bounds for analytic tails and their first and second derivatives in the lemniscate paper.

git.label: Git
git.preview: Git is a version-control system that records snapshots of files and the history connecting them.
git.card: A commit identifies a stored snapshot, its parent history, and a message. Branches name lines of development, and differences between commits show how tracked content changed.
git.rule: Uncommitted edits are part of a working copy, not yet part of a recorded commit.
git.deep: The repositories use Git revisions to identify the source behind a paper, check, or generated page. Sharing a revision lets another person obtain the same tracked content rather than an unspecified current copy.

git_branch.label: Git branch
git_branch.preview: A Git branch is a movable name that points to a commit and normally advances along one line of repository history.
git_branch.card: Creating a branch gives new commits a separate history label so work can diverge and later be compared or merged. The branch itself is a reference, not a copied directory or complete second repository.
git_branch.rule: Git branch identity consists of a movable reference and its commit history; working directories and worktrees are separate checkouts that may point at branches or detached commits.
git_branch.deep: The word branch also names a decision path, a tree limb, or an organizational division, but a Git branch has precise reference semantics. It points to one commit and moves when new commits are added or the reference is explicitly changed. Several branches can point to the same commit, and deleting a branch name does not immediately erase reachable commits. Merging combines histories according to Git’s rules; it does not prove semantic compatibility. A worktree may provide separate files, but that checkout is not the branch itself.

github.label: GitHub
github.preview: GitHub is a service for hosting Git repositories and tools for collaboration around them.
github.card: It provides interfaces for browsing files and history, discussing issues, reviewing changes, and publishing releases. GitHub Pages can serve static websites from a repository's published content.
github.rule: Git is the version-control system; GitHub is one service that hosts repositories using it.
github.deep: The links on this site lead to public source and related artifacts. A hosted file's presence establishes availability, while its correctness and evidence status must be assessed from the work itself.

govern.label: govern
govern.preview: To govern a process is to define how its decisions are made, authorised, and checked.
govern.card: In Plectis, this includes assigning source authority, setting rules for changes, and specifying evidence required before an action proceeds. The relevant rule should be discoverable where the action is performed.
govern.rule: A written rule and an enforced rule are different states of implementation.
govern.deep: To assess a governed process, inspect both its stated contract and the mechanism applying it. Recorded decisions can then show whether the rule had the intended effect in a particular case.

gradient.label: gradient
gradient.preview: For a differentiable real-valued function in Euclidean coordinates, the gradient is the vector of its first partial derivatives.
gradient.card: For \(u(x,y) = x^{2}+y^{2}\), the gradient is \((2x,2y)\). Where it is nonzero, its direction gives the steepest local increase per unit distance; the opposite direction gives the steepest decrease. At a zero gradient there is no such preferred first-order direction.
gradient.rule: On more general geometric spaces, the gradient depends on the chosen metric, which specifies how directions and lengths are compared.
gradient.deep: The Newton-flow discussion relates trajectories to gradients of real-valued quantities formed from a complex polynomial, such as \(|p|^{2}\). A gradient of such a quantity is different from the polynomial’s complex derivative.

gram_matrix.label: Gram matrix
gram_matrix.preview: The Gram matrix of vectors \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{n}\) has entries \(G_{ij}=\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\), recording every pairwise inner product.
gram_matrix.card: For two real vectors, the matrix contains their squared lengths on the diagonal and their dot product off the diagonal. Its determinant is the squared area of their spanned parallelogram.
gram_matrix.rule: Every Gram matrix is positive semidefinite. It is positive definite exactly when the listed vectors are linearly independent. The result depends on the chosen inner product and ordered family, although definiteness does not depend on reordering.
gram_matrix.deep: The paper forms a Gram matrix from finitely many analytic atoms. Positive definiteness certifies that no nontrivial linear combination of those atoms has zero norm, hence that the finite family is linearly independent.

graph.label: graph
graph.preview: A graph can mean vertices joined by edges, or the set of input–output pairs of a function.
graph.card: A dependency graph represents objects as vertices, also called nodes, and their relationships as edges. A function’s graph instead consists of pairs \((x,f(x))\); plotting those pairs draws a curve or surface when the setting permits it. The surrounding argument determines which meaning applies.
graph.rule: An abstract graph need not be drawn, connected, or contain any edges. A function graph need not be a continuous curve.
graph.deep: The website’s content graph uses the vertex-and-edge sense: pages, statements, and terms are objects connected by named relationships. A directed edge records an ordered relation, such as one statement depending on another. Drawing two vertices close together does not add an edge. In analysis, the graph of \(f(x)=x^{2}\) is the set of pairs \((x,x^{2})\), a different construction from this relationship network. Neither meaning makes the display’s visual appearance a substitute for its underlying definition.

edge.label: graph edge
edge.preview: A graph edge connects vertices according to the graph’s declared relation.
edge.card: In a dependency graph, an arrow from A to B might mean that A depends on B. An undirected edge has no preferred direction. Graph conventions determine whether a vertex can connect to itself and whether several edges can share the same endpoints.
edge.rule: The endpoints, direction, and relation type determine what an edge asserts; a connection alone does not establish causation or logical implication.
edge.deep: The site’s content graph distinguishes relations such as “defined in”, “depends on”, and “generated from”. Following an edge is meaningful only with its relation type: a citation is not automatically a proof dependency. Some mathematical graphs allow loops or multiple edges and others exclude them, so those conventions belong to the graph’s definition. An edge can exist without being drawn as a visible line, and two displayed nodes need not be connected merely because they are close together.

node.label: graph node
node.preview: A graph node, also called a vertex, is one of the objects that a graph’s edges can connect.
node.card: A node can represent a page, person, theorem, machine, or other object. Its identity makes it distinguishable within the graph; labels and other attributes are additional data. A node may have no incident edges and still belong to the graph.
node.rule: What a node represents comes from the graph’s definition; a node’s visual position does not by itself give its relationships.
node.deep: The website uses node identifiers to connect statements, proof declarations, and public pages across several views. One mathematical object can have more than one representation when the graph intentionally distinguishes versions or roles, but those distinctions must be explicit. A diagram is one way to display the structure rather than the structure’s definition. In other computing contexts, a network node can be a participating device or process; the graph interpretation depends on the network being modelled.

greatest_common_divisor.label: greatest common divisor
greatest_common_divisor.preview: For integers not all zero, the greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer dividing every one of them.
greatest_common_divisor.card: The common positive divisors of 12 and 18 are 1,2,3,6, so \(\gcd (12,18)=6\). Two integers are coprime exactly when their gcd is 1.
greatest_common_divisor.rule: Signs do not affect the nonnegative gcd. By convention \(\gcd (0,0) = 0\), and \(\gcd(a,0)=|a|\); these cases require care when describing the gcd as a largest positive divisor.
greatest_common_divisor.deep: The factorial paper uses gcds to measure cancellation, reduce denominators, and control how prime factors overlap across many terms.

green_function.label: Green function
green_function.preview: A harmonic function away from a specified pole, with a prescribed singularity there and prescribed boundary behaviour.
green_function.card: For a regular compact planar set K of positive capacity, the Green function of the unbounded component of its complement, with pole at infinity, vanishes on the boundary and behaves as \(\log |z|-\log \operatorname{cap}(K)+o(1)\). A finite pole instead has singularity \(-\log |z-a|\) in the positive planar convention.
green_function.rule: State the domain, pole, normalization and boundary condition. Green functions need not exist on every domain, and continuous vanishing at every boundary point requires boundary regularity. A pole at infinity is different from a finite pole.
green_function.deep: The #1041 capacity refinement sums exterior Green-function values at roots outside the chosen component. These values encode how the excluded roots reduce the component capacity, making the geometric hypothesis more precise than its root count.

grounding.label: grounding
grounding.preview: Grounding connects a statement or decision to the information that gives it meaning and support.
grounding.card: For a factual claim, that may be a source or observation. For a system term, it may be the code and records defining its local use. Plectis expects important explanations to retain those connections.
grounding.rule: The source must be relevant to the actual claim, not merely related to its subject.
grounding.deep: A source link improves inspectability but does not settle interpretation by itself. The reader still needs to check that the source supports the wording and scope.

guinea_pig.label: guinea pig
guinea_pig.preview: “Guinea pig” is an informal term for a person or case on which an experimental method is tried.
guinea_pig.card: The phrase draws attention to who bears the uncertainty, inconvenience, or consequences of the trial. In descriptions of this project, it concerns the experience of trying an unfinished workflow or method.
guinea_pig.rule: An experimental use should be understood through its actual conditions and limits.
guinea_pig.deep: The metaphor does not establish that a method works or that its effects generalise. A trial can reveal useful failures while leaving wider effectiveness and suitability unresolved.

haar_measure.label: Haar measure
haar_measure.preview: A Haar measure is a nonzero translation-invariant regular Borel measure, finite on compact sets, on a locally compact Hausdorff group.
haar_measure.card: A left Haar measure assigns the same mass to a measurable set and any left translate of it, and is finite on compact sets. It is unique up to a positive scale; on a compact group it can be normalized to total mass one.
haar_measure.rule: Specify left or right invariance when it matters. On a noncompact locally compact Hausdorff group, Haar measure has infinite total mass and cannot be normalized to a probability measure.
haar_measure.deep: The #257 note uses normalized Haar measure on the compact additive group of profinite integers. Each finite residue quotient is uniform, letting divisibility events be evaluated without choosing a finite truncation as the permanent probability model.

hankel_determinant.label: Hankel determinant
hankel_determinant.preview: A Hankel determinant is the determinant of a matrix whose entries are constant along each anti-diagonal.
hankel_determinant.card: For a sequence \(\mu _{0},\mu _{1},\ldots\), the \(N\times N\) moment matrix has entry \(\mu _{i+j}\) for \(0\le i,j<N\). At \(N=2\) its determinant is \(\mu _{0}\mu _{2}-\mu _{1}^{2}\).
hankel_determinant.rule: Some versions shift the starting index. The determinant need not be positive for an arbitrary sequence; positivity needs additional structure.
hankel_determinant.deep: For the positive geometric moments in #1049, the determinant expands over choices of distinct nodes with squared Vandermonde factors. The paper estimates that full sum, rather than treating one leading node choice as the entire asymptotic.

hard_coded.label: hard-coded
hard_coded.preview: Hard-coded means a value or choice is written directly into code or content instead of being supplied through configuration, input, or a separate source.
hard_coded.card: Hard-coding can cause drift when the value represents changing state, because updates require another manual edit. It can also be the clearest correct choice for stable constants, protocol markers, fixed limits, test fixtures, or behavior intentionally owned by that code.
hard_coded.rule: Judge hard-coding by the value’s authority and expected rate of change: fixed ownership can be appropriate, while copied runtime facts need a refresh path.
hard_coded.deep: The defect is not literal syntax by itself. A mathematical constant, file signature, compatibility token, or deliberately fixed policy default may belong directly in source. Trouble arises when independently changing information is copied without provenance, validation, or regeneration, producing several apparent authorities. Alternatives include configuration, lookup, dependency injection, computed projection, or generated code, each carrying different complexity and failure modes. A sound design states who owns the value, how changes propagate, and whether divergence can be detected.

harmonic_extension.label: harmonic extension
harmonic_extension.preview: A harmonic extension fills boundary data into a domain by a harmonic function that takes those boundary values, when the relevant Dirichlet problem is solvable.
harmonic_extension.card: On the unit disc, continuous boundary data can be extended using the Poisson integral. Constant boundary data extend constantly; oscillatory Fourier modes decay toward the center according to their frequency.
harmonic_extension.rule: Existence and uniqueness depend on the domain and the function class. “Extension” means agreement in the appropriate boundary sense, which may be continuous or almost everywhere. Harmonic does not mean holomorphic, though real and imaginary parts of holomorphic functions are harmonic.
harmonic_extension.deep: The paper extends boundary information harmonically so interior estimates can be derived from boundary averages and maximum principles. The extension acts as a controlled interpolant rather than introducing new independent analytic data.

harmonic_function.label: harmonic function
harmonic_function.preview: A harmonic function has continuous second derivatives and a zero Laplacian, the sum of its pure second partial derivatives.
harmonic_function.card: A harmonic function is locally balanced: its value at the centre of a sufficiently small ball equals its average over that ball or its boundary. For example, \(x^{2}-y^{2}\) is harmonic on the plane because its pure second derivatives, 2 and \(-2\), cancel.
harmonic_function.rule: Check the domain and regularity; in the plane, real and imaginary parts of holomorphic functions are harmonic, but a general harmonic function need not be globally the real part of one on a domain with holes.
harmonic_function.deep: A harmonic function u on an open region satisfies \(\Delta u=0\), where the Laplacian adds the second derivative in every coordinate direction. Harmonic functions obey the mean-value property: the value at the centre of a sufficiently small ball equals the average on its boundary or interior. Consequently, a nonconstant harmonic function cannot attain a maximum or minimum strictly inside a connected domain. In two dimensions, the real and imaginary parts of holomorphic functions are harmonic. A harmonic conjugate exists locally, and globally on simply connected domains, but topology can obstruct a single global conjugate.

harmonic_measure.label: harmonic measure
harmonic_measure.preview: A measure describing how strongly different parts of a domain boundary influence a harmonic value at a chosen interior point.
harmonic_measure.card: For a sufficiently regular bounded domain D, continuous boundary data h determine a harmonic extension \(u(z)=\int h(\xi )d\omega _D(z,\xi )\). The measure \(\omega _D(z,\cdot )\) depends on the base point z. At the centre of the disc it is uniform angular measure; elsewhere it is weighted by the Poisson kernel.
harmonic_measure.rule: Harmonic measure is generally different from uniform boundary length. Conformal maps transport it, but an arc-length density needs boundary regularity and the appropriate derivative factor. The domain and base point must be specified.
harmonic_measure.deep: In #1041, pushing the uniform circle measure through a Blaschke product produces harmonic measure seen from \(B(0)\). Comparing its density with the inverse-branch boundary weights gives a bound on the capacity of the selected polynomial component.

harness.label: harness
harness.preview: A test harness is the code and setup that runs a test and captures its result.
harness.card: It supplies inputs, prepares the environment, invokes the thing being tested, and records or compares outputs. Plectis uses harnesses to make a component's advertised check executable.
harness.rule: The harness is separate from both the component and the claim being tested.
harness.deep: Its own behaviour matters: a harness that runs the wrong command or ignores a failure can produce a misleading pass. Negative cases help check that relevant failures are actually detected.

hausdorff_measure.label: hausdorff measure
hausdorff_measure.preview: Hausdorff measure measures a set by covering it with arbitrarily small pieces and summing powers of their diameters.
hausdorff_measure.card: The one-dimensional version measures length: it agrees with arc length for a simple rectifiable curve, and also applies to connected sets with no chosen parametrisation.
hausdorff_measure.rule: Specify the dimension and normalization. The measure of a curve’s image counts each location once; the length of a parametrised path counts retraced portions again.
hausdorff_measure.deep: For dimension s, first minimize \(c_{s}\sum _{i}\operatorname{diam}(U_{i})^{s}\) over countable covers with diameters at most \(\delta\), then let \(\delta\) decrease to zero; \(c_{s}\) fixes the standard normalization. The #1041 counterexample bounds one-dimensional Hausdorff measure of connecting sets, a statement distinct from a bound on a particular parametrised path.

heine_determinant_identity.label: Heine determinant identity
heine_determinant_identity.preview: An identity expressing a moment determinant as an integral or sum of a squared Vandermonde product.
heine_determinant_identity.card: For \(n\ge 1\) and a finite positive measure \(\mu\) on the real line with finite moments through degree \(2n-2\), \(\det (\mu _{i+j})_{i,j<n}=1/n! \int \ldots \int \prod _{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^{2} d\mu (x_{1})\ldots d\mu (x_{n})\), where \(\mu _k=\int x^{k}d\mu\). For discrete weights, strictly increasing node indices remove the \(1/n!\) factor; pairwise distinct ordered tuples retain it.
heine_determinant_identity.rule: The moments and multiple integral must exist, with hypotheses justifying interchange. For a positive measure every summand is nonnegative, which is useful for limits and lower bounds. Signed weights remove that positivity advantage.
heine_determinant_identity.deep: In #1049 the nodes are powers of q and the weights are positive. The Heine expansion tracks displaced node tuples and shows why the initial tuple alone misses a nontrivial asymptotic constant. The identity is not Heine’s transformation of a basic hypergeometric series.

hereditary_property.label: hereditary property
hereditary_property.preview: A property is hereditary under a specified restriction if every allowed restriction of an object retains that property.
hereditary_property.card: Here, a support condition is hereditary when it passes from a set of exponents to each infinite subset. Removing nonnegative terms cannot increase a finite weighted sum.
hereditary_property.rule: State which restrictions are allowed. An irrational sum alone does not imply that every infinite subseries has an irrational sum.
hereditary_property.deep: The #257 criteria establish conditions that survive passage to infinite subsets. Applying the theorem anew to each such subset proves irrationality throughout that class; the mechanism is preservation of the hypothesis, not a general rule about irrational numbers.

hessian_matrix.label: hessian matrix
hessian_matrix.preview: The square matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar-valued function.
hessian_matrix.card: The Hessian records second-order change in a scalar-valued function. For \(f(x,y) = x^{2}-y^{2}\) it has diagonal entries 2 and \(-2\), showing upward curvature along one axis and downward curvature along the other at the origin.
hessian_matrix.rule: At a critical point of a twice continuously differentiable real function, positive or negative definiteness gives a strict local minimum or maximum, and indefiniteness gives a saddle.
hessian_matrix.deep: For n variables, the Hessian is the \(n\times n\) matrix of second partial derivatives. Under continuous second differentiability, equality of mixed partials makes it symmetric. Its quadratic form, multiplied by one half, gives the second-order Taylor term. A semidefinite Hessian with zero directions needs further analysis: higher-order terms can change the classification. A singular Hessian can still be indefinite and establish a saddle, so singularity alone is not the classification rule.

heuristic.label: heuristic
heuristic.preview: A heuristic is a practical rule or method that often finds a useful answer without guaranteeing the best or correct answer.
heuristic.card: Heuristics reduce search or decision cost by using patterns, estimates, or experience. They are valuable when exact calculation is too expensive, but their limits should be tested against representative cases.
heuristic.rule: Treat a heuristic result as a candidate or ranking signal until a stronger check establishes the required claim.
heuristic.deep: A heuristic may rank search results, choose a promising proof step, or estimate where to spend effort. It can be fast and useful while missing good answers on some inputs. A guaranteed algorithm also has assumptions; the distinction is whether the claimed guarantee has been established for the case at hand. Plectis uses heuristic retrieval and planning to choose work, then checks the resulting evidence separately.

hologram.label: hologram
hologram.preview: In Plectis, “hologram” means a structured, compressed view that preserves routes into the material it summarises.
hologram.card: Public JSON packets carry selected content, identities, and relationships so an assistant or reader can examine the collection without reconstructing the website page by page. Internal navigation uses the same idea at different levels of detail.
hologram.rule: The term is a project metaphor, not a claim about optical holography.
hologram.deep: The packet's declared coverage determines what it contains. Source links and preserved relationships make deeper inspection possible even when the packet deliberately omits large bodies of detail.

holomorphic_function.label: holomorphic function
holomorphic_function.preview: A complex-valued function that has a complex derivative at every point of an open domain.
holomorphic_function.card: Complex differentiation uses the same derivative regardless of the direction from which the increment approaches zero. Polynomials are holomorphic everywhere; complex conjugation is not. In one complex variable, being holomorphic on an open set is equivalent to having a convergent local power series.
holomorphic_function.rule: Real differentiability of the two coordinate functions is insufficient. A nonzero complex derivative gives a holomorphic inverse near that point, but does not make the map globally one-to-one.
holomorphic_function.deep: In #1041 a local inverse is extended across a domain from which critical values have been removed. Global inverse sheets need the covering and topology arguments as well as holomorphic regularity. Even a biholomorphic change of coordinates can distort lengths: preserving angles does not preserve the metric estimate needed for a short connection.

html.label: HTML
html.preview: HTML is the markup language used to describe the structure and meaning of web-page content.
html.card: Elements identify headings, paragraphs, links, lists, forms, and other parts that browsers and assistive technology can interpret. CSS controls presentation, while JavaScript can add behaviour.
html.rule: HTML structure affects how a page works as well as how it looks.
html.deep: The site's glossary references are links to definitions, enhanced with interactive previews. Keeping meaningful links in the page lets readers still reach an entry when the preview script is unavailable.

http.label: HTTP and HTTPS
http.preview: HTTP is the web protocol for exchanging requests and responses; HTTPS is HTTP carried through an authenticated encrypted connection.
http.card: A client sends a method, URL, headers, and sometimes a body. A server returns a status, headers, and sometimes a body. HTTPS protects the connection against ordinary interception and identifies the server through certificates.
http.rule: Interpret the status, headers, body, method, URL, and connection security together; successful transport does not validate the claims inside a response.
http.deep: HTTP defines how web messages are structured and what methods and status codes mean. HTTPS adds Transport Layer Security, commonly called TLS, around that exchange. Encryption protects data while it travels between endpoints, but the destination can still store or misuse it. Plectis publishes HTTPS links and static files; the protocol delivers those bytes without deciding whether their scholarly or technical content is correct.

hyperbolic_distance.label: hyperbolic distance
hyperbolic_distance.preview: In the unit-disc model, hyperbolic distance is the shortest path length measured with increasing stretching near the boundary.
hyperbolic_distance.card: With the usual curvature \(-1\) convention, a small Euclidean displacement \(|dz|\) at z has hyperbolic length \(2|dz|/(1-|z|^{2})\). The stretching grows without bound towards the unit circle; any path from an interior point to that boundary has infinite hyperbolic length.
hyperbolic_distance.rule: Some conventions rescale this metric by a constant, so numerical distance formulas must use the paper’s normalization. Holomorphic disc self-maps do not increase hyperbolic distance.
hyperbolic_distance.deep: Pairwise hyperbolic separation of selected points feeds packing and area estimates for critical-value connectors.

hypothesis.label: hypothesis
hypothesis.preview: A mathematical hypothesis is an assumption under which a statement is being considered or proved.
hypothesis.card: For example, “if n is prime and greater than 2, then n is odd” assumes both primality and the size condition. The conclusion is asserted for cases satisfying those assumptions.
hypothesis.rule: A hypothesis in a theorem need not be an unproved conjecture; it may simply define the cases covered.
hypothesis.deep: In conditional research results, a particular hypothesis may remain unresolved. The proof then establishes what follows from it, rather than establishing that it holds.

ide.label: IDE
ide.preview: An IDE, or integrated development environment, is an application combining tools for working on software.
ide.card: It commonly provides a code editor, project navigation, diagnostics, and ways to build or run programs. Support for a proof language can also show goals, errors, and declaration information while a proof is developed.
ide.rule: An IDE is useful for local work but is not required to read the website.
ide.deep: The repositories' command-line checks describe the reproducible operations. An editor interface can invoke or help inspect those operations without replacing their recorded inputs and results.

idempotency.label: idempotency
idempotency.preview: Idempotency is the property that repeating an operation with the same intended input has the same effect as performing it once.
idempotency.card: Idempotent operations make retries safer when a caller cannot tell whether an earlier attempt completed. Implementations may use stable request keys, existing-state checks, or naturally repeatable assignments.
idempotency.rule: Judge idempotency by observable effects, not merely by whether repeated calls return the same value.
idempotency.deep: Setting a field to a fixed value is idempotent; incrementing it is not. A function from a set to itself is mathematically idempotent when \(f(f(x))=f(x)\). For an API, the relevant question is whether repeating the same request accumulates an additional intended effect; responses and incidental logs may differ. Plectis queue fixtures check that repeated enqueue requests identify one job rather than creating duplicates.

identifier.label: identifier
identifier.preview: An identifier is a name or code used to distinguish one object from others within a stated system.
identifier.card: Identifiers include database keys, route IDs, filenames, package names, and DOI strings. They support reference and lookup; they do not necessarily describe the object in ordinary language.
identifier.rule: Judge an identifier inside its naming system, including its namespace, case rules, and stability promises.
identifier.deep: An identifier works only relative to rules that say what it identifies and whether it can change or be reused. Human-readable labels and identifiers may differ: a page title can change while its stable route ID remains fixed. Plectis preserves compatibility identifiers when renaming them would break links or tools. Possessing an identifier does not prove that the referenced object exists, is current, or is authoritative.

image_of_function.label: image of a function
image_of_function.preview: The set of output values a function actually attains.
image_of_function.card: If \(f(n)=n^{2}\) on the integers, its image contains 0,1,4,9,… but not 2. The image may be smaller than the announced set of possible outputs.
image_of_function.rule: For a subset A of inputs, \(f(A)\) means all \(f(a)\) with a in A.
image_of_function.deep: Image language identifies which outputs a recurrence or map actually reaches. “Range” often means this image, but some sources use it for the declared codomain; the source’s convention matters. A function is surjective exactly when its image equals its stated codomain.

immutability.label: immutable
immutability.preview: Immutable describes a value or record that cannot be changed after it is created.
immutability.card: An immutable object may be replaced by a new version, but its existing value remains fixed. Immutability simplifies comparison, caching, concurrency, and audit history when the boundary is real.
immutability.rule: Ask which object and boundary are immutable; a fixed record can still point to mutable external content.
immutability.deep: A language or storage system can prevent changes to an object, while an append-only policy can forbid them. A cryptographic hash serves a different purpose: changed bytes acquire a different hash, making a change detectable when identities are checked. Plectis records events as immutable history and builds changing views from them. New events can be added, and references can move, while the earlier records remain intact.

implementation.label: implementation
implementation.preview: An implementation is a concrete realization of a design, specification, algorithm, interface, or policy.
implementation.card: Implementation may take the form of executable code, configured services, data structures, generated artifacts, hardware, or an operational procedure. Several implementations can satisfy the same contract while using different internal methods, performance trade-offs, and dependencies.
implementation.rule: Evaluate an implementation against the requirements it claims to realize, the environment in which it operates, and evidence from its actual behavior.
implementation.deep: Specifications describe required relationships or outcomes; implementations choose concrete representations and steps. A correct algorithm can be implemented incorrectly, and a conforming implementation may still be insecure, slow, inaccessible, or unsuitable for a particular setting. Conversely, observed useful behavior without a stated contract makes conformance hard to judge. Source inspection explains how a realization is built, while tests, formal checks, and operational evidence address different aspects of whether it works. Version identity matters because implementation behavior can change without renaming the interface.

implication.label: implication
implication.preview: An implication says that if one statement holds, another follows.
implication.card: The notation \(P\to Q\) means “if P, then Q”. P is a sufficient condition for Q, and Q is a necessary condition for P. This alone does not say that Q implies P.
implication.rule: Proving the implication does not establish P itself.
implication.deep: The papers use implications to connect hypotheses and target results. To claim an equivalent reformulation, the reverse implication must also be proved under compatible assumptions.

independent_events.label: independent events
independent_events.preview: Events are mutually independent when the probability of every finite intersection is the product of its probabilities.
independent_events.card: For two events A and B, this says \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\). A family needs the corresponding identity for every finite subfamily. Pairwise independence alone does not guarantee mutual independence.
independent_events.rule: Independence depends on the chosen probability law. Disjoint positive-probability events are not independent, because their joint occurrence is impossible.
independent_events.deep: For a Haar-uniform profinite integer, the #257 note treats divisibility of \(x+1\) by distinct primes as independent. The Chinese remainder theorem supplies the product probabilities for finite collections, supporting the stated almost-sure argument.

index.label: index
index.preview: An index identifies a member of an indexed family or provides a lookup structure for locating information.
index.card: In a sequence \(a_{n}\), n is the index and \(a_{n}\) is the term at that position. A search or database index instead records information that helps locate matching items efficiently. The site uses both mathematical indices and generated lookup indexes.
index.rule: An index used as a label need not be a number; an index used for lookup is separate from the material it describes.
index.deep: The paper’s notation states which values an index can take, such as positive integers or elements of another set. Distinct indices can label equal values, so an index does not assert uniqueness of the value itself. A lookup index stores keys or references to selected content; it can omit items, become stale, or use approximate matching. The site’s declaration index helps locate proof declarations, while its coverage record states which source inventory was actually indexed.

indicator_function.label: indicator function
indicator_function.preview: An indicator function is 1 on a specified set and 0 outside it.
indicator_function.card: Writing \(1_A(x)\) means 1 if \(x\in A\) and 0 otherwise. Its sum over a finite index set counts the members of A in that set; multiplying a function by \(1_A\) restricts it to A.
indicator_function.rule: The set or condition being indicated must be specified. An indicator is a numeric function; a predicate states whether the condition is true.
indicator_function.deep: The #257 identity uses \(1_A\) for a selected exponent support, while \(1_{d\mid n}\) indicates a divisibility event. Summing the latter over a finite divisor set counts how many of its members divide n. Mathlib also names the restricted function itself an indicator: Set.indicator A f equals f on A and zero elsewhere.

inductive_type.label: inductive type
inductive_type.preview: An inductive type is specified by constructors that build its values and rules for reasoning about those values.
inductive_type.card: Natural numbers have zero and successor constructors; lists have an empty-list constructor and a constructor adding an element to a list. The associated induction or recursion principles let proofs and functions follow these constructions.
inductive_type.rule: Constructors must satisfy the proof system's formation rules. Writing a self-referential type equation is not enough to create a valid inductive type.
inductive_type.deep: The local Lean developments repeatedly use natural-number induction and finite structures built on such types. The logical mechanism explains why handling a base case and a successor case can establish a statement about every natural index.

inequality.label: inequality
inequality.preview: An inequality compares quantities using an order relation such as \(<,\le,>,\text{ or }\ge\).
inequality.card: The symbol \(\le\) means “less than or equal to”, so \(x \le M\) allows x to equal M. The strict inequality \(x < M\) excludes equality.
inequality.rule: The difference between strict and non-strict bounds can determine whether an endpoint is included.
inequality.deep: Inequalities in the papers often control an error or bound a sum. Each manipulation must respect sign conditions: multiplying both sides by a negative number reverses the order.

infimum.label: infimum
infimum.preview: The largest number less than or equal to every member of a set.
infimum.card: The open interval (0,1) has infimum 0 even though it has no smallest member. The infimum is the best lower bound: every element is at least 0, while any larger proposed lower bound fails.
infimum.rule: A minimum must belong to the set; an infimum need not. For an unbounded-below set the infimum may be \(-\infty\) in the extended real numbers, and an empty-set convention must be stated.
infimum.deep: Optimization thresholds in cover and matrix arguments are expressed as infima when competitors approach an optimal value without attaining it. Proving a lower bound for every competitor bounds the infimum; producing examples approaching it gives the reverse bound.

infinite.label: infinite
infinite.preview: An infinite set has more elements than any finite set; no finite count exhausts it.
infinite.card: Infinite sequences and series specify a term for every index in an unending index set. Statements about them are expressed through definitions, quantifiers, and limits rather than by carrying out infinitely many steps.
infinite.rule: “Infinitely many” is weaker than “all” and can also be weaker than “all sufficiently large”.
infinite.deep: For example, there are infinitely many even integers, but arbitrarily large odd integers remain. This distinction matters when interpreting the scope of a theorem.

injective_map.label: injective map
injective_map.preview: A function that never sends two different inputs to the same output.
injective_map.card: \(f(x)=2x\) on the integers is injective; \(f(x)=x^{2}\) is not, because 2 and -2 both map to 4.
injective_map.rule: To prove injectivity, assume \(f(x)=f(y)\) and show \(x=y\).
injective_map.deep: In the lemniscate arguments, an injective complex map gives different image points to different inputs. Having a nonzero derivative is only a local condition and does not by itself establish injectivity across the whole domain.

inner_product.label: inner product
inner_product.preview: An inner product pairs two vectors to measure their lengths and relative directions through an algebraic operation.
inner_product.card: For real coordinate vectors, the usual dot product adds the products of matching coordinates: \((a,b)\cdot (c,d) = ac+bd\). Its value on a vector paired with itself is the square of that vector's length and is positive unless the vector is zero.
inner_product.rule: An inner product is linear in one argument and symmetric over the reals; over the complexes it is conjugate-symmetric, with conjugate scaling in the other argument.
inner_product.deep: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds an inner product by the product of the two lengths. Function spaces can use integrals as inner products, allowing the same reasoning to compare functions rather than coordinate lists.

inspection.label: inspection
inspection.preview: Inspection means examining the actual material closely enough to assess a specific question about it.
inspection.card: Here that can involve reading a theorem statement, tracing its proof dependencies, examining a test, or comparing a result record with the command that produced it. The relevant depth depends on the question.
inspection.rule: Reading a summary is useful orientation but may leave the decisive detail unexamined.
inspection.deep: Plectis provides source and evidence routes to make that deeper reading possible. Inspection can reveal uncertainty as well as confirm a claim; it need not end in approval.

instance_resolution.label: instance resolution
instance_resolution.preview: Instance resolution searches for declared implementations that satisfy a type-class requirement.
instance_resolution.card: An instance may itself require other instances, so resolution can recursively assemble the needed structure. The search uses the language's declarations, priorities, and matching rules; it can fail when evidence is missing or parameters remain unknown.
instance_resolution.rule: Resolving an instance is not unrestricted theorem proving. A failed search can mean that a suitable declaration is absent rather than that the mathematical requirement is false.
instance_resolution.deep: In Lean's finite-index proofs, Fintype instances make enumeration available to generic operations. Reproducing such a proof therefore depends on the imported instance environment as well as the visible theorem statement.

integer.label: integer
integer.preview: An integer is one of the numbers \(\ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots\) .
integer.card: Integers have no fractional part. They include positive and negative whole numbers and zero, and are usually denoted collectively by ℤ.
integer.rule: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication preserve integers; division need not do so.
integer.deep: Number-theory statements often restrict integers further, for example to positive or nonnegative values. Those restrictions matter for divisibility, factorials, and sequence indices, so they are part of the mathematical claim rather than optional wording.

integer_partition.label: integer partition
integer_partition.preview: An integer partition writes a nonnegative integer as a sum of positive integers without counting different orders separately.
integer_partition.card: The partitions of 4 are 4, \(3+1\), \(2+2\), \(2+1+1\), and \(1+1+1+1\). They are often written as nonincreasing lists; trailing zeros may be added for indexing.
integer_partition.rule: This is different from a composition, which counts order, and from a set partition, which groups elements of a set. The empty partition represents zero.
integer_partition.deep: The #1049 proof indexes displaced moment nodes by partitions. Subtracting the baseline tuple \((0,1,\ldots,N-1)\) gives nonnegative increasing shifts, which become a partition after reversal. This puts the contributions for varying N on one index set so a common summable bound can justify passing to a limit.

integer_valued_polynomial.label: integer-valued polynomial
integer_valued_polynomial.preview: An integer-valued polynomial is a polynomial whose values are integers at every integer input, even if its coefficients are rational.
integer_valued_polynomial.card: For example, \(T(T-1)/2\) has rational coefficients but takes integer values for every integer T, because consecutive integers have an even product.
integer_valued_polynomial.rule: The input domain must be stated when using the term more generally. Integer values are different from integer coefficients: the latter imply the former, while the converse fails.
integer_valued_polynomial.deep: The #243 normalization gives \(Q(n)=(m/6)n(n+1)(n+2)+c\) with m,c integers. The product divided by six equals a binomial coefficient, so Q is integer-valued even when m/6 is not integral. This is the arithmetic property used for congruences and coprimality, rather than an assertion that Q belongs to \(\mathbb{Z}[T]\).

integrable_function.label: integrable function
integrable_function.preview: In Lebesgue integration, an integrable real or complex function is measurable and has finite integral of its absolute value.
integrable_function.card: The measure and domain are part of the claim. Scalar integrability allows a measurable representative agreeing almost everywhere. For a Banach space, a complete normed vector space, Bochner integrability requires almost-everywhere strong measurability and finite integral of the norm. Completeness ensures the integral lies in that space.
integrable_function.rule: Pointwise finiteness or existence of a conditionally convergent improper integral does not by itself establish Lebesgue or Bochner integrability.
integrable_function.deep: The #257 note keeps finite residue averages separate from a limiting profinite observable that is infinite almost everywhere. That limit cannot provide a finite integrable mean merely because selected integer inputs have finite values.

integral_basis.label: integral basis
integral_basis.preview: An integral basis is a basis over the integers: every element of the relevant free abelian group has a unique finite integer linear combination of the basis vectors.
integral_basis.card: The standard coordinate vectors form an integral basis of \(\mathbb{Z}^n\). A rational vector-space basis may fail to be integral because representing integer vectors can require fractions.
integral_basis.rule: The factorial-channel paper uses an integral basis for a specified lattice of relations. In algebraic number theory, the phrase usually names an integer-coordinate basis for a number field’s ring of integers. Both uses require unique integer coordinates in the stated object.
integral_basis.deep: An integral basis gives unique integer coordinates, unlike a rational basis which only promises rational coordinates. In algebraic number theory, an integral basis usually means a basis of the ring of integers over Z. The factorial-channel paper uses the same integer-coordinate idea for a specified relation lattice, making divisibility constraints visible in its coordinates.

integral_curve.label: integral curve
integral_curve.preview: An integral curve of a vector field is a parametrised curve whose velocity agrees with that field at every point.
integral_curve.card: It solves \(x'(t) = V(x(t))\). For the constant field \(V = 1\) on the real line, the curves are \(x(t) = t + c\), with the starting value determined by c.
integral_curve.rule: Existence and uniqueness require conditions on the field, such as local Lipschitz continuity for a standard uniqueness theorem.
integral_curve.deep: In the Newton-flow papers, the field is regular away from zeros of p′. A trajectory approaching an excluded point needs separate analysis before further continuation can be asserted.

intelligent.label: intelligent
intelligent.preview: Intelligent ordinarily describes an ability to learn, reason, understand, or adapt to a task.
intelligent.card: The word covers several capacities rather than one universally agreed measure. Performance can vary with the problem, available context, tools, and time.
intelligent.rule: Plectis's Type A and Type B labels describe access and authority, not intelligence.
intelligent.deep: An actor may reason well while lacking access to the evidence needed for a particular claim. Conversely, permission to run commands gives an opportunity to gather evidence without guaranteeing good judgement about the results.

interface.label: interface
interface.preview: An interface is a defined boundary through which a person, program, or component interacts with another system.
interface.card: A user interface exposes controls and feedback to people, while a programming interface exposes operations, inputs, outputs, and errors to software. Both establish what can cross a boundary without revealing every implementation detail.
interface.rule: An interface is determined by its participants, available operations, accepted inputs, returned outputs, and failure behaviour; its implementation may change while that contract remains stable.
interface.deep: An interface gives one party a usable way to interact with another while hiding details that need not be shared. Screens, forms, command lines, functions, file formats, and network APIs are all interfaces, but they serve different participants and carry different contracts. A stable interface specifies valid operations, data shapes, responses, and errors closely enough for independent use. It does not guarantee that the underlying implementation is simple or unchanged. A physical boundary may also be called an interface, so context must establish whether the interaction involves people, software, or material systems.

invariant.label: invariant
invariant.preview: An invariant is a quantity or property preserved by specified transformations or steps of a process.
invariant.card: For example, repeatedly adding 2 preserves an integer's parity. The unchanged property can connect distant stages without examining every intermediate operation separately.
invariant.rule: An invariant is preserved exactly in the stated sense; a quantity merely increasing or decreasing is instead monotone.
invariant.deep: The papers use preserved arithmetic relationships to constrain possible trajectories of a recurrence. Which transformation is allowed matters: a property invariant under one update need not survive a different operation or change of coordinates.

inverse_branch.label: inverse branch
inverse_branch.preview: A single-valued local choice of inverse for a map that may have several preimages globally.
inverse_branch.card: Near \(w=1\), one branch of the square root takes value 1 and another takes value \(-1\). Each is a consistent single-valued local inverse of squaring. Choosing a branch specifies which preimage is followed as w changes.
inverse_branch.rule: For a holomorphic map, a nonzero derivative gives a local holomorphic inverse branch. Its domain and starting preimage matter, and extending the branch requires avoiding the relevant obstructions.
inverse_branch.deep: If f is locally one-to-one near \(z_0\) and \(w_0=f(z_0)\), an inverse branch is a function g on a neighbourhood of \(w_0\) satisfying \(f(g(w))=w\) and \(g(w_0)=z_0\). For a holomorphic f with \(f'(z_0)\) nonzero, the inverse function theorem gives a holomorphic branch. A polynomial of degree greater than one has several possible preimages, so there is generally no single global inverse. Continuing a chosen branch can encounter a critical value or can return to another branch after travelling around a branch point.

inverse_function.label: inverse function
inverse_function.preview: An inverse function undoes a function, returning each output to the unique input that produced it.
inverse_function.card: The map \(f(x) = 2x\) on the reals has inverse \(y \mapsto y/2\). Squaring on all real numbers has no inverse function because 2 and \(-2\) have the same square; restricting the domain to nonnegative reals removes that ambiguity.
inverse_function.rule: A function has a two-sided inverse between its domain and codomain exactly when it is bijective.
inverse_function.deep: The notation \(f^{-1}(B)\) can instead mean the preimage of a set B, which is defined even without an inverse function. The papers' inverse branches make an inverse choice on a suitable restricted region.

irrational.label: irrational
irrational.preview: A real number is irrational if it cannot equal \(a/b\) for any integers a and nonzero b.
irrational.card: For example, \(\sqrt 2\) is irrational. In any fixed integer base greater than one, an irrational number's digit expansion never becomes permanently periodic.
irrational.rule: An infinite expansion alone does not imply irrationality: \(1/3\) has an infinite repeating decimal expansion.
irrational.deep: An irrationality proof must rule out every possible rational representation. Computing many digits or checking many candidate denominators can provide evidence, but it does not on its own exclude all fractions.

irrationality_criterion.label: irrationality criterion
irrationality_criterion.preview: An irrationality criterion is a proved condition that can be used to establish that a number is irrational.
irrationality_criterion.card: It may require a pattern of rational approximations, denominators, or scaled tails that a rational number cannot have. The criterion gives a route to irrationality when its requirements are verified.
irrationality_criterion.rule: Some criteria are sufficient conditions; stronger characterisations give both necessary and sufficient conditions.
irrationality_criterion.deep: The papers state these logical roles separately. Proving a criterion is useful, but applying it to an open problem still requires establishing the condition for the particular number under study.

irrationality_exponent.label: irrationality exponent
irrationality_exponent.preview: The irrationality exponent is the supremum of the approximation powers achieved infinitely often by rational approximations to an irrational number.
irrationality_exponent.card:
For an irrational \(\xi\), consider exponents \(
u\) for which \(|\xi -p/q| < 1/q^
u\) holds for infinitely many coprime integers \(p,q\) with \(q > 0\). The supremum of those \(
u\) is at least 2 and can be infinite. Larger values allow unusually close rational approximations.
irrationality_exponent.rule: A supremum need not itself satisfy the defining inequality infinitely often, and a finite approximation sample cannot establish the exponent.
irrationality_exponent.deep: Lambert-series approximation estimates yield explicit upper bounds on how well the target values can be approximated.

irreducible_polynomial.label: irreducible polynomial
irreducible_polynomial.preview: An irreducible polynomial over a field is a nonconstant polynomial that cannot be factored into two polynomials of positive degree over that field.
irreducible_polynomial.card: The polynomial \(T^{2}-2\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb{Q}\) but factors over \(\mathbb{R}\). Irreducibility therefore always refers to a specified coefficient field.
irreducible_polynomial.rule: For degrees two and three over a field, irreducibility is equivalent to having no root in that field. This root test is insufficient in higher degrees.
irreducible_polynomial.deep: The #243 argument excludes a rational root of its cubic by reducing that root modulo suitable persistent primes and contradicting coprimality. The cubic root test then supplies irreducibility, allowing the proof to pass to a degree-three number field.

jacobi_matrix.label: Jacobi matrix
