jacobi_matrix.preview: The tridiagonal matrix representing multiplication by the variable in an orthonormal polynomial basis.
jacobi_matrix.card: For orthonormal polynomials on the real line, \(xp_n=a_{n+1}p_{n+1}+b_n p_n+a_n p_{n-1}\). The associated real symmetric matrix has \(b_n\) on the diagonal and positive \(a_n\) on neighbouring diagonals. Its finite truncations give quadrature nodes as eigenvalues.
jacobi_matrix.rule: This row uses the symmetric orthonormal convention. A differently normalized polynomial basis can yield a nonsymmetric tridiagonal recurrence matrix. The Jacobi matrix is also distinct from a Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives.
jacobi_matrix.deep: The #1049 finite moment construction becomes a Jacobi matrix after choosing an orthonormal polynomial basis. The paper explicitly distinguishes this positive-node quadrature construction from a different coefficient matrix pencil whose roots can include negative values.

jacobian_matrix.label: jacobian matrix
jacobian_matrix.preview: The matrix of all first partial derivatives of a map between finite-dimensional coordinate spaces.
jacobian_matrix.card: For \(F(x,y) = (x+y,xy)\), the Jacobian has rows \((1,1)\) and \((y,x)\). When F is differentiable, this matrix represents the linear map describing its first-order local change; the existence of individual partial derivatives alone is not enough.
jacobian_matrix.rule: For n inputs and m outputs, the Jacobian is \(m\times n\). A square Jacobian with nonzero determinant gives a local differentiable inverse when the map is continuously differentiable nearby.
jacobian_matrix.deep: Each entry records how one output changes with one input coordinate. The inverse function theorem uses both local regularity and a nonzero determinant. A zero determinant does not exclude every kind of local inverse: \(x \mapsto x^{3}\) is invertible near zero, but its inverse is not differentiable there. Some prose uses “Jacobian” for the determinant; the matrix and that scalar must be distinguished. Hessians instead collect second derivatives of a scalar-valued function.

javascript.label: JavaScript
javascript.preview: JavaScript is a programming language used in web browsers and many server and tooling environments.
javascript.card: Browsers use JavaScript to respond to actions such as clicks, update a page, and communicate through web APIs. Other environments use the same language for servers, scripts, and development tools. Its core language is standardized as ECMAScript.
javascript.rule: JavaScript being enabled permits code to run; it does not establish that the code is safe, correct, or necessary.
javascript.deep: The host environment supplies facilities beyond the core language: a browser provides documents, events, and timers, while a server runtime can provide file or network access. Plectis uses JavaScript to add glossary previews, search, maps, and navigation controls to generated HTML. Direct links and readable content remain useful when those enhancements are unavailable. JavaScript and Java are separate languages.

jitter.label: jitter
jitter.card: In networking, jitter often means unwanted variation in packet arrival times. Retry jitter deliberately varies waiting times: clients that failed together choose different delays, reducing another simultaneous traffic spike.
jitter.rule: Distinguish unwanted timing variation from the deliberate randomness used to spread retry attempts.
jitter.deep: Retry jitter is often combined with exponential backoff. One scheme draws a delay anywhere between zero and the current backoff limit; another varies around a planned delay. The variation need not be small. Plectis provider-routing discussions use this scheduling sense, where several clients may otherwise retry together after a shared rate limit. The delay changes timing; it does not make an unsafe operation safe to repeat.

jordan_domain.label: jordan domain
jordan_domain.preview: A Jordan domain is the bounded open region enclosed by a simple closed curve in the plane.
jordan_domain.card: The inside of a circle or any non-self-intersecting closed loop is a Jordan domain. A figure-eight boundary is excluded because it crosses itself and encloses more than one lobe rather than one simple inside region.
jordan_domain.rule: A Jordan domain is the bounded open component enclosed by a simple closed plane curve. The Jordan curve theorem supplies exactly one inside and one outside component, sharing that curve as boundary.
jordan_domain.deep: When a polynomial sublevel component is a Jordan domain, conformal maps can transfer it to the unit disc and boundary behavior becomes tractable. The term is topological; the boundary need not be smooth, circular, or convex.

json_format.label: JSON
json_format.preview: JSON is a text format for representing structured values as objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.
json_format.card: JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. People can inspect it as text, while programs parse its defined grammar. It is widely used beyond JavaScript. A separate schema or contract explains allowed fields, relationships, and version changes for a particular application.
json_format.rule: JSON syntax being valid says nothing about whether its values are true, complete, safe, current, or meaningful for a particular consumer.
json_format.deep: JSON deliberately supports a small value vocabulary and has no native comments, dates, binary blobs, or object identity. Applications encode those ideas by convention. Member ordering usually has no semantic force, duplicate-name handling differs among parsers, and numbers may lose precision across implementations. A durable JSON interface therefore documents encoding, schema, required and optional fields, identifier stability, compatibility rules, and validation behavior. Human readability aids inspection but does not replace those contracts or establish the authority of the contained claims.

kernel.label: kernel
kernel.preview: Here, kernel can mean Lean's proof checker or the repository's kernel.py command router.
kernel.card: In Lean, the kernel checks terms against a small core type theory. In ai_workflow, kernel.py is a command entry point selecting files, records, tools, and state views. Both are central interfaces, but they answer different questions.
kernel.rule: Read proof acceptance as a Lean-kernel claim and navigation or status output as a repository-router response. Qualify the name when both appear together.
kernel.deep: The router helps an agent find the source controlling a question; its response does not establish a theorem. Lean's checker establishes that a term has its declared type in its environment, including the assumptions on which it depends.

koebe_distortion_theorem.label: Koebe distortion theorem
koebe_distortion_theorem.preview: The Koebe distortion theorem gives explicit bounds on the size and derivative of a normalized univalent holomorphic function inside the unit disc.
koebe_distortion_theorem.card: If f is one-to-one on the unit disc with \(f(0)=0\) and \(f'(0)=1\), then points well inside the disc cannot be stretched or compressed arbitrarily; the bounds worsen as \(|z|\) approaches 1.
koebe_distortion_theorem.rule: Normalization matters: general univalent functions are reduced to the standard form by translating and scaling. The theorem controls interior distortion, not arbitrary behavior on the boundary, and it depends essentially on global injectivity on the disc.
koebe_distortion_theorem.deep: The paper applies a Koebe estimate to an inverse branch on a one-root lobe. Once univalence and the available disc radius are established, the theorem converts analytic normalization into quantitative control of the corresponding path pieces.

kronecker_approximation_theorem.label: Kronecker approximation theorem
kronecker_approximation_theorem.preview: A theorem describing which simultaneous phases can be approached by a linear motion modulo integers.
kronecker_approximation_theorem.card: For a continuous flow \(t\omega\) on \(\mathbb{R}^{d}/\mathbb{Z}^{d}\), its closure consists of the phases satisfying every integer relation \(k\cdot x=0\) modulo 1 for which \(k\cdot \omega =0\). In particular, if no nonzero integer relation among the frequencies exists, the flow is dense in the whole torus.
kronecker_approximation_theorem.rule: For a discrete orbit \(n\alpha\), relations \(k\cdot \alpha\) that are integers must also be respected. Full density then requires rational independence of 1 and the coordinates of \(\alpha\). The continuous and discrete forms must not be interchanged.
kronecker_approximation_theorem.deep: The #269 proof uses the continuous form to identify its orbit closure as a subtorus determined by the rational relations among reciprocal logarithms. It then searches inside that subtorus. Qualitative approximation gives arbitrarily close returns; a numerical return-time bound would require additional estimates.

laboratory.label: laboratory
laboratory.preview: In Plectis, a laboratory is a controlled setting for trying a proposed mechanism before relying on it in live work.
laboratory.card: It runs candidate checks, rules, or workflows against selected fixtures and records what happens. The small, explicit setting makes it easier to investigate failures and compare proposed changes.
laboratory.rule: Laboratory evidence covers the experiment that was actually run.
laboratory.deep: A successful trial can justify further testing or a proposed integration. It does not automatically change a governing rule or establish that the mechanism will behave the same way on every live input.

lambert_series.label: Lambert series
lambert_series.preview: A Lambert series has the form \(\sum a_n x^n/(1-x^n)\), usually summed over positive integers n where it converges.
lambert_series.card: At \(x = 1/b\), its terms become \(a_{n}/(b^{n} - 1)\). Expanding the denominators as geometric series connects the coefficients to sums over divisors, under conditions that justify rearranging the terms.
lambert_series.rule: A power series \(\sum a_{n}x^{n}\) is a different expression and is not automatically a Lambert series.
lambert_series.deep: That distinction matters here: the totient power series and the sums with denominators \(b^n-1\) are related number-theory objects, but their definitions and convergence arguments must be read separately.

large_language_model.label: large language model
large_language_model.preview: A large language model is a statistical model trained to predict and generate sequences of tokens from context.
large_language_model.card: Such models can write, summarize, reason, call tools, and transform information, but their outputs depend on training, prompting, context, sampling, and external tools. Fluent language does not by itself establish factual accuracy, understanding, authorship, or authority.
large_language_model.rule: Judge an LLM-assisted result through its sources, checks, and reproducible artifacts; the model name alone supplies no evidence for a claim.
large_language_model.deep: A large language model learns statistical regularities over token sequences and generates continuations conditioned on supplied context. Scale refers to training data, computation, and parameters rather than a guarantee of broad competence. Models can assist with language, code, search, and tool use, yet may fabricate details, inherit bias, follow malicious instructions, or reason inconsistently. Sampling settings and surrounding systems affect outputs. Therefore authority belongs to inspectable sources, executable checks, formal proofs, or accountable human decisions as appropriate; fluency and model identity alone do not validate a conclusion.

latency.label: latency
latency.preview: Latency is the elapsed time between the start of an action or request and a defined response or completion point.
latency.card: Latency measures how long one operation waits, separately from throughput, which measures how much work a system handles per unit time. Queueing, network transfer, computation, storage, and rendering may all contribute.
latency.rule: A latency measurement is defined by its start and end events, workload, environment, and summary distribution; percentiles expose slow cases that an average can conceal.
latency.deep: Latency is an end-to-end delay between two specified events, such as sending a request and receiving its first byte or final response. Different endpoint choices produce different measurements. Total latency may contain queueing time, network travel, server computation, database access, and client rendering. Throughput and latency are related but not equivalent: a system can complete many jobs each second while an individual job waits in a long queue. Because delays are often skewed, median, high percentiles, maximum, and timeout rate can reveal behaviour that a simple arithmetic mean obscures.

latex.label: LaTeX
latex.preview: LaTeX is a system for writing structured documents that a typesetting engine turns into formatted output, usually a PDF.
latex.card: Authors write text together with commands for sections, equations, references, and layout. This is widely used for mathematical papers because complex notation and cross-references can be maintained in source form.
latex.rule: The source file and rendered document serve different purposes and should correspond to the same version.
latex.deep: The site publishes readable paper views alongside source material where available. A successful typesetting run checks document construction, not the correctness of the mathematics.

lattice.label: lattice
lattice.preview: In Plectis, the lattice is the network of relationships between rules, skills, concepts, code, and evidence.
lattice.card: Its connections state how items relate: a standard may govern a skill, a component may implement a mechanism, and a record may support a claim. This lets a reader follow meaning across different kinds of artifact.
lattice.rule: This project usage does not assert the axioms of a mathematical lattice.
lattice.deep: In order theory, a lattice instead requires a greatest lower bound and least upper bound for every pair. The local term is a name for the system's relationship graph.

lattice_transposition.label: lattice transposition
lattice_transposition.preview: Lattice transposition moves a reusable lesson into the kind of system record that can apply it to future work.
lattice_transposition.card: A local failure may reveal a missing instruction, validation rule, or concept. Plectis retains the original case and places the general refinement in the narrowest existing skill, standard, or other owner that can carry it.
lattice_transposition.rule: The lesson's scope must survive the move.
lattice_transposition.deep: For example, a faulty glossary preview may justify changing the shared glossary rule. It does not automatically justify changing how every kind of document is written.

launch_scope_decision.label: launch-scope decision
launch_scope_decision.preview: A launch-scope decision determines what is ready and authorised to be published or made available.
launch_scope_decision.card: It considers the intended audience, included material, evidence, and unresolved limitations. In Plectis, component checks provide information for this decision but do not independently grant publication authority.
launch_scope_decision.rule: A passing technical check answers its own conditions, not every question about release readiness.
launch_scope_decision.deep: The person responsible for the release must make the decision within the authorised scope. A published selection should then match the material and evidence on which that decision was based.

lay_person.label: lay person
lay_person.preview: A lay person is someone who is not a specialist in the subject being discussed.
lay_person.card: The term concerns subject knowledge, not intelligence or general ability. A mathematician can be a lay reader of software architecture, just as an experienced programmer can be new to number theory.
lay_person.rule: The glossary aims to explain unfamiliar terms without requiring specialist training.
lay_person.deep: Readers can still contribute useful questions, corrections, or work with tools. Specialist judgement may be needed for particular claims, and the project should make that need clear rather than assume a reader's background.

lean.label: Lean
lean.preview: Lean is a programming language and proof assistant used to state mathematics and check formal proofs.
lean.card: Authors supply definitions, theorem statements, and proofs, often with tactics that help construct the proof object. Lean then checks that the object establishes the encoded proposition under its assumptions.
lean.rule: Successful checking applies to that precise formal statement.
lean.deep: Admissions, added axioms, or an incorrectly translated problem can limit what acceptance establishes. The papers therefore need readable statements and evidence of the relevant checks alongside the Lean source.

lean_kernel.label: Lean kernel
lean_kernel.preview: The Lean kernel checks that a formal term has its declared type under Lean's logical rules.
lean_kernel.card: Lean translates source syntax and tactics into terms in a core dependent type theory. The kernel checks those terms before declarations enter its environment. Proof construction and proof checking are separate operations.
lean_kernel.rule: Read acceptance together with the exact theorem and its axiom dependencies. An admitted statement can type-check because its gap is represented by an axiom.
lean_kernel.deep: This separation lets complex automation propose proofs without requiring the kernel to reproduce the search. Readers still assess whether the encoded statement matches the intended mathematics. The repository's kernel.py supplies navigation and has no such proof-checking role.

lean_standard_axioms.label: Lean's standard axioms
lean_standard_axioms.preview: The three usual mathematical axioms permitted here are propext, Quot.sound, and Classical.choice.
lean_standard_axioms.card: Propositional extensionality equates logically equivalent propositions; quotient soundness identifies quotient representatives related by the defining relation; classical choice selects an element from a nonempty type. A theorem may use only some of them.
lean_standard_axioms.rule: Compare reported axiom dependencies with the project's allowed set. Here, 'no added axioms' means no dependencies beyond that set, not an axiom-free theorem.
lean_standard_axioms.deep: Lean's manual also lists sorryAx among its standard implementation axioms, but it represents unfinished proofs and is excluded from finished results here. Native-evaluation proofs can introduce additional trust dependencies, which also need explicit treatment in an audit.

least_common_multiple.label: least common multiple
least_common_multiple.preview: For positive integers, the least common multiple is the smallest positive integer divisible by all of them.
least_common_multiple.card: For example, the least common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12. In prime factorisation, it keeps the highest exponent of each prime appearing in the inputs.
least_common_multiple.rule: Positivity matters because zero is also a common multiple but is not the intended minimum here.
least_common_multiple.deep: Least common multiples combine periodic conditions: an event repeating every 4 steps and one repeating every 6 steps align every 12 steps. Definitions involving zero or empty collections need their stated conventions.

lebesgue_measure.label: Lebesgue measure
lebesgue_measure.preview: Lebesgue measure generalises length on the real line, area in the plane, and volume in higher dimensions.
lebesgue_measure.card: For an interval it gives the usual length, but it also applies to many fragmented or irregular sets. A set can contain infinitely many points and still have measure zero.
lebesgue_measure.rule: Claims using Lebesgue measure apply to measurable sets in the stated space.
lebesgue_measure.deep: The papers use it to distinguish the size of a set from its number of points or its topological shape. Positive measure, containing an interval, and being infinite are different properties.

lemma.label: lemma
lemma.preview: A lemma is a proved statement introduced mainly to support another argument.
lemma.card: It has the same need for a valid proof as a theorem. The label describes its role in the exposition, not a lower standard of correctness or a guarantee that it is easy.
lemma.rule: Read its hypotheses before applying it to a later step.
lemma.deep: A lemma may isolate the main difficulty, provide a reusable technical fact, or organise a long proof. Counting lemmas therefore gives little information by itself about the number of distinct mathematical ideas.

lemniscate.label: lemniscate
lemniscate.preview: A polynomial lemniscate is a set defined by the size of a complex polynomial, commonly the curve \(|p(z)| = c\).
lemniscate.card: The term is also used, with qualification, for a sublevel region such as \(|p(z)| < c\) or \(|p(z)| \le c\). These regions can have several components surrounding the polynomial's roots.
lemniscate.rule: Check whether the paper means the level curve, the open region, or the filled closed region.
lemniscate.deep: In the Erdős #1041 material, paths inside the open unit region \(|p(z)| < 1\) are central. Being on its boundary is different from being inside it.

curve_length.label: length of a curve
curve_length.preview: A curve’s length is the supremum of the lengths of polygonal paths through successive points on the curve.
curve_length.card: A segment from (0,0) to \((3,4)\) has length 5. For a parametrised curve, each ordered partition gives a polygonal approximation. Curve length is the supremum over all these lengths; suitable successive partitions approach that supremum, whereas an arbitrary choice of samples need not.
curve_length.rule: A continuous curve may have infinite length; finite-length curves are called rectifiable. Retracing a segment counts its length again, even though no new points are added.
curve_length.deep: Problem 1041 is quantitative: connecting roots is insufficient unless the path inside the lemniscate also meets a degree-dependent length bound.

level_curve.label: level curve
level_curve.preview: A level curve is a curve along which a real-valued function has a constant value.
level_curve.card: Contour lines on a height map connect points at the same height. For \(g(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}\), the level at 1 is the unit circle. For \(g(x,y)=x^{2}-y^{2}\), the level at 0 instead crosses at the origin, so a level set need not form one smooth curve.
level_curve.rule: For a continuously differentiable planar function, a nonzero gradient at a point gives a continuously differentiable local level curve through that point.
level_curve.deep: The papers study curves where a polynomial’s magnitude has a fixed value. Away from critical points, local regularity gives a well-defined tangent, perpendicular to the gradient of the real-valued magnitude function when that gradient is defined. Critical levels can have crossings or changes in the number of components. The general term level set also covers higher-dimensional surfaces and isolated points; calling something a level curve requires the curve geometry in the passage to be justified.

level_set.label: level set
level_set.preview: All inputs at which a function takes one specified value.
level_set.card: For a real-valued function g, its level set at c is \(\{x : g(x)=c\}\). The level \(x^{2}+y^{2}=1\) is a circle; \(x^{2}-y^{2}=0\) is two crossing lines. A level set can also be empty or contain isolated points.
level_set.rule: Smoothness of the function alone does not make every level a smooth curve. For a continuously differentiable planar function, a nonzero gradient gives a smooth local curve through that point.
level_set.deep: In the lemniscate paper the function is \(g(z)=|p(z)|\), so \(|p(z)|=c\) names the level and \(|p(z)|<c\) names a region. At positive levels one can equally use the smooth function \(|p|^{2}\). A critical point on the level can create a crossing and invalidate arguments that need a single tangent.

limit.label: limit
limit.preview: “Limit” can mean a restriction or, in mathematics, the value approached by a sequence or function.
limit.card: On the system pages, a scope limit states how far a claim or action reaches. A service limit instead restricts use of a resource. Mathematical limits describe behaviour as an input approaches a point or infinity.
limit.rule: The surrounding phrase determines which meaning applies.
limit.deep: For a mathematical example, 1/n tends to the limit zero as n increases, although every term is positive. The separate mathematical-limit entry explains that precise sense in more detail.

limit_inferior.label: limit inferior
limit_inferior.preview: The limit inferior is the limiting lower bound obtained by discarding longer and longer finite beginnings of a sequence.
limit_inferior.card: For the oscillating sequence 1,0,1,0,…, the limit inferior is 0 while the limit superior is 1. For 1/n, both equal 0, matching the ordinary limit. Thus liminf records persistent low behavior.
limit_inferior.rule: Form the infimum of each tail \(\{a_{k}:k\ge n\}\); these tail infima increase, and their limit is liminf \(a_{n}\), possibly infinite. No term needs equal the result, and a one-time early minimum is irrelevant.
limit_inferior.deep: A finite liminf for consecutive prime gaps says gaps at most slightly above that level recur arbitrarily far out. It does not bound every sufficiently late gap, so large gaps may coexist with the bounded recurring subsequence.

limit_superior.label: limit superior
limit_superior.preview: The limit superior is the limiting upper bound obtained by discarding longer and longer finite beginnings of a sequence.
limit_superior.card: For 1,0,1,0,…, the limit superior is 1 and the limit inferior is 0. If a sequence converges, both values equal its limit; disagreement records lasting oscillation rather than a single early fluctuation.
limit_superior.rule: Take the supremum of each tail \(\{a_{k}:k\ge n\}\); these tail suprema decrease, and their limit is \(\limsup a_{n}\), allowing infinite values. The limsup need not occur as an actual term.
limit_superior.deep: The reciprocal-tail analysis uses limsup to control the worst ratios or jumps that recur arbitrarily late without assuming full convergence. A limsup bound is eventual in an approximate sense, not necessarily a pointwise bound at the limiting constant.

lineage.label: lineage
lineage.preview: Lineage records where an item came from and which transformations led to its present form.
lineage.card: For a generated page, it may identify source records, the builder, and the relevant versions. For a claim, it may connect an interpretation to earlier results or observations.
lineage.rule: Origin and correctness are separate questions: a traceable item can still contain an error.
lineage.deep: Plectis uses lineage to make copies and summaries inspectable. When a source changes, those connections help identify which derived artifacts may need to be rebuilt or reconsidered.

linear_combination.label: linear combination
linear_combination.preview: A linear combination is a finite sum of vectors multiplied by scalar coefficients.
linear_combination.card: Given vectors u and v, the expression 3u-2v is a linear combination: multiply each object by a scalar, then add. A finite linear combination may use many vectors, with zero coefficients effectively omitting some.
linear_combination.rule: The objects must belong to a common vector space, and coefficients must come from its scalar field, such as the rationals or reals. 'Nontrivial' means at least one coefficient is nonzero.
linear_combination.deep: The papers ask whether arithmetic sequences, functions, or series channels obey a nontrivial rational linear relation. Showing every zero linear combination has all coefficients zero proves independence; displaying one nonzero coefficient relation proves dependence.

torus_flow.label: linear flow on a torus
torus_flow.preview: Motion at constant velocity with each coordinate read modulo its period.
torus_flow.card: On \(\mathbb{R}^{d}/\mathbb{Z}^{d}\) it has the form \(\theta (t)=\theta _{0}+t\omega\) modulo \(\mathbb{Z}^{d}\). One coordinate behaves like a clock repeatedly wrapping around its circle. Rational relations among the velocity coordinates can confine the motion to a smaller subtorus.
torus_flow.rule: Continuous time t and sampled integer time n give different density tests. A continuous flow can fill a torus even though its time-one map visits only part of it.
torus_flow.deep: The #269 flow \(\Theta(s)=(s\bmod\log q)\) simultaneously records phases for several primes. A crossing of the q-coordinate marks a power of q; changing the starting phase can interchange two crossings. The proof uses recurrence and density inside the actual orbit closure, without assuming density in the full product.

linear_form.label: linear form
linear_form.preview: A linear form is an expression \(a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots +a_{n}x_{n}\), or equivalently a linear map from a vector space to its scalar field.
linear_form.card: In two variables, 3x-2y is an integer linear form. Evaluating it at particular numbers can create a small nonzero quantity; irrationality proofs exploit that a rational target cannot admit certain integer linear forms that approach zero too quickly.
linear_form.rule: A homogeneous linear form has no constant term. Authors sometimes call \(a_{0}+a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots\) an affine linear form, while number-theory prose may include 1 among the variables and still say linear form. “Integral” describes the coefficients, not necessarily the value.
linear_form.deep: The paper constructs integer combinations of 1 and \(F(a/b)\) whose absolute values tend to zero. If \(F(a/b)\) were rational, clearing its fixed denominator would force every nonzero combination to stay a definite distance from zero.

linear_independence.label: linear independence
linear_independence.preview: A family is linearly independent if no finite combination of its members equals zero unless every scalar coefficient is zero.
linear_independence.card: For example, \(a(1,0) + b(0,1) = (0,0)\) forces \(a = b = 0\), so those two plane vectors are independent. The vectors \((1,0)\) and \((2,0)\) are dependent because twice the first minus the second is zero.
linear_independence.rule: Always state the scalar field; rational independence can differ from real independence.
linear_independence.deep: Disjoint supports and nonsingular evaluation matrices certify that families of arithmetic sequences are independent.

linear_map.label: linear map
linear_map.preview: A linear map preserves vector addition and multiplication by scalars.
linear_map.card: Writing L for the map, \(L(u+v) = L(u)+L(v)\) and \(L(cu) = cL(u)\). For example, \(L(x,y) = (2x,2y)\) is linear over the reals; adding a fixed nonzero translation produces an affine map instead.
linear_map.rule: The vector spaces and allowed scalar field are part of the definition, and every linear map sends zero to zero.
linear_map.deep: Matrices represent linear maps after bases are chosen. The derivative of a differentiable function is also a linear map describing its first-order local change, even when the original function is nonlinear.

linear_recurrence.label: linear recurrence
linear_recurrence.preview: A linear recurrence expresses a sequence term as a linear combination of a fixed number of earlier terms, possibly with a separate forcing term.
linear_recurrence.card: The homogeneous order-two form is \(u_{n+2}=A_{n}u_{n+1}+B_{n}u_{n}\). Coefficients may depend on the index; constant-coefficient recurrences are a special case.
linear_recurrence.rule: Linearity concerns the unknown sequence for fixed coefficients. A system whose coefficients themselves depend on another evolving sequence can need additional analysis beyond the linear recurrence.
linear_recurrence.deep: Eliminating the denominator sequence in #243 yields \(u_{n+2}=(a_{n}+a_{n+1})u_{n+1}-a_{n}^{2}u_{n}\). This is linear in u once the multiplier sequence a is fixed. The relation is then combined with the exact eventual cubic and congruence constraints; it is not a constant-coefficient recurrence.

little_o_notation.label: little-o notation
little_o_notation.preview: A comparison saying one quantity becomes negligible relative to another.
little_o_notation.card: The function \(\log n\) is \(o(n)\) because \(\log n/n\) tends to zero. Although both grow without bound, \(\log n\) becomes negligible on the scale of n. In contrast, \(3n\) is \(O(n)\) but not \(o(n)\).
little_o_notation.rule: When g is nonzero near the stated limit, \(f=o(g)\) means \(f/g\to 0\). The limit and fixed parameters are part of the assertion. Little-o is strictly stronger than Big-O at the same comparison scale.
little_o_notation.deep: A block length \(o(\log \log X)\) may still increase, but its ratio to \(\log \log X\) vanishes. The notation controls relative size only; it supplies neither a universal numerical cutoff nor a rate of convergence unless further estimates are given.

living_system_posture.label: living system posture
living_system_posture.preview: Living system posture means treating claims about a changing system as statements about an identifiable state or version.
living_system_posture.card: A report can remain a valid record of an earlier run after the implementation has changed. Plectis distinguishes that historical record from evidence about the system as it exists now.
living_system_posture.rule: The relevant source and refresh rule determine whether an old observation still applies.
living_system_posture.deep: This does not make every mathematical theorem time-dependent. It concerns facts such as which proof version was checked, which files were published, or which behaviour a particular run demonstrated.

locus.label: locus
locus.preview: A locus is a place where something occurs or is defined; in mathematics, it can mean all points satisfying a condition.
locus.card: In the system documentation, a code locus identifies the file or function implementing a behaviour. In geometry, the locus of points at distance one from the origin is the unit circle.
locus.rule: The subject determines whether the word means a source location or a mathematical set.
locus.deep: Both uses help make a description precise: they replace an unspecified “somewhere” with a location or condition that can be examined directly.

log_file.label: log file
log_file.preview: A log file stores timestamped or ordered records produced while a program, service, or job runs.
log_file.card: Logs can record events, warnings, errors, identifiers, and diagnostic context. Their contents and retention depend on configuration, and absence of a log does not prove that nothing happened.
log_file.rule: Treat logs as scoped observations from the code that emitted them; correlate them with other evidence and protect sensitive data.
log_file.deep: Log files help reconstruct execution after the fact, but they can be incomplete, delayed, rotated, altered, or lost. A useful log states time, event, source, and correlation identity without exposing credentials or private payloads. Plectis queue reconciliation checks whether a claimed job’s log is present and current. That supports a liveness diagnosis; it does not by itself establish the job’s full result.

logarithm.label: logarithm
logarithm.preview: For a positive base b other than 1, the real logarithm \(\log_b(x)\) is the exponent y satisfying \(b^y=x\), for \(x > 0\).
logarithm.card: For example, \(\log_2(8)=3\) because \(2^{3}=8\). In advanced mathematics, \(\log\) without a base usually means the natural logarithm with base e.
logarithm.rule: For positive inputs, logarithms turn products into sums and real powers into multipliers: \(\log (xy) = \log x + \log y\) and \(\log (x^{a}) = a \log x\). Complex logarithms require separate branch choices.
logarithm.deep: The papers take logarithms of products and least common multiples to compare multiplicative growth efficiently using additive estimates and asymptotic scales.

logarithmic_capacity.label: logarithmic capacity
logarithmic_capacity.preview: A notion of size for a compact planar set, defined through the smallest logarithmic interaction energy of measures supported on it.
logarithmic_capacity.card: For a compact set K, set \(\operatorname{cap}(K)=\exp(-\inf I(\mu))\), where \(\mu\) ranges over probability measures on K and \(I(\mu )=\int \int \log (1/|z-w|) d\mu (z)d\mu (w)\). A disc of radius r has capacity r. Sets with infinite minimum energy have capacity zero.
logarithmic_capacity.rule: Capacity differs from area, perimeter and diameter. Scaling a set by a complex number a scales its capacity by \(|a|\), while area scales by \(|a|^{2}\). A root count alone does not determine capacity.
logarithmic_capacity.deep: The #1041 paper bounds the capacity of a selected lemniscate component and then converts that bound into an area estimate. Its component-capacity hypothesis measures a geometric saving that is stronger than merely having few roots in the component.

lower_semicontinuity.label: lower semicontinuity
lower_semicontinuity.preview: Lower semicontinuity means a function’s value at a limit point is no larger than the limit inferior of nearby values.
lower_semicontinuity.card: For real-valued functions on metric spaces, \(x_{n} \to x\) implies \(F(x) \le \liminf F(x_{n})\). A downward dip is allowed: \(F(0) = 0\) and \(F(x) = 1\) elsewhere is lower semicontinuous. Reversing those values creates an upward spike and fails the condition.
lower_semicontinuity.rule: The direction matters: lower semicontinuity helps minimise a function, because passing to a limit cannot increase its value above the limiting lower bound.
lower_semicontinuity.deep: It ensures the limiting polynomial competitor has path length no larger than the limiting lengths of approximating competitors.

machine_checked.label: machine-checked
machine_checked.preview: Machine-checked means software has verified a stated property of the supplied material.
machine_checked.card: The strength of that verification depends on the checker. A Lean kernel check concerns a formal proof; a schema check concerns a file's structure; a test run concerns behaviour on particular inputs.
machine_checked.rule: Always identify what was checked and by which method.
machine_checked.deep: The phrase alone does not mean that every surrounding claim is true. The encoded statement, assumptions, source version, and connection to the informal explanation determine how far a mathematical checking result reaches.

machine_readable.label: machine-readable
machine_readable.preview: Machine-readable information is structured so software can reliably parse and act on it.
machine_readable.card: JSON, CSV, typed records, and documented APIs can be machine-readable when their grammar and field meanings are explicit. Human-readable prose may still be processed by software, but ambiguity makes it a weaker contract. Machine readability concerns form, not truth or quality.
machine_readable.rule: Consistent interpretation depends on an agreed syntax and field meanings; stable identifiers and version rules matter when records are referenced or the format evolves.
machine_readable.deep: Machine-readable information has enough explicit structure for software to parse it consistently without relying on visual layout or open-ended human interpretation. Formats such as JSON, CSV, XML, typed records, and APIs can qualify when their syntax, encoding, field meanings, identifiers, and version rules are documented. Merely placing prose in a digital file does not provide the same contract. Successful parsing establishes structural acceptance, not truth, completeness, safety, or semantic agreement. Independent consumers also need evolution and compatibility rules when producers may add, remove, or reinterpret fields.

manifest.label: manifest
manifest.preview: A manifest is a structured inventory of the files or objects included in a build, package, or release.
manifest.card: It may record paths, versions, content digests, sizes, and relationships. Plectis uses such inventories to describe what a published collection contains and to support consistency checks.
manifest.rule: The manifest's listed content should agree with the actual files.
manifest.deep: A manifest helps detect missing, unexpected, or changed artifacts. It does not itself establish the correctness of their contents, and its own source and generation process need to remain identifiable.

map.label: map
map.preview: A map presents a collection and the relationships that help someone navigate it.
map.card: Plectis's software maps are generated views of stored objects, such as components and their dependencies. The view lets a reader choose a part before opening its detailed sources.
map.rule: In a mathematical passage, “map” commonly means a function instead.
map.deep: For a generated system map, completeness depends on what the underlying analysis captures. Links to source and a refresh record help readers understand both the represented relationships and the limits of the view.

mathematical_continuity.label: mathematical continuity
mathematical_continuity.preview: A function is continuous when sufficiently close inputs always produce sufficiently close outputs.
mathematical_continuity.card: For a function between metric spaces, continuity at x means that every output tolerance \(\varepsilon > 0\) has an input tolerance \(\delta > 0\): whenever y is less than \(\delta\) from x, \(f(y)\) is less than \(\varepsilon\) from \(f(x)\). For real or complex functions, these distances are written \(|y-x|\) and \(|f(y)-f(x)|\).
mathematical_continuity.rule: Continuity allows bending and changing speed but forbids jumps. A continuous path is a continuous function from an interval into the space being studied.
mathematical_continuity.deep: The lemniscate problem requires a path whose every point stays inside \(\{|f|<1\}\); continuity makes it one unbroken connection between the selected roots.

mathematical_induction.label: mathematical induction
mathematical_induction.preview: Mathematical induction proves a claim for every natural-number index by establishing a starting case and a valid step to the next case.
mathematical_induction.card: The step assumes the claim for an arbitrary index n and proves it for \(n+1\). Together with the base case, that gives the claim throughout the stated range.
mathematical_induction.rule: The starting index and induction hypothesis must match the statement being proved.
mathematical_induction.deep: Strong induction allows the step to use all earlier cases. The papers use these methods to establish recurrence formulas, divisibility propagation, and finite identities later used in arguments about limits.

mathematical_limit.label: mathematical limit
mathematical_limit.preview: A mathematical limit describes the value a sequence or function approaches as its index or input approaches a specified point or infinity.
mathematical_limit.card: For a real sequence with limit L, every positive tolerance around L eventually contains all later terms. The terms need not ever equal L; 1/n tends to zero while staying positive.
mathematical_limit.rule: The limit and the value at a particular input are different concepts.
mathematical_limit.deep: For functions, the relevant domain and direction of approach matter. An argument about an infinite sum uses the limit of its finite partial sums.

mathematical_priority.label: mathematical priority
mathematical_priority.preview: Mathematical priority concerns who first established or discovered a result, as supported by the scholarly record.
mathematical_priority.card: It can involve dated manuscripts, publications, communications, and careful comparison of what each source actually proved. Closely related results may have different hypotheses, conclusions, or forms of contribution.
mathematical_priority.rule: The project's own contribution records cannot settle an unresolved priority question by declaration.
mathematical_priority.deep: When this site says it asks for no priority on someone else's solution, it means using the project as a starting point does not give the project authorship of that person's result.

mathematician.label: mathematician
mathematician.preview: A mathematician studies mathematical structures and questions through definitions, reasoning, and proof.
mathematician.card: The term covers many specialisms and forms of work, including research, teaching, exposition, and applications. Expertise relevant to one paper may differ from the expertise needed for another.
mathematician.rule: The site invites mathematical judgement about correctness, context, significance, and useful next questions.
mathematician.deep: A contribution may clarify a proof, identify prior work, refute a proposed step, or find a new result. Its value depends on the work itself rather than on agreement with the project's current direction.

mathematics.label: mathematics
mathematics.preview: Mathematics studies patterns, quantities, structures, and relationships through precise definitions and logical reasoning.
mathematics.card: Its results are established by proof, while examples, computation, and conjectures help discover what might be true. The mathematical pages here focus on selected problems associated with Erdős and related formal work in Lean.
mathematics.rule: That collection is one research programme within a much wider subject.
mathematics.deep: The site distinguishes proved results, finite calculations, conditional arguments, and open questions so readers can understand what each artifact contributes without treating every mathematical-looking output as a theorem.

mathlib.label: Mathlib
mathlib.preview: Mathlib is the community-maintained library of mathematical definitions, theorems, and tools for Lean.
mathlib.card: It supplies reusable material across many fields, along with notation and tactics that help authors build further proofs. A local project can import the relevant modules instead of developing all foundations itself.
mathlib.rule: The Mathlib version is part of a formal project's reproducible environment.
mathlib.deep: Using a theorem from the library requires matching its assumptions and types. New declarations built on Mathlib should distinguish the project's contribution from results already supplied by the library.

matrix.label: matrix
matrix.preview: A matrix is a rectangular array of entries, often representing numerical data, simultaneous equations, or a linear map.
matrix.card: The matrix [[1,2],[3,4]] has two rows and two columns. Multiplying it by a coordinate vector forms prescribed linear combinations.
matrix.rule: Entries can be numbers or other elements of a specified algebraic system. Rows and columns have distinct roles; transposition interchanges them.
matrix.deep: Evaluation matrices record arithmetic functions at selected inputs so modular diagonal patterns can certify independence.

maximal_ideal.label: maximal ideal
maximal_ideal.preview: A maximal ideal is a proper ideal contained in no larger proper ideal.
maximal_ideal.card: In the integers, the maximal ideals are exactly the multiples of a prime p; the quotient is arithmetic modulo p. For a commutative ring with identity, an ideal is maximal exactly when its quotient is a field. The whole ring is excluded by the word proper.
maximal_ideal.rule: Maximal implies prime in a commutative ring with 1, but prime need not imply maximal. The zero ideal of Z is the simplest counterexample: Z has no zero divisors, yet Z itself is not a field.
maximal_ideal.deep: At a maximal ideal, the general residue-field construction simplifies: \(\kappa (m)=R/m\). This is why quotienting the ring of integers of a number field by a nonzero prime ideal directly produces a finite field.

maximum_principle.label: maximum principle
maximum_principle.preview: A maximum principle says that a function satisfying specified equations or inequalities cannot have a strict interior maximum, and often places its largest value on the boundary.
maximum_principle.card: For a nonconstant holomorphic function, the maximum modulus principle rules out an interior maximum of its absolute value. A harmonic function has an analogous principle for its value. On a closed disc, continuity at the boundary lets the corresponding maximum be located there.
maximum_principle.rule: For a harmonic function, a local interior maximum forces constancy on the connected component. For a holomorphic function, the analogous statement concerns its modulus. Boundary conclusions need additional hypotheses, especially on unbounded domains.
maximum_principle.deep: Each version needs its own hypotheses, including the domain and the equation or regularity condition on the function. A boundary statement on an unbounded region also needs control at infinity. The papers use the holomorphic and harmonic versions to carry a boundary estimate into the interior. For \(f(z)=z\) on the closed unit disc, the maximum modulus is 1, attained on its boundary.

mechanism.label: mechanism
mechanism.preview: A mechanism is the process or arrangement through which an outcome is produced.
mechanism.card: Explaining a mechanism means identifying relevant parts, inputs, steps, and interactions. In Plectis, that explanation connects a component’s stated behaviour to its implementation and evidence.
mechanism.rule: A label for an outcome does not explain the process that produces it.
mechanism.deep: For example, “detects drift” becomes inspectable when the explanation identifies two sources, the comparison rule, and the record produced when they disagree. A mechanism can exist before it is fully understood or documented.

mechanism_contract.label: mechanism contract
mechanism_contract.preview: A mechanism contract states what a component is expected to do and how that expectation can be checked.
mechanism_contract.card: It identifies the component's purpose, inputs or conditions, outputs, evidence, and scope limits. Plectis uses this information on component cards so readers can inspect different mechanisms with a consistent set of questions.
mechanism_contract.rule: The contract states the expectation; source and execution evidence show whether it is met.
mechanism_contract.deep: If the implementation or supported use changes, the contract needs to be reviewed with it. A broader description should not inherit evidence collected for an earlier, narrower behaviour.

meromorphic_function.label: meromorphic function
meromorphic_function.preview: A function holomorphic on its domain except at isolated poles.
meromorphic_function.card: Locally a meromorphic function can be written as a quotient of holomorphic functions with a denominator that is not identically zero. Rational functions are examples, but a meromorphic function on the complex plane need not be rational: it may have infinitely many poles.
meromorphic_function.rule: Poles cannot accumulate inside the domain. An essential singularity in the domain prevents meromorphicity there. A quotient may have removable points after common factors cancel, so its unreduced denominator alone does not locate genuine poles.
meromorphic_function.deep: The #1049 companion constructs a generating function with genuine poles at \(q^{-k}\), for \(0<q<1\). These points escape to infinity and show that the function is not rational. That structural fact still does not decide whether a chosen special value is rational.

mersenne_number.label: Mersenne number
mersenne_number.preview: A Mersenne number has the form \(2^n-1\) for a positive integer n.
mersenne_number.card: The sequence begins 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. Some are prime, but many are composite; “Mersenne prime” is the more specific term for a prime of this form.
mersenne_number.rule: In base two, \(2^n-1\) is written as n consecutive ones.
mersenne_number.deep: The Erdős #257 material studies reciprocal sums involving these denominators. Expressions \(b^n-1\) use a similar construction at another base, but the unqualified name Mersenne conventionally refers to base two.

metabolism.label: metabolism
metabolism.preview: “Metabolism” is Plectis's name for the recurring work that keeps stored knowledge and generated views in step with their sources.
metabolism.card: The process identifies changes, queues bounded work, refreshes affected artifacts, and records the checks. It covers upkeep such as rebuilding an index or incorporating a supported lesson into an existing rule.
metabolism.rule: The biological word is a metaphor for maintenance and renewal in the software.
metabolism.deep: The process should have explicit owners and stopping conditions. A refresh that runs successfully still needs to preserve source meaning and satisfy the checks governing its output.

metadata.label: metadata
metadata.preview: Metadata is information that describes other data, a file, a record, or an event.
metadata.card: Metadata can name a title, author, date, format, identifier, size, source, or status without containing the described material itself. It helps people and programs find, sort, validate, and interpret records.
metadata.rule: Read metadata as a description of an object or event; inspect the underlying content when the claim depends on that content.
metadata.deep: Metadata ranges from simple file properties to structured catalogue records and run summaries. It can support discovery and checking, but its accuracy depends on how it was produced and maintained. Plectis pages use metadata for identifiers, source routes, dates, counts, and declared status. A metadata record is evidence about those fields, not a substitute for the source body or the event it describes.

metadata_only.label: metadata-only
metadata_only.preview: Metadata-only means a record contains information about material or a run without including the underlying bodies themselves.
metadata_only.card: It may list counts, identifiers, classifications, digests, and outcomes while omitting the source text or inputs. This can make a record smaller or limit what it discloses.
metadata_only.rule: The omitted content may still be necessary to independently inspect or repeat the work.
metadata_only.deep: A digest can identify a file but cannot reconstruct it. A metadata-only result therefore needs an appropriate source route if readers are expected to examine the evidence behind its verdict.

metric.label: metric
metric.preview: A metric is either a defined performance measure or, in mathematics, a distance function satisfying the metric axioms.
metric.card: Response time and error rate are evaluation metrics. A mathematical metric assigns a distance \(d(x,y)\) to each pair of points, with zero only for identical points, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
metric.rule: A performance metric has a formula, units, population, and interpretation; a mathematical metric instead defines distances and must satisfy non-negativity, identity, symmetry, and triangle inequality.
metric.deep: The two senses should remain separate. Evaluation metrics summarize speed, accuracy, coverage, cost, or risk and can be useful without behaving like distances. A mathematical metric creates a geometry: it determines which points are near, which sequences converge, and which sets are open. Different metrics on the same objects can produce different numerical distances. Optimizing a performance metric can also worsen the underlying goal when the number is only a proxy, omits important cases, changes incentives, or hides trade-offs between groups.

metric_space.label: metric space
metric_space.preview: A metric space is a set equipped with a distance satisfying the standard rules of separation, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
metric_space.card: A distance is zero exactly between identical points, gives the same answer in either direction, and is no greater than the sum of distances through a third point. The real line with distance \(|x-y|\) is an example.
metric_space.rule: The distance is part of the space: the same underlying points can carry different metrics.
metric_space.deep: This lets analysis discuss closeness, continuity, convergence, and compactness beyond the ordinary plane. The lemniscate papers compare Euclidean and hyperbolic distances, whose lengths differ even when drawn using the same disc.

microcosm.label: Microcosm
microcosm.preview: Microcosm is an earlier public name for Plectis that remains in some technical paths and compatibility identifiers.
microcosm.card: Existing package names, schemas, files, and links may retain the old spelling to preserve compatibility and traceability. Current reader-facing descriptions use Plectis for the project.
microcosm.rule: The presence of the old name does not by itself identify a separate project or release.
microcosm.deep: An ordinary phrase such as “a microcosm of a larger system” has a different meaning: a small representative example. The glossary keeps that everyday sense separate from this historical project identifier.

minimal_polynomial.label: minimal polynomial
minimal_polynomial.preview: The minimal polynomial of an algebraic element over a field is the monic polynomial of least positive degree over that field that vanishes at the element.
minimal_polynomial.card: Over \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\sqrt 2\) has minimal polynomial \(T^{2}-2\). Every polynomial over the same field that vanishes at \(\sqrt 2\) is divisible by it.
minimal_polynomial.rule: The base field is part of the definition: over \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt 2)\), the same element has minimal polynomial \(T-\sqrt 2\). Transcendental elements have no such nonzero polynomial.
minimal_polynomial.deep: In #243, \(z=\alpha +\beta\) generates the cubic field K. Its minimal polynomial over \(\mathbb{Q}\) therefore has degree three. The proof writes it as \(T^{3}+bT^{2}+dT+w\) and compares its coefficients with those of the polynomial for \(z^{-1}\).

mining.label: mining
mining.preview: Here, “mining” means sustained searching through candidate arguments and experiments for useful mathematical results or failures.
mining.card: A person or agent follows a research direction, tries approaches, checks candidates, and preserves useful outcomes. The term describes repeated exploration rather than a single answer to a prompt.
mining.rule: The amount of computation does not determine the value of what is found.
mining.deep: Results still need verification, explanation, and attribution. A failed approach can be useful when it records a precise obstruction, while many unchecked drafts may add little to the understanding of a problem.

minor_of_matrix.label: minor of a matrix
minor_of_matrix.preview: A determinant obtained by selecting equally many rows and columns from a matrix.
minor_of_matrix.card: Select two rows and two columns from a larger matrix; the determinant of the resulting \(2\times2\) square is a minor. Different selections can produce zero or nonzero minors of the same order.
minor_of_matrix.rule: A nonzero \(k\times k\) minor proves matrix rank at least k. Depending on convention, 'minor' may name the selected square submatrix or its determinant, so formulas and context should disambiguate.
minor_of_matrix.deep: The running-LCM paper constructs nonsingular minors of every order. Each such certificate supplies a finite independent family; having them for arbitrarily large k rules out any fixed finite-dimensional bound.

model.label: model
model.preview: A model is a representation used to describe, predict, or reason about something.
model.card: Here the word often refers to an AI model used by an agent. In mathematics, a model may instead be a structure satisfying a theory's axioms; in software, a data model specifies how information is organised.
model.rule: The surrounding qualifier identifies the intended meaning.
model.deep: An AI model is only one part of an agent's working setup. Tools, instructions, available evidence, and permissions also affect what the agent can do and what its answers can establish.

module.label: module
module.preview: A module is a unit of code or written material organised around a subject or responsibility.
module.card: A code module groups related definitions and exposes interfaces to other code. A Plectis paper module explains a subsystem and links its concepts, implementation, and evidence.
module.rule: The module's dependencies determine what else is needed to understand or use it.
module.deep: The same word also has a separate algebraic meaning, generalising a vector space from a field to a ring. That mathematical use must be read from its own definitions and context.

modulus.label: modulus
modulus.preview: Modulus means the integer defining a modular-arithmetic relation, or the magnitude of a complex number.
modulus.card: Modulo 5, integers fall into five classes represented by 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Changing the modulus changes these classes and the divisibility information they retain.
modulus.rule: In a complex-number passage, “modulus” instead means magnitude: \(|z|\) is the distance of z from zero.
modulus.deep: Both meanings occur in these papers. A phrase such as “critical-value modulus” refers to a complex magnitude, while “modulo m” refers to arithmetic with integer remainders.

moment_sequence.label: moment sequence
moment_sequence.preview: A moment sequence records integrals of successive powers against a measure, whenever those integrals are finite.
moment_sequence.card: The nth moment is \(\mu _{n}=\int x^{n}d\mu (x)\). For point masses with weights \(w_{k}\) at nodes \(x_{k}\), it becomes \(\sum _{k}w_{k}x_{k}^{n}\). A positive measure need not have total mass one.
moment_sequence.rule: Specify the measure, nodes, weights, and range of finite moments. These are power moments, not necessarily moments about the mean of a probability distribution.
moment_sequence.deep: The #1049 paper rewrites coefficients as moments on geometric nodes \(q^{k}\), with \(0<q<1\). Positivity of the weights allows a determinant expansion with nonnegative contributions and supports the subsequent asymptotic estimates.

monic.label: monic
monic.preview: A polynomial is monic if its leading coefficient is 1.
monic.card: The leading coefficient multiplies its highest-degree nonzero term. For example, \(z^{3} + 2z - 7\) is monic, while \(3z^{3} + 2z - 7\) is not.
monic.rule: This normalisation concerns the polynomial's scale, not the positions of its roots alone.
monic.deep: In lemniscate questions, multiplying a polynomial by a constant changes sets defined by \(|p(z)| < 1\) or \(|p(z)| = 1\). A monic hypothesis therefore matters to geometric statements about those sets.

monodromy.label: monodromy
monodromy.preview: Monodromy describes how a locally defined branch changes when analytically continued around loops; the monodromy theorem gives path independence under suitable simply connected hypotheses.
monodromy.card: A square root chosen near 1 returns with the opposite sign after continuation once around 0, showing nontrivial monodromy on the punctured plane. On a simply connected region avoiding 0, a consistent square-root branch can be chosen.
monodromy.rule: Local uniqueness of analytic continuation need not give one branch around every loop. The monodromy theorem gives conditions for path independence; monodromy describes what happens when path independence fails as well.
monodromy.deep: The paper invokes monodromy to turn a local inverse into one branch on a disc after excluding finite branch points and escape. The term names the global compatibility step, not merely the act of extending a function.

monodromy_theorem.label: monodromy theorem
monodromy_theorem.preview: The monodromy theorem says that a holomorphic function defined near one starting point extends to a single-valued function on a simply connected domain if it can be continued along every path there.
monodromy_theorem.card: A logarithm chosen near 1 can be continued consistently throughout the slit plane \(\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,0]\), which is simply connected and avoids 0. On the punctured plane \(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\), going once around 0 changes a continued logarithm by \(2\pi i\), so the conclusion fails because the domain has a hole.
monodromy_theorem.rule: Fix a base point and an initial holomorphic germ. One must know that analytic continuation exists along every path from that base point inside the domain. Simple connectivity then makes continuations along paths with the same endpoint agree. Local invertibility at the starting point alone supplies neither global continuation nor path independence.
monodromy_theorem.deep: A germ means a function specified near a point, with two such descriptions considered equivalent when they agree on some smaller neighbourhood. Continuations along paths deformable into one another with endpoints fixed give the same final germ, under the continuation hypotheses. In a simply connected domain, paths with the same endpoints are related this way, so the local functions agree and assemble into one holomorphic function. Singularities, escape of inverse branches, or failure of continuation along even one path can prevent the theorem from applying.

monotone_sequence.label: monotone sequence
monotone_sequence.preview: A monotone sequence is either nondecreasing at every step or nonincreasing at every step.
monotone_sequence.card: 1,2,2,5 is nondecreasing; 5,3,3,0 is nonincreasing. 'Strictly increasing' requires each next term to be larger.
monotone_sequence.rule: State whether equality is allowed and whether the direction is increasing or decreasing.
monotone_sequence.deep: The papers use increasing sequences to list selected exponents in order. Strict increase additionally prevents repetitions. A proof using only monotonicity cannot silently assume this stronger condition.

morse_chart.label: Morse chart
morse_chart.preview: A Morse chart is a local coordinate system near a nondegenerate critical point in which a smooth function becomes a quadratic form with plus and minus squares.
morse_chart.card: Near a saddle on a surface, suitable coordinates make the function look like \(c+x^{2}-y^{2}\). Its level set at c crosses at the critical point, while nearby levels form branches whose connections change across that value.
morse_chart.rule: The Morse lemma requires a nondegenerate Hessian. The number of negative squares is the Morse index and does not depend on the chosen chart. A degenerate critical point need not admit this normal form.
morse_chart.deep: The paper uses a Morse chart around an index-one critical point to model the local saddle. The audit then notes that the local quadratic picture alone cannot determine how branches reconnect through a surrounding annulus.

morse_saddle.label: Morse saddle
morse_saddle.preview: A Morse saddle is a critical point of a smooth real-valued function whose second-order form is nondegenerate and has both positive and negative directions.
morse_saddle.card: In two dimensions, the local behaviour resembles \(x^{2} - y^{2}\) after a suitable change of coordinates: the value rises in some directions and falls in others. Nondegeneracy rules out flat second-order directions.
morse_saddle.rule: At a planar saddle, the level set through the point has four local half-branches.
morse_saddle.deep: The lemniscate arguments use this local geometry. It must be distinguished from the behaviour of a singular flow or a degenerate critical point, where additional analysis is required.

multinomial_coefficient.label: multinomial coefficient
multinomial_coefficient.preview: A multinomial coefficient counts ways to divide a finite set into labelled groups of prescribed sizes.
multinomial_coefficient.card: For nonnegative integers \(k_{1},\ldots ,k_{r}\) with total n, it equals \(n!/(k_{1}!\cdots k_{r}!)\). For two groups this is the ordinary binomial coefficient.
multinomial_coefficient.rule: The group labels matter, but the order within each group does not. The factorial quotient is an integer because it counts these allocations.
multinomial_coefficient.deep: In #68, writing \(n=kd+r\) identifies \(n!/(d!)^{k}\) as \(r!\) times the multinomial coefficient with k groups of size d and one of size r. This directly proves the channel weight is integral, an essential input before small-tail estimates can force an integer contradiction.

multiple.label: multiple
multiple.preview: In arithmetic, a multiple of an integer d is a number d·k for some integer k.
multiple.card: For example, 12 is a multiple of 3 because \(12 = 3\cdot 4\). A common multiple of several positive integers is divisible by every one of them.
multiple.rule: The adjective “multiple” also means “more than one” in ordinary prose.
multiple.deep: In phrases such as “multiple root”, it has a more specific algebraic role: a root occurs with multiplicity greater than one. The surrounding noun therefore matters when reading this word in a paper.

multiple_root.label: multiple root
multiple_root.preview: A multiple root of a nonzero polynomial is a root appearing with multiplicity at least two.
multiple_root.card: For example, \(z^{2} - 2z + 1 = (z - 1)^{2}\) has 1 as a double root. In general, multiplicity k means \((z - a)^{k}\) divides the polynomial but the next power does not.
multiple_root.rule: Over the real or complex numbers, every multiple root is also a root of the derivative.
multiple_root.deep: This changes local geometry and root counting. A polynomial's degree counts roots over the complex numbers with multiplicity, while the number of distinct root locations can be smaller.

multiplicative_function.label: multiplicative function
multiplicative_function.preview: An arithmetic function f is multiplicative if \(f(1) = 1\) and \(f(mn) = f(m)f(n)\) whenever m and n are coprime.
multiplicative_function.card: Euler’s totient is multiplicative: since 3 and 5 are coprime, \(\varphi (15) = \varphi (3)\varphi (5) = 2\cdot 4 = 8\). Sharing a prime changes matters: \(\varphi (9) = 6\), whereas \(\varphi (3)\varphi (3) = 4\).
multiplicative_function.rule: An arithmetic function f is multiplicative when \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(mn)=f(m)f(n)\) for coprime m,n. Completely multiplicative functions obey the product rule without the coprimality restriction.
multiplicative_function.deep: The totient papers split values into independent local prime factors by arranging coprime inputs. The distinction between multiplicative and completely multiplicative prevents applying a valid coprime factorization across overlapping prime powers.

multiplicative_order.label: multiplicative order
multiplicative_order.preview: For b coprime to a positive modulus Q, the multiplicative order is the least positive k for which \(b^{k} \equiv 1\) modulo Q.
multiplicative_order.card: It measures the repetition period of powers of b in modular arithmetic. For example, the order of 2 modulo 7 is 3, since \(2^{3}\) leaves remainder 1 and no smaller positive exponent does.
multiplicative_order.rule: Finding an exponent with remainder 1 gives a period, which need not be the least one.
multiplicative_order.deep: Exact order requires a minimality argument. The papers use this distinction when connecting denominator arithmetic with periodic digit patterns and finite certificates.

mutability.label: mutable
mutability.preview: Mutable describes a value, object, or record that can change after it is created.
mutability.card: Mutation can be useful for updating live state, but readers need to know who may change it and how past versions or concurrent readers are handled.
mutability.rule: Do not use a mutable projection as permanent evidence unless the relevant version or source identity is fixed.
mutability.deep: Mutable state can change in place, so two observations at different times may disagree without either observation being fabricated. Programs manage this through ownership, locks, transactions, versioning, or immutable snapshots. Plectis rejects claims that treat a generated mutable projection as source authority. Mutability is not itself a defect; it becomes a problem when a consumer assumes stability that the producer does not promise.

mobius_function.label: möbius function
mobius_function.preview: The Möbius function \(\mu\) assigns each positive integer a value determined by its prime factorisation: zero for repeated prime factors, otherwise a sign.
mobius_function.card: The Möbius function has \(\mu (1)=1\). It is zero when a prime square divides n; otherwise \(\mu (n)=(-1)^k\) for a product of k distinct primes. Thus \(\mu (6)=1\), \(\mu (30)=-1\), and \(\mu (12)=0\).
mobius_function.rule: Its square \(\mu (n)^{2}\) is the indicator of squarefree integers. Under Dirichlet convolution, \(\mu\) inverts the constant-one function, yielding Möbius inversion formulas that recover data from divisor sums.
mobius_function.deep: The totient-series work uses Möbius-square terms to select squarefree indices and translate arithmetic identities into coprimality-probability coordinates. This arithmetic function is unrelated to Möbius transformations from complex geometry.

named_basis.label: named basis
named_basis.preview: A named basis identifies the exact inputs, assumptions, or sources on which a claim rests.
named_basis.card: Plectis uses the phrase to make a result reproducible and inspectable: the supporting material should be specified precisely enough for another checker or reader to examine it.
named_basis.rule: This is a statement of support, distinct from a vector-space basis in linear algebra.
named_basis.deep: A path without a version may not identify the bytes used in an earlier run. Source revisions, content digests, and explicit hypotheses help preserve the intended basis as files and explanations change.

namespace.label: namespace
namespace.preview: A namespace is a scope within which names identify objects without colliding with the same names used elsewhere.
namespace.card: Two components can use the same local name without collision when each name belongs to a different namespace. Namespaces appear in programming languages, XML, package systems, and route registries.
namespace.rule: Interpret an identifier together with its namespace; the same text in another namespace may denote something else.
namespace.deep: Namespaces organise names rather than copying the objects those names identify. A qualified name usually combines a namespace with a local identifier. Plectis uses route and registry namespaces so stable IDs can be resolved by the correct owner. Changing a namespace or dropping its qualifier can break references even when the local text remains unchanged.

natural_number.label: natural number
natural_number.preview: A natural number is a counting number; in Lean, the natural numbers include zero: 0, 1, 2, 3, … .
natural_number.card: Mathematical authors differ on whether their notation \(\mathbb{N}\) starts at zero or one. Lean's type `Nat` starts at zero, and positivity must be stated separately when needed.
natural_number.rule: Check the convention in a paper rather than inferring it from the phrase alone.
natural_number.deep: This matters for factorials, denominators, and sequence indices. A theorem valid for positive n may need a separate hypothesis or a separate zero case when encoded over `Nat`.

navigation.label: navigation
navigation.preview: Navigation is the process of finding and moving between relevant parts of a body of information.
navigation.card: Plectis provides collections, summaries, search, links, and command routes to help a reader reach the source needed for a task. Different levels of detail let the reader narrow the question before opening large files.
navigation.rule: Navigation should preserve the identity and meaning of the selected object across views.
navigation.deep: A good route reduces unnecessary reading while keeping evidence accessible. It cannot replace the underlying material when the task requires checking a claim or changing an implementation.

necessary_and_sufficient.label: necessary and sufficient
necessary_and_sufficient.preview: A condition is necessary and sufficient for a statement when each implies the other.
necessary_and_sufficient.card: Necessary means the statement cannot hold without the condition. Sufficient means the condition guarantees the statement. Together they give an equivalence, often written “if and only if” or \(\leftrightarrow\).
necessary_and_sufficient.rule: A condition can have one of these roles without having the other.
necessary_and_sufficient.deep: For example, divisibility by 4 is sufficient for an integer to be even but is not necessary: 6 is even. Distinguishing the directions prevents a stronger research target from being mistaken for the original problem.

negative_case.label: negative case
negative_case.preview: A negative case is a test input designed to exercise a failure or refusal that the system should detect.
negative_case.card: It accompanies valid inputs so a checker cannot appear successful simply by accepting everything. Plectis may plant a forged result, missing action, or invalid condition and verify that the appropriate finding is produced.
negative_case.rule: The expected response must be stated for the particular case.
negative_case.deep: Rejecting one planted error supports that detection path. It does not establish that every possible error will be detected, and valid inputs are also needed to check for inappropriate refusals.

neighbourhood.label: neighbourhood
neighbourhood.preview: A set containing an open set around a specified point or subset.
neighbourhood.card: For a point x in the plane, any set containing a small open disc centred at x is a neighbourhood of x. Its size may depend on x.
neighbourhood.rule: Authors sometimes say neighbourhood for the open disc itself and sometimes for any set containing one; the common content is local room around the target.
neighbourhood.deep: The paper needs neighbourhoods where analytic expansions converge and saddle geometry has a controlled local form before connecting it to global paths.

newton_flow.label: Newton flow
newton_flow.preview: For a complex polynomial p, the Newton flow studied here follows the differential equation \(z' = -p(z)/p'(z)\) where \(p'(z) \ne 0\).
newton_flow.card: It is a continuous analogue of Newton's root-finding iteration. Along a regular trajectory, the chain rule gives \(d(p(z(t)))/dt = -p(z(t))\), so the polynomial value decays exponentially.
newton_flow.rule: The displayed vector field is undefined at critical points where p′ vanishes.
newton_flow.deep: This limitation matters in the lemniscate arguments: local trajectories and their behaviour near critical points require separate justification. The decay identity applies only along intervals where the trajectory is defined and p′ does not vanish.

newton_identities.label: Newton identities
newton_identities.preview: Newton identities relate the sums of powers of a polynomial’s roots to its coefficients, through the elementary symmetric sums.
newton_identities.card: If a monic polynomial begins \(T^{d}+c_{1}T^{d-1}+c_{2}T^{d-2}\), and \(s_{j}\) is the sum of jth powers of its roots, then \(s_{1}+c_{1}=0\) and \(s_{2}+c_{1}s_{1}+2c_{2}=0\).
newton_identities.rule: The identities themselves hold over commutative rings. Solving them by division requires the relevant integers to be invertible; characteristic-zero fields permit this.
