simulation.card: Simulation permits controlled experiments when direct observation is costly, slow, dangerous, or impossible. Its results describe the modelled system and inherit the model's assumptions, simplifications, and parameter choices.
simulation.rule: A simulation result is conditional on the model, initial conditions, parameters, numerical method, and random inputs; agreement within the simulation is distinct from validation against observations of the target system.
simulation.deep: A simulation represents selected features of a process and calculates how that representation evolves. Deterministic simulations replay fixed equations or rules, while stochastic simulations sample uncertain events, often many times, to estimate a distribution of outcomes. Resolution, discretization, parameter choice, and random seeds can materially change the result. Verification asks whether the program implements the intended model; validation asks whether that model adequately represents the real system for the proposed use. A simulation can expose consequences, sensitivities, and failure modes without establishing that the same behaviour occurs outside the model.

skill.label: skill
skill.preview: In this system, a skill is a reusable set of instructions for carrying out a recognisable kind of task.
skill.card: It states when it applies, the steps to follow, relevant constraints, and routes to governing material. Agents can discover and reuse it instead of reconstructing the workflow from scratch.
skill.rule: A skill is procedural guidance; a component is implemented machinery that may carry out part of it.
skill.deep: The skill should stay aligned with the tools and rules it names. An instruction pointing to an obsolete command needs repair even if its general advice remains sound.

slice.label: slice
slice.preview: A slice is a selected part of a larger collection or system.
slice.card: Plectis uses the word for bounded sets of files, records, or components included in a task or public release. Naming the selection makes it clear what can be inspected or changed.
slice.rule: The selection's boundary should be explicit rather than inferred from its title.
slice.deep: A public slice can be independently runnable while the wider system remains unpublished. Evidence about that slice applies to its included material and tested interactions, with any broader conclusions requiring additional support.

smoke_check.label: smoke check
smoke_check.preview: A smoke check is a quick test for major failures in basic operation.
smoke_check.card: It might confirm that an application starts, an example command runs, or a key page loads. The aim is to catch obvious breakage before investing in more detailed checks.
smoke_check.rule: A smoke check deliberately has limited coverage.
smoke_check.deep: Its success is a useful first signal, not a comprehensive assessment of correctness. Plectis should identify the basic behaviour exercised so readers can tell which further checks are needed for a particular change.

smooth_function.label: smooth function
smooth_function.preview: A smooth function has continuous derivatives of every finite order in its stated mathematical setting.
smooth_function.card: Every polynomial is smooth, including at points where its first derivative is zero. Smoothness allows repeated differentiation but does not imply that a real function equals its Taylor series. A function can therefore be smooth without being analytic.
smooth_function.rule: Read smooth as C-infinity unless the source explicitly gives a finite differentiability class such as C-one or C-two.
smooth_function.deep: A smooth, or C-infinity, function has derivatives of every order and all those derivatives are continuous. For maps between Euclidean spaces, this means every iterated partial derivative exists and is continuous. On manifolds the definition is made through smooth coordinate charts. Smoothness is a regularity condition, not a claim of analyticity, convexity, or absence of critical points. In optimization prose, a smooth cell often means a region where the active formula and its derivatives vary smoothly; boundaries where the active branch changes may fail to share that regularity.

smooth_number.label: smooth number
smooth_number.preview: A smooth number is a positive integer whose prime factors all lie below a stated bound, or in a stated allowed prime set.
smooth_number.card: Relative to the set {2,3}, numbers such as 1, 8, 12, and 27 are smooth, while 10 is not. Repeated prime factors are allowed.
smooth_number.rule: Specify the bound or allowed prime set. Some conventions use primes \(\le y\) and others primes \(<y\); mathlib’s Nat.smoothNumbers uses the strict bound.
smooth_number.deep: The #257 P-part extracts all allowed prime factors with their multiplicities. The #269 running LCM likewise uses integers built from a specified prime set. Smoothness limits which primes occur; squarefreeness limits their multiplicities.

snapshot.label: snapshot
snapshot.preview: A snapshot is a captured representation of data or system state associated with a particular point or version.
snapshot.card: A database snapshot can preserve records as they appeared at noon; a repository snapshot can preserve one commit. Later changes do not make that snapshot inaccurate, but they do make it stale as a description of current state.
snapshot.rule: Snapshot meaning depends on capture time, scope, consistency guarantees, source version, included external state, and whether content is copied or referenced immutably.
snapshot.deep: Snapshots support comparison, recovery, audit, and reproducibility by fixing a view that would otherwise change. They may be full copies, incremental differences, filesystem references, database-consistent views, or application exports. Capturing related systems at different moments can create an internally inconsistent composite. A snapshot also may omit caches, secrets, running processes, external services, or uncommitted changes. Restoring it recreates only the state actually captured, and a successful restore does not establish that newer dependent systems remain compatible.

software.label: software
software.preview: Software consists of programs and related data used by computers to perform tasks.
software.card: On this site, the software section presents Plectis's reusable research components and the machinery supporting its workflow. It is distinguished from the mathematical reading routes, although formal proofs also use software tools.
software.rule: Each published component needs its own description, dependencies, and evidence.
software.deep: A repository can make implementation available without demonstrating every advertised use. The source, runnable example, and recorded check together help a reader assess the particular behaviour being claimed.

library.label: software library
library.preview: A software library is a reusable collection of code, interfaces, or formal definitions intended for other programs or developments to use.
library.card: Libraries can be source packages, compiled objects, runtime modules, or formal collections such as Mathlib. Their exposed interfaces supply reusable operations or results. Consumers depend on the relevant version, behaviour, licence, and compatibility with other parts of their program or proof development.
library.rule: When a result depends on a software library, record the exact package, version or revision, relevant interface assumptions, and environment used.
library.deep: A library differs from an application because it primarily supplies capabilities to consumers rather than owning the whole interaction, although packages can contain both. Public interfaces form the supported contract; internal implementation may change between compatible releases. Static and dynamic libraries link differently, while interpreted packages load through a runtime. Formal libraries contribute checked definitions and theorems. Dependency updates can alter behavior or proof meaning, so reproducibility requires pinned identity and transitive dependencies, not merely the library’s familiar name.

source.label: source
source.preview: A source is the original or controlling material from which a particular claim or artifact is drawn.
source.card: Here it often means code, a structured record, a theorem declaration, or a document linked from a generated page. Which source matters depends on the question being asked.
source.rule: Source for implementation and source for human intent need not be the same material.
source.deep: A reliable explanation identifies the relevant source precisely, including a version where necessary. Opening it lets a reader check the detail that a summary may simplify or omit.

source_body.label: source body
source_body.preview: A source body is the actual content of the code or document being referenced.
source_body.card: In a component bundle, it can be the full function or module implementation, as distinct from its signature, description, path, or digest. Including the body makes direct inspection possible.
source_body.rule: The body needs an identifiable version and context to explain which material it represents.
source_body.deep: A function may also depend on imports, configuration, or other files outside its displayed body. The bundle should make those dependencies clear if readers are expected to reproduce its behaviour.

source_file.label: source file
source_file.preview: A source file contains material from which another artifact is built or defined.
source_file.card: Source files can be written by people or generated by tools. Their role as source is relative to the build or transformation being discussed.
source_file.rule: Being a source file does not automatically make it the editable authority for every workflow.
source_file.deep: Plectis identifies the owning source and builder so generated material can be refreshed correctly. Editing a generated source copy may be overwritten by the next update unless its upstream owner is changed.

source_slice.label: source slice
source_slice.preview: A source slice is the explicitly selected source material included in a task, package, or public release.
source_slice.card: It can contain files and dependencies needed to support particular pages, components, or results. Plectis publishes bounded slices so readers can inspect relevant machinery without receiving the entire private working repository.
source_slice.rule: The inventory determines what the slice includes and excludes.
source_slice.deep: Its claims should fit that selection. If an example relies on omitted material, the dependency must be disclosed or included before the example can be described as independently reproducible.

span.label: linear span
span.preview: In linear algebra, the span of a set of vectors is the set of all finite linear combinations of them.
span.card: A linear combination scales vectors by allowed scalars and adds the results. For example, two nonparallel vectors in the ordinary plane span the plane; one nonzero vector spans a line through the origin.
span.rule: A spanning family may contain redundant vectors and need not be a basis.
span.deep: The underlying field and vector space matter. Claims about dimension concern the amount of independent structure in the span, not merely how many vectors were listed.

sparse_checkout.label: sparse checkout
sparse_checkout.preview: A sparse checkout limits which tracked files Git places in the working directory.
sparse_checkout.card: It lets someone work on selected directories while the repository's history and object database may still cover a larger project. This can make a large checkout easier to navigate and use.
sparse_checkout.rule: Sparse checkout alone does not mean that only those files were downloaded.
sparse_checkout.deep: Reducing downloads is a separate capability of partial or filtered clones. The public instructions should distinguish those operations so readers understand which files are present locally and which data may still need to be fetched.

specification.label: specification
specification.preview: A specification states the requirements an implementation or result is expected to satisfy.
specification.card: It can define behaviour, data structure, interfaces, inputs, outputs, or permitted assumptions. A test or formal verification then checks some relationship between the implementation and those requirements.
specification.rule: The specification must itself express the intended task accurately.
specification.deep: A perfectly checked implementation of the wrong requirement can still fail the user's goal. Plectis therefore links requirements, source, and evidence so reviewers can examine both the check and the meaning of what it checks.

squarefree.label: squarefree
squarefree.preview: Squarefree means having no repeated prime factor for an integer, or no repeated irreducible factor for a nonzero polynomial.
squarefree.card: The integer \(30=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\) is squarefree, while \(12=2^{2}\cdot 3\) is not. Over the complex numbers, a nonzero polynomial is squarefree exactly when every root is simple: \((z-1)(z+1)\) qualifies, while \((z-1)^{2}\) does not.
squarefree.rule: The integer 1 and nonzero constant polynomials are squarefree; zero is not. Polynomial factors are taken over the specified coefficient field.
squarefree.deep: The same idea removes repeated factors in two settings. An irreducible polynomial factor cannot be split into lower-degree factors over its coefficient field. Over the complex numbers every nonconstant polynomial splits into linear factors, so squarefreeness becomes distinctness of roots, equivalently no common root of p and p′. The number-theory papers use squarefree integers in counting arguments, while the lemniscate papers use squarefree polynomials to control root geometry. These applications share a factorisation property without treating integers and polynomials as the same objects.

stack_trace.label: stack trace
stack_trace.preview: A stack trace is a recorded list of active function calls at or near the point where a program failed or was inspected.
stack_trace.card: It usually names functions, files, and line numbers from the newest call back through its callers. It helps locate an execution path but may expose local paths or sensitive values.
stack_trace.rule: A stack trace locates a sequence of calls. The error, inputs, code, and environment supply the further evidence needed to explain why that path failed.
stack_trace.deep: A stack trace is diagnostic evidence about control flow, not a complete explanation of a failure. Optimisation, asynchronous execution, omitted frames, or generated code can make it incomplete or indirect. Plectis distinguishes reporting a degraded provider result from terminating with a stack trace. Public reports should redact private paths and secrets while retaining enough frames to diagnose the failure.

standard.label: standard
standard.preview: A standard specifies requirements that items or processes are expected to meet.
standard.card: Plectis stores standards as structured contracts covering fields, meanings, authority, validation, and maintenance. They give people and tools a common basis for writing and checking particular artifact kinds.
standard.rule: A standard states the requirement; evidence shows whether an item satisfies it.
standard.deep: The applicable version matters when rules change. A record valid under an earlier contract may need migration or a documented compatibility rule before it can be treated as valid under the current one.

star_shaped_domain.label: star-shaped domain
star_shaped_domain.preview: A domain containing every straight segment from one chosen centre to each of its points.
star_shaped_domain.card: A set U is star-shaped about a if \((1-t)a+tx\) belongs to U for every x in U and \(0\le t\le 1\). A convex set is star-shaped about each of its points, but a star-shaped set can have indentations and need not be convex.
star_shaped_domain.rule: The centre matters: being star-shaped about one point does not establish the property about another. A nonempty star-shaped domain is contractible by straight-line contraction and hence simply connected.
star_shaped_domain.deep: The square-root coordinate in #1041 has a star-shaped target, enabling a global inverse after the covering argument. The paper separately warns that a full polynomial lemniscate need not be star-shaped; one useful coordinate domain does not establish that property for every original component.

statement_node.label: statement node
statement_node.preview: A statement node is one identified mathematical statement in a graph of results and their relationships.
statement_node.card: The graph can connect it to formal declarations, evidence, implications, and open obligations. Several declarations may support the same mathematical statement when they express equivalent versions or serve different implementation roles.
statement_node.rule: Grouping statements requires a justified correspondence, not just similar wording.
statement_node.deep: Plectis uses this distinction to make a large proof corpus easier to interpret. The number of declaration names need not equal the number of distinct claims or research ideas represented in the graph.

static_site.label: static site
static_site.preview: A static site serves prebuilt files rather than generating each page in response to a reader’s request.
static_site.card: A builder can create HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and media files ahead of publication. A web server then returns those files, although JavaScript may still add interaction in the browser.
static_site.rule: Static describes how pages are produced and served; it does not mean the content never changes or that the site contains no scripts.
static_site.deep: Static generation makes published output inspectable as files and can reduce runtime infrastructure. Changes usually require rebuilding and publishing new files. Plectis uses a static public site whose builders derive many pages from source registries while preserving stable routes. Some interactive features run in the browser, but no server-side page generation is needed for each visit.

stationary_bootstrap.label: stationary bootstrap
stationary_bootstrap.preview: The stationary bootstrap resamples a time series in blocks of randomly chosen lengths to retain some of its temporal dependence.
stationary_bootstrap.card: In the standard construction, block lengths have a geometric distribution and starting points are sampled from the observed series, with circular continuation at its end. Joining such blocks creates a resampled series.
stationary_bootstrap.rule: Block length choices and assumptions about dependence affect the method's validity.
stationary_bootstrap.deep: It preserves local stretches of observations rather than exactly preserving every dependence in the original data. Statistical conclusions still require the sampling assumptions appropriate to the analysis.

stochastic.label: stochastic
stochastic.preview: Stochastic describes a process or model whose outcomes involve probability or randomness.
stochastic.card: A stochastic procedure can follow precise rules while producing different outcomes across runs because it samples random choices. Analysis describes distributions, expectations, variability, or event probabilities rather than one guaranteed path. Pseudorandom software also depends on a generator and seed.
stochastic.rule: Separate randomness in the model from uncertainty about the model, and record seeds when exact computational repetition matters.
stochastic.deep: A stochastic process, model, or algorithm includes outcomes governed by probability. Its rules may be exact even though individual runs differ, so analysis concerns distributions, expected values, variability, dependence, or event probabilities rather than one fixed path. Computational randomness is normally pseudorandom and becomes repeatable when the generator, seed, implementation, and relevant ordering are fixed. Stochastic variation differs from ignorance about model choice or data quality. A reported sample illustrates possible behavior; it does not alone characterize the underlying probability law or justify a causal conclusion.

stub.label: stub
stub.preview: A stub is a placeholder representing an item or interface whose full contents or behaviour are not yet supplied.
stub.card: It may allow navigation, compilation, or planning to proceed while showing where further work belongs. In testing, a stub can provide a simplified replacement for a dependency.
stub.rule: The placeholder's limitations should be explicit wherever its output is used.
stub.deep: A stub appearing in a catalog does not establish that the intended mechanism exists. Replacing it with an implementation requires the same source, interface, and validation checks as other substantive work.

subcover.label: subcover
subcover.preview: A subcover is a selection from a collection of covering sets that still covers the same target set.
subcover.card: If three open intervals cover \([0,1]\) and two of those intervals already cover every point of \([0,1]\), those two form a subcover. A finite subcover uses finitely many members of the original collection; it need not be the smallest possible choice.
subcover.rule: The selected sets must come from the given cover; replacing them with a newly invented covering set does not produce a subcover.
subcover.deep: Compactness requires a finite subcover for every open cover. The condition is stronger than the existence of one finite open cover: any subset of the real line is covered by the whole real line, but many subsets are not compact. The empty collection covers the empty set, so it is a finite subcover when the target is empty. These distinctions keep the quantifiers in compactness arguments precise.

subexponential_growth.label: subexponential growth
subexponential_growth.preview: Growth slower than every fixed exponential \(c^n\) with \(c>1\).
subexponential_growth.card: Polynomial growth \(n^{10}\) is subexponential because \(n^{10}/c^{n}\to 0\) for every fixed \(c>1\). The faster function \(\exp (\sqrt n)\) is also subexponential, showing that subexponential does not mean polynomial or practically small.
subexponential_growth.rule: For positive sequences \(a_{n}\ge 1\), a standard equivalent condition is \(\log (a_{n})/n\to 0\). The comparison must hold against every fixed exponential base greater than one, rather than against just one especially large base.
subexponential_growth.deep: In the reciprocal-tail analysis, normalized vanishing can constrain denominator states to subexponential growth. That scale restriction then limits how frequently strict divisibility changes can occur, but it does not make the states bounded or convergent.

subharmonic_function.label: subharmonic function
subharmonic_function.preview: A subharmonic function never exceeds its average on a small surrounding circle and satisfies an upper-semicontinuity condition that rules out downward jumps at a point.
subharmonic_function.card: For example, \(|z|^{2}\) is subharmonic: its average around a circle centred at z is larger than its value at z. A harmonic function has equality. Subharmonic functions may take the value \(-\infty\), as \(\log |f|\) does at a zero of a holomorphic function f.
subharmonic_function.rule: For twice differentiable real functions on a planar domain, subharmonicity is equivalent to a nonnegative Laplacian. The average condition is the more general definition and requires upper semicontinuity; it is not ordinary convexity along every line.
subharmonic_function.deep: On a plane domain, the standard definition requires upper semicontinuity, local integrability, and the sub-mean inequality on discs contained in the domain; one usually excludes the function identically \(-\infty\). Upper semicontinuity means nearby limiting values cannot exceed the value at the point. The papers apply subharmonicity to squared moduli of analytic quantities, bounding an interior value by an average that can be evaluated using coefficients.

sublevel_set.label: sublevel set
sublevel_set.preview: The region where a real-valued function is at most a chosen level; the strict version uses less than.
sublevel_set.card: For g and a threshold c, the sublevel set is \(\{x : g(x)\le c\}\); its strict version is \(\{x : g(x)<c\}\). If g is continuous, the first is closed and the second is open. Neither need be connected.
sublevel_set.rule: State whether equality is allowed. A path permitted to touch the boundary of a closed sublevel set can fail to lie in the corresponding strict sublevel set.
sublevel_set.deep: Erdős #1041 asks for a connection inside \(|p(z)|<1\). The paper also constructs paths in smaller closed regions \(|p(z)|\le a\) with \(a<1\); these do lie in the required open region. A construction only in \(|p(z)|\le 1\) needs a separate argument to remove boundary contact.

subsequence.label: subsequence
subsequence.preview: A sequence formed by retaining terms at increasing indices.
subsequence.card: From 1,2,3,4,…, selecting indices 2,4,6,… produces the subsequence 2,4,6,…. Selecting square indices produces 1,4,9,16,…. Terms retain their original order although the gaps between chosen indices may grow.
subsequence.rule: A subsequence has form \(a_{n_{1}}\), \(a_{n_{2}}\), … with \(n_{1} < n_{2} < \ldots\). It need not be consecutive, but it preserves order. Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit.
subsequence.deep: Sparse exceptional behavior may survive along a subsequence even when its proportion among all indices tends to zero. Consequently, typical or density-one estimates may be insufficient when a proof must exclude infinitely recurring exceptional denominator states.

subseries.label: subseries
subseries.preview: A subseries is formed by selecting terms from a series and keeping them in their original order.
subseries.card: For example, retaining only the even-indexed terms of \(\sum a_{n}\) gives \(a_{2} + a_{4} + a_{6} + \cdots\) . Its value, when defined, is a subsum of the original series.
subseries.rule: Selection differs from rearrangement: a rearrangement keeps all terms but changes their order.
subseries.deep: The Erdős #257 work asks about sums selected by infinite sets of exponents. The arithmetic pattern of the selected indices matters even when every such subseries converges.

subset.label: subset
subset.preview: A set A is a subset of B if every element of A also belongs to B.
subset.card: The notation \(A\subseteq B\) permits equality. For example, \(\{2,4\}\) is a subset of the even integers, and every set is a subset of itself. A proper subset excludes equality and therefore leaves at least one member of the larger set outside it.
subset.rule: The empty set is a subset of every set because it has no element that could violate the condition.
subset.deep: The papers use subsets to specify allowed indices, regions, and candidate families. Inclusion alone does not say that the subset is large, connected, dense, or representative of the larger set.

subsum.label: subsum
subsum.preview: A subsum is the value obtained by selecting some terms of a series and adding them.
subsum.card: For a selected index set A, the expression is \(\sum_{n\in A}a_n\), when that sum is defined. The selected series is a subseries; its value is one subsum.
subsum.rule: Convergence of a conditionally convergent series does not guarantee convergence of every subseries. Absolute convergence does, and nonnegative convergent series have all subsums between zero and their full sum.
subsum.deep: The achievement set collects all possible subsum values. In #257, it includes the empty and finite selections as well as infinite selections. The universal irrationality question concerns the infinite selections, so rational values from finite selections are not counterexamples.

sum.label: sum
sum.preview: A sum is the result of adding quantities together.
sum.card: A finite sum adds a specified number of terms. An infinite series uses the limit of finite partial sums when that limit exists. The symbol \(\sum\) abbreviates a sum with its index and range stated alongside it.
sum.rule: The range and order of summation can be part of the mathematical claim.
sum.deep: The papers distinguish exact finite arithmetic from conclusions about infinite sums. Passing from one to the other requires convergence and, when terms are rearranged, the appropriate justification for that rearrangement.

summability.label: summability
summability.preview: Summability means that a family of terms has a sum under a specified definition of infinite summation.
summability.card: For a nonnegative sequence, it means the partial sums are bounded and hence converge to a finite total. For real or complex families indexed without an order, the usual unconditional notion corresponds to absolute summability.
summability.rule: The terms, weighting, and summation convention are part of the claim.
summability.deep: In Lean, `Summable` has a formal meaning that should be checked for the relevant index and space. A convergent ordered series need not be summable in every stronger, order-independent sense.

divisor_cover.label: summable divisor cover
divisor_cover.preview: In the #257 paper, a summable divisor cover groups exponents into finite sets with nonnegative divisor bounds whose full costs have finite sum.
divisor_cover.card: For a finite exponent set F, let \(f_F(n)\) count members of F dividing n. The criterion bounds \(f_F(n)^\alpha\) by \(\sum_{d\mid n}c_d\), with \(c_d\ge 0\) and \(0<\alpha \le 1\). Its cost depends on \(C=\sum_d c_d/d\).
divisor_cover.rule: A separate finite cover exists for every finite F. The theorem requires summability across the entire sequence of finite sets, including the scale and fractional-power factors.
divisor_cover.deep: Precisely, for finite \(F_{j}\) and coefficients \(c_{j,d}\) as above, the paper requires \(\sum_j C_j2^{j\alpha_j}/(2^{\alpha_j}-1)<\infty\). It then proves irrationality of \(\sum_{a\in A}1/(b^{a}-1)\) for every infinite \(A\subseteq \bigcup _{j}F_{j}\) and integer \(b\ge 2\). This is a specific criterion, distinct from a topological open cover or a claim that all infinite supports qualify.

summation_by_parts.label: summation by parts
summation_by_parts.preview: Summation by parts is a finite-sum identity that transfers differences from one factor to partial sums of the other.
summation_by_parts.card: If \(A_{k}=\sum _{j=1}^{k}a_{j}\), then \(\sum _{k=1}^N a_{k}b_{k}=A_N b_N+\sum _{k=1}^{N-1}A_{k}(b_{k}-b_{k+1})\), with the endpoint retained.
summation_by_parts.rule: Passing to infinite sums requires convergence and control of that endpoint. Dropping it without proving its limit can change the identity.
summation_by_parts.deep: The #251 paper transforms the weighted prime series into a weighted prime-gap series by this identity. Its Lean-bound finite formula keeps the last prime term. Polynomial growth then makes the dyadic endpoint tend to zero, producing the infinite affine relation and equivalent irrationality statements.

superior_predictive_ability.label: superior predictive ability
superior_predictive_ability.preview: Hansen's superior predictive ability test assesses whether any candidate forecasting method has lower expected loss than a benchmark.
superior_predictive_ability.card: It compares a collection of methods jointly rather than treating the best observed performer as if it had been selected in advance. The procedure accounts for sampling variation and the comparison across candidates under its assumptions.
superior_predictive_ability.rule: The loss function, candidate set, dependence model, and resampling choices affect the inference.
superior_predictive_ability.deep: A rejection provides evidence against the benchmark's equal-or-better expected performance in the tested setting. It does not prove a particular method will outperform forever or explain why a difference occurs.

support.label: support
support.preview: For a sequence, support is the set of indices with nonzero terms; in evidential prose it means what backs a claim.
support.card: In #257, the support A selects which exponents appear in \(\sum_{a\in A}1/(b^{a}-1)\). Writing the series with zero-or-one coefficients makes A exactly their nonzero index set.
support.rule: For a series support, membership selects a term; it does not assert that the terms form a finite set or satisfy the paper’s weighted hypothesis.
support.deep: For a function on a topological space, support commonly means the closure of the nonzero set. On discrete positive-integer indices this gives the same set. In prose about evidence, “support” instead means reasons or records backing a claim; its evidential strength must be judged separately.

supremum.label: supremum
supremum.preview: The smallest number greater than or equal to every member of a set.
supremum.card: The open interval (0,1) has supremum 1 even though it has no largest member. Every element is at most 1, and any smaller proposed upper bound is exceeded by points sufficiently close to 1.
supremum.rule: A maximum must be attained; a supremum need not be. Unbounded-above sets may have supremum \(+\infty\) in the extended reals, and conventions for the empty set must be stated.
supremum.deep: The irrationality exponent is a supremum over approximation exponents achieved infinitely often. Calling it a supremum allows a sharp boundary value even when no single family of rational approximations attains that boundary exponent.

surjective_map.label: surjective map
surjective_map.preview: A function that attains every element of its stated codomain.
surjective_map.card: The map \(f(n)=n+1\) from integers to integers is surjective because each target m has preimage m-1. The same formula from nonnegative integers to nonnegative integers is not surjective, since zero is never reached.
surjective_map.rule: Surjectivity depends on the stated codomain: every allowed target must have at least one input mapping to it. It says nothing about uniqueness of that input; uniqueness belongs to injectivity.
surjective_map.deep: The Lambert analysis proves certain coefficient maps are onto the integers, so every desired integer correction can be represented. Changing the domain, codomain, coefficient range, or degree bound can destroy that conclusion and must be tracked explicitly.

sylvester_sequence.label: Sylvester's sequence
sylvester_sequence.preview: Sylvester's sequence starts with 2, and each later term is one plus the product of all preceding terms.
sylvester_sequence.card: It begins 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807. With \(a_{0} = 2\), the same rule can be written \(a_{n+1} = a_{n}(a_{n} - 1) + 1\), so each next term can be calculated directly from the previous one.
sylvester_sequence.rule: The starting value and indexing convention should be checked when comparing formulas.
sylvester_sequence.deep: Its terms are pairwise coprime and grow rapidly. Reciprocal identities associated with the sequence make it useful in questions about unit fractions and the values of structured infinite sums.

synth_seed.label: synth seed
synth_seed.preview: A synth seed is a concise, replaceable brief for the current phase of work.
synth_seed.card: It gathers the goal, reasons for the work, success conditions, relevant sources, and next planned activity. Plectis derives it from durable intent and current state so an agent can start without rereading all earlier material.
synth_seed.rule: It describes the current phase rather than preserving the operator's original words.
synth_seed.deep: As the work changes, the brief can be replaced while the underlying source and historical records remain. Its usefulness depends on staying aligned with the live objective and evidence.

synthetic.label: synthetic
synthetic.preview: Synthetic data is deliberately generated rather than directly observed from the real situation being studied.
synthetic.card: It may model typical inputs, isolate an edge case, or contain a known fault. Plectis uses synthetic fixtures to make particular checks repeatable and their expected outcomes explicit.
synthetic.rule: Generated data is useful when its relationship to the intended behaviour is clear.
synthetic.deep: A successful synthetic test establishes what happened under the constructed conditions. Extending that result to real use requires evidence that the relevant conditions and failure mechanisms have been represented adequately.

tactic.label: tactic
tactic.preview: A proof tactic is an instruction that transforms proof goals or constructs part of a formal proof.
tactic.card: A tactic may introduce a hypothesis, rewrite an expression, apply a theorem, or solve a goal through a decision procedure. A tactic script organizes these steps; its visible commands are not the final core proof object.
tactic.rule: Success must culminate in an accepted proof of the stated goal. The tactic's name alone does not identify its assumptions or scope.
tactic.deep: The local Lean sources use commands such as simp and rw, while verification receipts record which tactics discharged propositions. Automation can shorten proof construction without changing the need to inspect the resulting statement and dependencies.

taylor_series.label: Taylor series
taylor_series.preview: A Taylor series is the power series whose coefficients are determined by a function’s derivatives at a chosen point.
taylor_series.card: For one variable, the coefficient of \((x-c)^{n}\) is \(f^{(n)}(c)/n!\). The exponential has Taylor series \(1+x+x^{2}/2!+\ldots\) at zero. Its partial sums give polynomial approximations, with error controlled by a separate remainder estimate.
taylor_series.rule: Having derivatives of all orders does not ensure that the Taylor series converges or equals the function. Analyticity supplies local equality.
taylor_series.deep: For example, \(\exp (-1/x^{2})\), extended by zero at \(x = 0\), is smooth and has every derivative zero there, yet it is positive elsewhere. Its Taylor series at zero therefore misses those values. Finite Taylor approximations and infinite series equality make different claims.

telemetry.label: telemetry
telemetry.preview: Telemetry is automatically collected operational data sent or stored for observing a system away from the point where events occur.
telemetry.card: Request counts, error rates, timings, resource use, and selected event traces can be telemetry. It describes instrumented observations, not a complete or neutral record of everything the system did.
telemetry.rule: Telemetry is defined by its events, sampling, fields, aggregation, retention, transmission, access controls, and relationship to the system state being inferred.
telemetry.deep: Telemetry can reveal failures, performance changes, and usage patterns across many machines, but instrumentation choices determine what remains invisible. Sampling can miss rare events; aggregation can hide individual cases; clock skew and dropped messages can distort sequences. Collection may also carry privacy, security, and cost constraints. A dashboard is a presentation of telemetry rather than the raw evidence itself. Interpreting a change requires checking definitions and collection changes before concluding that the underlying system or user behavior changed.

telescoping_identity.label: telescoping identity
telescoping_identity.preview: A telescoping sum is one in which cancellations reduce a long sum to a few endpoint terms.
telescoping_identity.card: For example, \((b_1-b_2)+(b_2-b_3)+\cdots+(b_N-b_{N+1})\) equals \(b_1-b_{N+1}\). The intermediate terms cancel in this finite identity.
telescoping_identity.rule: For an infinite series, the remaining endpoint term must have the appropriate limit.
telescoping_identity.deep: This method turns certain factorial fractions or recurrence differences into exact formulas. Writing down the finite cancellation first prevents an infinite argument from assuming, without proof, that its final boundary term disappears.

terminal.label: terminal
terminal.preview: A terminal provides a text interface for interacting with programs, commonly through a command-line shell.
terminal.card: A terminal displays text and passes keyboard input to the program using it. That program may be a shell with a command prompt, a text editor, or another interactive application. A terminal emulator supplies this interface in a desktop window.
terminal.rule: The terminal is the interface; the shell interprets the command and starts the requested process.
terminal.deep: The site's runnable instructions use this route so readers can repeat named operations. A command's exit status and saved outputs help establish what happened beyond the text displayed while it ran.

test.label: test
test.preview: A test examines whether something behaves as expected under specified conditions.
test.card: Software tests supply inputs or setup, execute code, and compare the result with an assertion or other expectation. Plectis publishes tests alongside components to make the advertised behaviour inspectable.
test.rule: A passing test covers its particular conditions and assertions.
test.deep: Formal proof checking is a different form of verification and can establish a quantified statement under explicit assumptions. Both are valuable, but their guarantees should be described according to what the underlying method actually checks.

theorem.label: theorem
theorem.preview: A theorem is a mathematical statement established by proof within stated assumptions and definitions.
theorem.card: Its conclusion applies to every case covered by those assumptions. The word describes a proved result; importance, difficulty, and originality are separate questions.
theorem.rule: Read the theorem together with its hypotheses and the evidence for its proof.
theorem.deep: In Lean, a declaration labelled `theorem` can still depend on admissions or added axioms unless these are audited. The keyword alone is therefore insufficient evidence that the intended result has been fully proved on the permitted foundations.

threshold.label: threshold
threshold.preview: A threshold is a boundary value at which a classification, condition, or behavior changes.
threshold.card: A temperature may cross a physical threshold, a theorem may apply when x exceeds 10, or a score may trigger an alert above 0.8. The boundary can arise from nature, mathematics, convention, or policy.
threshold.rule: A threshold includes a measured quantity, comparison direction, boundary value, and consequence; equality at the boundary must be specified when it matters.
threshold.deep: Some thresholds are discovered properties, such as the value where a mathematical regime changes. Others are chosen decision rules that trade missed cases against false alarms, cost, delay, or risk. A threshold need not be selected by policy, and a policy threshold need not reveal a natural discontinuity in the underlying phenomenon. Units, calibration, population, and uncertainty affect interpretation. Crossing a noisy threshold once may not indicate a stable change, while hysteresis or repeated evidence can prevent rapid switching near the boundary.

throughput.label: throughput
throughput.preview: Throughput is the amount of work a system completes per unit of time.
throughput.card: Throughput may count requests, records, tasks, tokens, or other units. It differs from latency, which measures how long one operation takes, and the two can change independently.
throughput.rule: State the work unit, time window, load, and success criteria when reporting throughput.
throughput.deep: A system can increase throughput by parallelising work, batching operations, or reducing cost per item. Higher throughput may increase queueing, resource use, or error rates, so the measure needs conditions and quality bounds. Plectis research prose discusses agent throughput as completed work over time while warning that review and maintenance capacity must grow with it.

timeout.label: timeout
timeout.preview: A timeout ends or changes waiting behavior when a defined time limit expires before the awaited event is observed.
timeout.card: A client may stop waiting after 30 seconds so one slow call cannot block forever. The server or background job may nevertheless continue and later produce a result.
timeout.rule: Timeout semantics specify which clock starts, the duration, the event being awaited, whether underlying work is cancelled, and how late completion or repeated attempts are handled.
timeout.deep: Connection, read, idle, operation, and overall timeouts measure different intervals. Expiry means the waiting side did not observe completion in time; it does not prove that remote work failed, stopped, or had no side effects. Retrying after a timeout can therefore duplicate effects. Short limits improve responsiveness but may reject legitimate slow work, while long limits consume resources and delay recovery. Cancellation support, idempotency, status lookup, and late-result reconciliation determine whether timeout handling remains correct under uncertainty.

tls.label: TLS
tls.preview: Transport Layer Security, or TLS, is a protocol that encrypts and authenticates a network connection.
tls.card: HTTPS uses TLS to protect HTTP traffic while it travels between client and server. Certificates help the client verify the server identity associated with a hostname.
tls.rule: TLS protects transport between endpoints; it does not make endpoint software, stored data, or response content trustworthy.
tls.deep: During a TLS handshake, peers agree on cryptographic parameters, establish session keys, and usually authenticate the server with a certificate chain. The resulting channel protects confidentiality and integrity against ordinary network interception. Certificate checks, supported protocol versions, and key management affect the guarantee. Plectis HTTPS links depend on this transport layer, while content evidence and publication authority remain separate questions.

tonelli_theorem.label: Tonelli theorem
tonelli_theorem.preview: Tonelli’s theorem allows the order of integration of a nonnegative measurable function to be exchanged, even when the value is infinite.
tonelli_theorem.card: On a product of \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces, the product integral and both iterated integrals agree for nonnegative measurable functions. Counting measure gives the familiar equality of the two orders of a nonnegative double sum.
tonelli_theorem.rule: Nonnegativity is essential to this version. For signed or complex terms, exchanging summations usually requires an absolute-convergence or integrability argument instead.
tonelli_theorem.deep: The #257 divisor-incidence identity expands \(1/(b^{a}-1)=\sum_{j\ge1}b^{-aj}\) and exchanges the nonnegative sums. Regrouping terms by \(n=aj\) then gives \(X_A(b)=\sum_{n\ge1}c_A(n)b^{-n}\). The positivity makes the exchange legitimate before any separate estimate of the final sum’s size.

toolchain.label: toolchain
toolchain.preview: A toolchain is the collection of tools used to turn source material into a built, runnable, or checked result.
toolchain.card: It may include a compiler, interpreter, package manager, document builder, and verifier. Their versions and configuration determine how the process behaves.
toolchain.rule: Reproducing a result often requires the same supported toolchain or a demonstrably compatible one.
toolchain.deep: The formal repositories identify Lean and dependency versions so proofs can be checked in the intended environment. A toolchain update can require source changes or a fresh validation even when the mathematical statement is unchanged.

torus_character.label: torus character
torus_character.preview: A continuous homomorphism from a torus to the complex unit circle.
torus_character.card: On \(\mathbb{R}^{d}/\mathbb{Z}^{d}\), every character has the form \(\chi _k(x)=\exp (2\pi i k\cdot x)\) for an integer vector k. Integer coordinates ensure that adding a lattice vector does not change the value. The zero vector gives the constant character one.
torus_character.rule: A character is a function on the torus, not a coordinate value or an orbit. Noninteger k generally fails to descend from Euclidean space to the quotient. The integer vector indexing convention depends on the torus coordinate periods.
torus_character.deep: In #269, averaging every nonconstant character along the sampled crossing phases gives a geometric sum whose average tends to zero. Approximation by these Fourier functions then proves visits to every open phase region, providing late crossing interchanges.

total_variation_distance.label: total variation distance
total_variation_distance.preview: Total variation distance is the supremum of the absolute difference between the probabilities two distributions assign to the same event.
total_variation_distance.card: For finite outcomes, total variation distance is half the sum of the absolute differences between two probability tables. It ranges from 0 for identical distributions to 1 when the distributions concentrate on disjoint events.
total_variation_distance.rule: Equivalently, take the largest difference in probability assigned to the same measurable event. Any test valued between 0 and 1 changes in expectation by at most this distance, but arithmetic properties of particular outcomes need not be preserved.
total_variation_distance.deep: The prime-gap countermodel keeps short-block empirical laws close in total variation while altering the target denominator behavior. This demonstrates that strong statistical resemblance can coexist with decisive arithmetic difference. Total variation here compares probability measures, not the variation of a curve or function.

curve_total_variation.label: total variation of a curve
curve_total_variation.preview: The supremum of sums of successive distances along ordered samples of a parametrized curve.
curve_total_variation.card: For \(\gamma :[a,b]\to X\) in a metric space, take the supremum of \(\sum d(\gamma(t_i),\gamma(t_{i-1}))\) over all partitions \(a=t_0<\cdots<t_n=b\). For a continuous curve this is its metric length and counts every traversal, including retraced pieces.
curve_total_variation.rule: A curve that goes along a segment and then returns has twice the segment length, while its image is only one segment. This quantity differs from Hausdorff measure of the image and from total variation distance between probability distributions.
curve_total_variation.deep: The #1041 records distinguish a short parametrized path from a small one-dimensional set containing roots. Image-length lower bounds can exclude paths of small total variation, but identifying the two quantities requires controlling repeated traversal and the geometric setting.

totient.label: totient
totient.preview: Euler's totient \(\varphi (n)\) counts the integers from 1 through n that are coprime to the positive integer n.
totient.card: For example, \(\varphi (6) = 2\) because only 1 and 5 are coprime to 6 in that range. The definition gives \(\varphi (1) = 1\); for n greater than 1, the qualifying integers are all strictly smaller than n.
totient.rule: The input must be a positive integer in this definition.
totient.deep: The papers use the totient in arithmetic series. Its values encode how prime factors restrict coprimality, linking multiplicative structure with questions about sums and digit expansions.

transaction.label: transaction
transaction.preview: A transaction groups related operations behind a stated validation and commitment boundary, with guarantees that depend on the system.
transaction.card: A database transaction may promise ACID properties at a documented isolation level. A user or workflow transaction may instead stage actions, validate them, obtain authorization, and commit or abandon selected changes. Those looser uses must not silently inherit strict database guarantees.
transaction.rule: Readers should ask which actions participate, when commitment occurs, what concurrent observers can see, and which effects rollback can actually reverse.
transaction.deep: Transaction is a family of consistency patterns rather than a universal promise of database ACID behavior. A database transaction may provide atomicity, consistency constraints, isolation, and durability at a stated level. A user or workflow transaction may instead stage changes, validate them, request authorization, then commit or abandon the operation, with weaker recovery guarantees. External messages, network calls, files, and irreversible effects may sit outside the boundary. Readers should ask which actions participate, what validation precedes commitment, how concurrent activity is handled, and what rollback can truly restore.

transcendental.label: transcendental
transcendental.preview: A number is transcendental if it is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.
transcendental.card: Equivalently, it is not algebraic over the rational numbers. Familiar examples include \(\pi\) and e. Every real transcendental number is irrational, but some irrational numbers, such as \(\sqrt 2\), are algebraic.
transcendental.rule: The polynomial must be nonzero: the zero polynomial vanishes at every number.
transcendental.deep: Proving irrationality alone therefore does not establish transcendence. A transcendence argument must rule out every nonzero integer-coefficient polynomial relation, which is a stronger requirement than ruling out fractions.

transcript.label: transcript
transcript.preview: A transcript is a textual record of speech or an interaction.
transcript.card: It can preserve what was said, typed, or reported during a session, sometimes with timings and speaker labels. Plectis uses transcripts as inspectable records and source material for later explanation.
transcript.rule: The recording method determines what the transcript captures and where errors may occur.
transcript.deep: Speech recognition can mishear words, and an interaction transcript may omit events outside the captured channel. Important quotations or claims should therefore be checked against the appropriate original recording or execution evidence.

triangle_inequality.label: triangle inequality
triangle_inequality.preview: The distance directly between two points is at most the length of any route through a third.
triangle_inequality.card: For numbers, \(|x+y|\le |x|+|y|\). Geometrically, traveling from A to C through B cannot be shorter than the direct distance from A to C. Equality needs the two steps to align without backtracking.
triangle_inequality.rule: The triangle inequality combines upper bounds after decomposing a quantity. Its reverse form, \(||x|-|y||\le |x-y|\), gives a lower bound on separation from differing sizes. Both depend on the relevant absolute value, norm, or metric.
triangle_inequality.deep: Path and polynomial estimates assemble local pieces using triangle inequalities. The step can lose crucial cancellation, so a proof needing a sharp constant may require additional angle, sign, orthogonality, or convexity information rather than repeated triangle bounds.

trinomial.label: trinomial
trinomial.preview: A trinomial is a polynomial written as the sum of three nonzero terms.
trinomial.card: For example, \(z^{5}+2z^{2}-7\) is a trinomial. The exponents need not be consecutive, and a missing power simply has coefficient zero. The paper studies the form \(z^{n}+az^{m}+b\).
trinomial.rule: Count nonzero terms after combining like powers. A nominal three-term expression can simplify to a binomial if coefficients cancel. “Monic trinomial” additionally says the coefficient of the highest-degree term is one.
trinomial.deep: Trinomial describes presentation by three terms, not irreducibility, degree three, or possession of three roots. A cubic is classified by degree; a trinomial is classified by how many nonzero monomials appear.

truth_maintenance.label: truth maintenance
truth_maintenance.preview: Truth maintenance tracks claims together with their reasons and dependencies so they can be reconsidered when evidence changes.
truth_maintenance.card: In AI and knowledge systems, this concerns managing beliefs and justifications. Plectis applies the idea to source records, checks, uncertainty, and decisions that depend on particular claims.
truth_maintenance.rule: Tracking a belief is not a guarantee that the belief is true.
truth_maintenance.deep: The useful behaviour is responding to a failed assumption or contradictory observation: identify affected conclusions, change their status, and review actions that relied on them rather than preserving an unsupported conclusion unchanged.

trying.label: trying
trying.preview: Trying means attempting an action whose outcome is not yet established.
trying.card: In research, an attempt can produce a proof, counterexample, useful failure, or no decisive result. Plectis keeps relevant evidence from attempts so later work can assess what was learned.
trying.rule: The account should distinguish effort from the outcome actually obtained.
trying.deep: A failed route is useful when its failure is explained precisely enough to guide another decision. Merely recording that an agent spent time on a task does not establish progress on the mathematical or software question.

type_a.label: Type A
type_a.preview: Type A is the local name for an AI actor with live access and assigned authority over the working system.
type_a.card: A Type A actor can inspect current repository state and perform permitted operations. It may be a controller or delegated agent. Write access, test access, and task ownership depend on the tools and permissions assigned to its session.
type_a.rule: Classify the actor by access and authority for this substrate. Delegation, intelligence level, and seniority are separate axes.
type_a.deep: An actor working from a packet may need Type A to collect evidence or apply a proposal. A delegated agent with live repository tools can already be Type A. A deterministic script is not an AI actor merely because it touches files.

type_a_judgment.label: Type A judgment
type_a_judgment.preview: Type A judgement is the practical reasoning an agent uses when acting on the live system.
type_a_judgment.card: It includes noticing a missing connection, checking current evidence, choosing the appropriate owner, and deciding the smallest useful change within the task. Plectis expects the agent to use context rather than wait for every routine step to be prescribed.
type_a_judgment.rule: That discretion remains bounded by permissions, source authority, and consequences.
type_a_judgment.deep: For example, an agent can repair a directly affected instruction while preserving unrelated edits. A broader rule change needs evidence that the local lesson actually generalises.

type_a_metabolism.label: Type A metabolism
type_a_metabolism.preview: Type A metabolism names the maintenance work that requires judgement about the system's structure or rules.
type_a_metabolism.card: It addresses situations where an established routine is insufficient, such as resolving a contradiction, defining a missing object, or changing how a standard applies. The result should make later work more explicit and repeatable.
type_a_metabolism.rule: This is a workflow category rather than a measure of an actor's intelligence.
type_a_metabolism.deep: Because the work changes guidance that other actions rely on, its evidence, scope, and validation matter. A local ambiguity should lead to the narrowest justified structural refinement.

type_a_operating_register.label: Type A operating register
type_a_operating_register.preview: The Type A operating register describes the conduct expected of an agent working directly on the system.
type_a_operating_register.card: It includes understanding the user's aim, caring for the material touched, checking outcomes, preserving unrelated work, and recording useful lessons where future work will find them.
type_a_operating_register.rule: “Register” here means a style of working, not a database or processor register.
type_a_operating_register.deep: The named traits, such as care and common sense, should produce observable decisions and follow-through. They do not replace explicit instructions, permissions, or evidence that a task has actually been completed.

type_b.label: Type B
type_b.preview: Type B is the local name for an AI actor reasoning without direct authority over the working system.
type_b.card: Type B works from supplied context or externally available evidence. It may research, criticise, or propose a proof or patch using its own tools, but cannot inspect or change private live state it has not been given access to.
type_b.rule: Treat its output as candidate material until an authorised actor checks it against the relevant source and applies any required change.
type_b.deep: The distinction measures neither intelligence nor delegation. Web tools and a separate execution environment can enrich evidence without granting repository authority. If an actor receives live substrate access, classify it by the authority it actually has.

type_b_metabolism.label: Type B metabolism
type_b_metabolism.preview: Type B metabolism names the routine upkeep of structures whose rules, inputs, and expected outputs have already been defined.
type_b_metabolism.card: Examples include refreshing an index, filling a prescribed summary field, or checking that references still resolve. The process follows an established contract and records whether its result satisfies the required checks.
type_b_metabolism.rule: This workflow label should be distinguished from the Type B actor-access label.
type_b_metabolism.deep: Any actual write still requires an actor or tool authorised to make it. Repeated work can be bounded and checkable without every operation being deterministic or safe to repeat under changed inputs.

type_checker.label: type checker
type_checker.preview: A type checker checks whether an expression obeys a formal language's typing rules.
type_checker.card: For a programming language, this can establish that operations receive values of suitable types. In a propositions-as-types proof system, checking a term against a proposition's type also checks the corresponding formal derivation.
type_checker.rule: A type check establishes only the rules of the chosen system. It does not automatically prove a program satisfies its intended specification.
type_checker.deep: The systems paper cites independent checking of Lean declarations. Such checkers can cross-check a core environment without reproducing the tactics that found a proof, while the informal-to-formal correspondence remains a separate mathematical question.

type_class.label: type class
type_class.preview: A type class specifies operations or properties that can be supplied by instances for particular types.
type_class.card: It supports using common notation or generic code with different implementations. A mathematical class can bundle algebraic operations and laws; another can provide finite enumeration or a method for deciding a predicate.
type_class.rule: A class states what must be provided. An instance supplies those data or proofs; declaring a requirement is different from finding a suitable instance.
type_class.deep: Lean's finite-family arguments use Fintype information for bounded index types. Class-based resolution supplies it where required, so the theorem can use generic finite sums without manually passing every supporting implementation.

type_theory.label: type theory
type_theory.preview: Type theory studies formal systems in which expressions have types governing how they can be combined.
type_theory.card: A type distinguishes kinds of object, such as natural numbers or functions. Typing rules specify which expressions are meaningful. Some type theories also represent propositions by types, so constructing an inhabitant corresponds to proving a proposition.
type_theory.rule: The rules and available axioms depend on the particular type theory; sharing the word type does not make different systems interchangeable.
type_theory.deep: Lean's mathematical declarations live in a dependent type theory. This explains why the local methodology checks a proof term against its proposition rather than asking a program to judge the paper's prose.

typed_refusal.label: typed refusal
typed_refusal.preview: A typed refusal is a structured result saying that an operation could not proceed, with a specific reason.
typed_refusal.card: It distinguishes cases such as missing evidence, unsupported input, failed validation, or timeout. Plectis uses these categories so later work can choose a suitable response instead of receiving a plausible-looking invented value.
typed_refusal.rule: The refusal reports the operation's limitation; it need not refute the underlying claim.
typed_refusal.deep: A timeout, for example, means the check did not finish within its budget. It is different from the checker finding a counterexample or completing with a failure verdict.

typed_relation.label: typed relation
typed_relation.preview: A typed relation is a connection that states how two identified items are related.
typed_relation.card: In a mathematical map, the type might be implication, equivalence, finite instance, or obstruction. In system records, it might identify implementation, ownership, or a source relationship.
typed_relation.rule: The relation type and direction are part of the information being recorded.
typed_relation.deep: Two statements merely sharing a topic do not establish an implication between them. Plectis's mathematical edges need supporting evidence so navigation does not silently promote an association into a logical result.

unconditional_result.label: unconditional result
unconditional_result.preview: An unconditional result needs no additional unresolved hypothesis beyond its stated mathematical setting.
unconditional_result.card: It still has definitions, domain restrictions, and logical foundations. The word distinguishes it from a result whose intended application depends on an open conjecture or other unestablished condition.
unconditional_result.rule: Unconditional does not mean assumption-free or that the original research problem is fully solved.
unconditional_result.deep: A proved equivalence or a theorem about a special case can be unconditional while the broader question remains open. The papers should say both what the result establishes and how it relates to the original target.

uniform_convergence.label: uniform convergence
uniform_convergence.preview: Functions converge uniformly when one sufficiently late stage makes the error small simultaneously at every point of the stated domain.
uniform_convergence.card: For every positive tolerance \(\varepsilon\), there must be an N such that \(|f_{n}(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon\) for all \(n \ge N\) and all x in the domain. The same N works for every x.
uniform_convergence.rule: Pointwise convergence instead allows the threshold N to depend on x.
uniform_convergence.deep: Uniform convergence preserves continuity of continuous functions in the usual metric setting. Passing strict inequalities or derivative bounds to a limit needs additional care; uniform convergence alone does not preserve every property.

uninterpretable.label: uninterpretable
uninterpretable.preview: Here, uninterpretable describes work for which readers do not yet have an adequate account of what it says or why it works.
uninterpretable.card: A formal proof can check while its main idea, relationship to prior work, or intended meaning remains poorly explained. The missing task is to make that content understandable at an appropriate level of expertise.
uninterpretable.rule: The term describes a current gap in understanding, not a proof that understanding is impossible.
uninterpretable.deep: Useful exposition states the exact result, exposes the decisive argument, and preserves attribution and limits. Community understanding and use require further engagement beyond a machine's acceptance.

unit_disc.label: unit disc
unit_disc.preview: The open unit disc is the set of complex numbers z with \(|z| < 1\).
unit_disc.card: It consists of points at distance less than one from the origin in the complex plane. The closed unit disc uses \(|z| \le 1\) and includes its boundary, the unit circle \(|z| = 1\).
unit_disc.rule: Open and closed versions differ precisely at that boundary.
unit_disc.deep: The lemniscate papers use conditions such as \(|p(z)| < 1\). That says the polynomial's value lies in the open unit disc; it does not necessarily say the input point z lies there.

univalent_function.label: univalent function
univalent_function.preview: A univalent function is a holomorphic function that is one-to-one on its domain.
univalent_function.card: The function \(z\mapsto z^{2}\) is not univalent on the whole complex plane because z and -z have the same image, but it is univalent on a suitably chosen half-plane. A univalent map has no self-overlap on its stated domain.
univalent_function.rule: Univalence is domain-relative and stronger than having nonzero derivative at one point. A holomorphic function with nonzero derivative is locally one-to-one, yet may still take the same value at distant points.
univalent_function.deep: The paper needs the continued inverse branch to remain injective throughout a disc. That permits distortion and area estimates for its image; a many-to-one analytic map would count overlaps and invalidate that geometric reading.

universal_quantifier.label: universal quantifier
universal_quantifier.preview: A universal quantifier states that a property holds for every element of a specified domain.
universal_quantifier.card: The symbol \(\forall\) means “for every.” For example, \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, n+1 > n\) says that adding one increases every natural number. One counterexample would refute the statement; a finite sample usually cannot prove it.
universal_quantifier.rule: The domain and the order of quantifiers determine the claim, including whether later choices can depend on earlier inputs.
universal_quantifier.deep: “For every n, there exists m greater than n” permits a different m for each n. “There exists m greater than every n” asks for one choice working for all n. These statements have different truth values over the natural numbers.

unramified_prime.label: unramified prime
unramified_prime.preview: A prime is unramified in a number-field extension when its factorization upstairs contains no repeated prime-ideal power, equivalently every ramification index is one.
unramified_prime.card: In \(Q(i)/Q\), odd rational primes are unramified. The prime 2 ramifies because the ideal (2) is the square of the prime ideal generated by \(1+i\). Only finitely many rational primes ramify in a fixed number field.
unramified_prime.rule: For a base prime p, “unramified in L” means that every prime ideal P above p has ramification index \(e(P/p)=1\). This does not mean there is only one P above p. In the number-field setting the residue extensions are finite-field extensions and hence separable.
unramified_prime.deep: In a number-field extension, the ideal generated by p factors as a product \(\prod P_i^{e_i}\). Ramification occurs when some exponent \(e_i\) exceeds one. The cited argument selects rational primes for which every exponent is one before prescribing Frobenius behavior. This provides the controlled residue-field symmetry used later.

up_propagate.label: up-propagate
up_propagate.preview: To up-propagate is to place a reusable lesson in the shared source that should guide future relevant work.
up_propagate.card: Plectis uses the move when a local correction reveals a missing rule, instruction, or relationship. The lesson is expressed with its evidence and limits, then attached to an existing owner such as a skill or standard.
up_propagate.rule: The appropriate destination is the narrowest one that can carry the supported lesson.
up_propagate.deep: This prevents repeated rediscovery without converting every local fix into a system-wide rule. The changed source should be discoverable through the workflow that needs it.

upper_asymptotic_density.label: upper asymptotic density
upper_asymptotic_density.preview: Upper asymptotic density is the limit superior of the fraction of positive integers up to N belonging to a set.
upper_asymptotic_density.card: For \(A\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots \}\), it is \(\limsup_{N\to\infty}|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N\). It exists even when the fractions oscillate and ordinary density does not.
upper_asymptotic_density.rule: Upper density zero forces ordinary density zero. This uses intervals starting at 1; upper Banach density also controls translated intervals and is a stronger sparsity condition.
upper_asymptotic_density.deep: An infinite set can have upper density zero, as the squares do. Density describes frequency, not the size of a weighted series: a density-zero set can still have a divergent reciprocal sum. The #251 paper uses the stronger upper Banach density zero for its correction support.

upper_banach_density.label: upper Banach density
upper_banach_density.preview: Upper Banach density measures the largest asymptotic proportion of a set inside long intervals, wherever those intervals start.
upper_banach_density.card: For \(S\subseteq \mathbb{N}\), it is \(\lim_{H\to\infty}\sup_{u\ge0}|S\cap\{u,\ldots,u+H-1\}|/H\). Density zero means every sufficiently long interval has a small proportion of points in S, uniformly in its starting position.
upper_banach_density.rule: Upper Banach density zero is stronger than upper asymptotic density zero. Widely separated blocks of consecutive integers with unbounded block lengths can have asymptotic density zero but upper Banach density one.
upper_banach_density.deep: The #251 correction theorem puts every correction support inside one set of upper Banach density zero. This uniform sparsity helps control how often a fixed-length block can encounter a changed index, even when the observation window moves.

upstream.label: upstream
upstream.preview: Upstream describes a source or earlier stage whose output, changes, or decisions flow into a specified consumer.
upstream.card: An upstream repository can supply imported code, an upstream service can answer requests, and an upstream pipeline stage can produce input for later stages. The direction is always relative to a named flow.
upstream.rule: An object is upstream only with respect to a particular dependency or data path, and the same object may be downstream in another relationship.
upstream.deep: Upstream names direction in a flow of code, data, work, or authority. A fork receives changes from its upstream repository; a processing stage receives records from an earlier producer; a service may depend on an upstream service for responses. Changes or failures can propagate to downstream consumers even when their local files or configuration remain untouched. The word does not identify ownership or superiority, and it has no absolute direction outside a stated relationship. In physical geography it retains its river meaning, while technical prose usually supplies repository, service, dependency, or pipeline context.

url.label: URL
url.preview: A URL is a structured identifier for a resource, commonly giving a network address and a way to access it.
url.card: A web URL can contain a scheme such as `https`, a host, a path, a query, and a fragment. Not every URL names a remote file: a `data:` URL carries content directly, and a relative URL gets part of its meaning from a base URL.
url.rule: Treat a stable URL as a route to a resource, not proof that its current content is unchanged or trustworthy.
url.deep: An absolute URL includes a scheme; a relative reference is resolved against a base, usually the current page. Queries can select a response, while fragments identify a part or view of the resource and are not included in an HTTP request. Plectis uses stable URLs and fragments so a link can return to the same guide, theorem, or glossary entry after the source files are reorganized.

validation.label: validation
validation.preview: Validation checks fitness for an intended use; data validation also checks records against declared constraints.
validation.card: Systems engineering validation asks whether a result serves its intended purpose under relevant conditions. A JSON validator uses the same word for checking data against a schema. Local tools perform both structural and behavioural checks.
validation.rule: Identify which sense and acceptance criteria a run uses. Schema acceptance does not establish that data are true or a result meets the user's intended need.
validation.deep: A generated glossary can have valid row shapes while explaining a term badly. A source-faithful page can also fail the reader's task. Structural checks, behavioural checks, and intended-use review therefore complement one another rather than contributing interchangeable passes.

validator.label: validator
validator.preview: A validator checks whether supplied material satisfies a declared set of requirements.
validator.card: It can examine a schema, input constraints, relationships, or other properties and report a pass, failure, warning, or inability to complete. Plectis connects these outcomes to the rules being applied.
validator.rule: Validation is only as broad as those rules and the evidence examined.
validator.deep: A file may be structurally valid while containing a false claim, and a blocked validation may simply lack a dependency. Clear result categories help distinguish these situations and identify the next appropriate action.

vandermonde_determinant.label: Vandermonde determinant
vandermonde_determinant.preview: A Vandermonde determinant is formed from successive powers of specified nodes and equals a product of their pairwise differences.
vandermonde_determinant.card: For nodes \(x_{0},\ldots ,x_{n-1}\), the matrix \(V_{ij}=x_{i}^{j}\) has determinant \(\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)\). With two nodes, the rows are \((1,x_{0})\) and \((1,x_{1})\), giving \(x_{1}-x_{0}\).
vandermonde_determinant.rule: Over a field, it is nonzero exactly when the nodes are distinct. Swapping two nodes changes the sign; squaring the determinant removes that sign.
vandermonde_determinant.deep: The #1049 moment expansion contains \(\prod_{i<j}(q^{k_i}-q^{k_j})^2\). This factor excludes repeated nodes and makes each positive-weight contribution nonnegative, while its exact size influences the determinant asymptotic.

variable.label: variable
variable.preview: A variable is a symbol or name whose value is supplied, quantified, or allowed to vary within a stated setting.
variable.card: In mathematics, n may range over natural numbers while x ranges over real numbers. In a program, a variable names a value held or computed during execution.
variable.rule: The name alone does not determine its meaning or permitted values.
variable.deep: This matters when reading formulas across papers: the same letter can denote different objects in different sections. Use the local definition and hypotheses rather than assigning a universal meaning to a familiar symbol.

vector_space.label: vector space
vector_space.preview: A vector space allows vector addition and multiplication by scalars from a field, with operations obeying the linear-algebra axioms.
vector_space.card: A vector space has a zero vector and an additive inverse for every vector.
